paragraphs.text: The water on Earth is always moving. The same water has been used again and again for millions of years. Its journey from the ground to the sky and back again is called the water cycle.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “sequencing a process with headings and a diagram”?

paragraphs.text: Evaporation: When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of the water turns into an invisible gas called water vapor. The vapor rises up into the air.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “sequencing a process with headings and a diagram”?

paragraphs.text: Condensation: High in the sky, the air is cooler. The water vapor cools down and turns back into tiny drops of water. Millions of these drops join together to form clouds.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “sequencing a process with headings and a diagram”?

paragraphs.text: Precipitation: When the drops in a cloud get too big and heavy, they fall to the ground. This is called precipitation. It can be rain, snow, sleet, or hail, depending on how cold the air is.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “sequencing a process with headings and a diagram”?

paragraphs.text: Collection: The water collects in oceans, lakes, and rivers, or it soaks into the ground. Then the sun heats it again, and the cycle starts all over.

paragraphs.text: Caption: The picture shows water rising from a lake, forming a cloud, and falling back down as rain.

paragraphs.text: Last spring, the Garden Club at Riverside Elementary planted milkweed in the school garden. Milkweed is the only plant that monarch caterpillars can eat. Without it, monarch butterflies have no place to lay their eggs.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “making an inference from a text and graph”?

paragraphs.text: Every Friday from June to October, club members counted the monarch butterflies they saw in the garden. They added up their counts for each month and made a bar graph.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “making an inference from a text and graph”?

paragraphs.text: In June, the milkweed plants were still small, and the club saw only a few butterflies. By August, the milkweed was tall and full of pink flowers. Club members even found tiny striped caterpillars munching on the leaves. In September, the days grew shorter and cooler. Monarchs in the eastern United States begin a long trip south to the mountains of Mexico at this time of year, where they spend the winter in warm forests. By late October, the garden was quiet again.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “making an inference from a text and graph”?

paragraphs.text: Fact box — Did you know? A monarch can fly about 50 miles (80 kilometers) in one day!
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “making an inference from a text and graph”?

paragraphs.text: In the early 1800s, Baltimore was a busy port city, but moving goods to the West was slow and hard. Wagons pulled by horses took weeks to cross the mountains. Business leaders worried that other cities, like New York, would get more trade because of a new canal there.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using a timeline table and headings”?

paragraphs.text: A Bold Idea: In 1827, a group of Baltimore leaders started the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, called the B&O. It was one of the first railroads in the United States to carry both people and goods. Workers began building the track in 1828.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using a timeline table and headings”?

paragraphs.text: A Famous Race: In 1830, a small steam engine named Tom Thumb raced a horse pulling a train car. The engine was winning until a belt slipped off, and the horse won the race! Still, people saw that steam engines could be fast and strong.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using a timeline table and headings”?

paragraphs.text: Reaching the River: Building the track over mountains and rivers took many years. Finally, in 1852, the track reached the Ohio River. Today, visitors can see old trains at a railroad museum in Baltimore.

paragraphs.text: Text 1: The Sonoran Desert
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing two texts”?

paragraphs.text: The Sonoran Desert stretches across parts of Arizona, California, and Mexico. It gets very little rain, usually less than 12 inches in a whole year. Days can be hotter than 100 degrees Fahrenheit, but nights can be chilly. Plants like the saguaro cactus store water inside their thick stems. Many animals, such as the kangaroo rat, hide underground during the day and come out at night when it is cooler.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing two texts”?

paragraphs.text: Text 2: The Amazon Rainforest
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing two texts”?

paragraphs.text: The Amazon Rainforest covers much of Brazil and parts of several other countries in South America. It rains there almost every day, often more than 80 inches a year. The air is warm and wet all year long. Tall trees grow so close together that their leaves form a roof called the canopy. Monkeys, parrots, and sloths live high in the trees, where they find fruit and leaves to eat.

paragraphs.text: Every Sunday morning, Valeria helps her grandmother make arepas. Arepas are round, flat corn cakes that are popular in Venezuela and Colombia. Abuela says the secret is to mix the dough with your hands until it feels as soft as clay.

paragraphs.text: Steps: First, pour the warm water into a large bowl and stir in the salt. Next, add the cornmeal a little at a time while you mix with your hands. Let the dough rest for five minutes so it can soak up the water. Then, roll the dough into balls and press each ball into a flat circle about as wide as your palm. After that, an adult cooks the arepas in a hot pan with a little oil for about five minutes on each side, until they are golden brown. Finally, cut them open and fill them with cheese, beans, or avocado.

paragraphs.text: What Is a Volcano? A volcano is an opening in Earth's surface where melted rock, gas, and ash can escape. Deep underground, it is so hot that some rock melts. This melted rock is called magma.

paragraphs.text: How Does a Volcano Erupt? Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. It collects in a space called a magma chamber. When too much pressure builds up, the magma bursts through cracks to the surface. Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Over many eruptions, layers of cooled lava and ash pile up and build a mountain.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “summarizing with headings”?

paragraphs.text: Are Volcanoes Helpful? Volcanoes can be dangerous, but they also help people. Ash from old eruptions breaks down into rich soil that is good for growing crops. In Iceland, people use heat from deep underground near volcanoes to warm their homes and make electricity.

paragraphs.text: On a July afternoon last summer, students in Ms. Achebe's science class carried thermometers to two blocks near our school. paragraphs.text: Our city should plant trees on every residential street that has fewer than five trees per block. The difference our class measured is not unusual. paragraphs.text: Trees offer other benefits as well. Their leaves trap dust and pollution, and their roots soak up rainwater that would otherwise flood storm drains. paragraphs.text: On December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks, a seamstress and an experienced civil rights activist, refused to give up her seat to a white passenger on a city bus in Montgomery, Alabama. Under the city's segregation laws, she was arrested. Her arrest became the spark for one of the most important protests of the civil rights movement.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “selecting all valid inferences from a history text”?

paragraphs.text: Within days, Black leaders in Montgomery organized a boycott: they asked Black residents to stop riding city buses until the rules changed. This was a powerful choice, because Black riders made up about three-quarters of the bus company's passengers. A young minister named Martin Luther King Jr. was chosen to lead the new Montgomery Improvement Association.

paragraphs.text: Tardigrades, sometimes called water bears, are animals smaller than a grain of sand. They have eight stubby legs, each ending in tiny claws, and a round body that makes them look like miniature bears under a microscope. They were first described by a German scientist in 1773, and today scientists know of more than 1,300 species.

paragraphs.text: Tardigrades live almost everywhere on Earth, from the tops of the Himalayas to the bottom of the deep sea, and even in the damp moss growing on a city sidewalk. Most of them eat by piercing plant cells or tiny animals and sucking out the liquid inside. If you collect a clump of moss, soak it in water, and look at a few drops under a microscope, you have a good chance of finding one.

paragraphs.text: In early 2018, the city of Cape Town, South Africa, faced a frightening possibility. After three years of very low rainfall, the reservoirs that supplied the city's four million people had dropped to about one-quarter of their capacity. City officials warned of "Day Zero," the day the taps in homes would be shut off and residents would have to collect a daily ration of water at public collection points.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “determining the meaning of an academic word from context”?

paragraphs.text: Because water had become so scarce, the city limited each resident to 50 liters a day, about the amount used in a five-minute shower plus one toilet flush. Families collected the water from their showers in buckets and reused it to flush toilets. Farmers who relied on the same reservoirs agreed to reduce how much they took, and businesses installed equipment to recycle water.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “determining the meaning of an academic word from context”?

paragraphs.text: The measures worked. By the time rain returned in mid-2018, Cape Town had cut its water use roughly in half, and Day Zero never arrived. Scientists who study water point to Cape Town as a warning and as a model. Climate change is making droughts longer in many regions, and cities that plan ahead, fix leaking pipes, and teach residents to conserve will be better prepared when water runs low.

paragraphs.text: Historians credit Cai Lun, an official in China's Han dynasty, with improving papermaking around the year 105 CE. He mixed tree bark, old rags, and hemp with water, pressed the mixture flat, and dried it into thin sheets. For centuries, China guarded the method closely.

paragraphs.text: The secret did not leave East Asia for more than six hundred years. According to traditional accounts, after the Battle of Talas in 751 CE, Chinese prisoners who knew how to make paper were brought to Samarkand, a trading city on the Silk Road. Soon, Samarkand became famous for its paper.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering historical events from an informational text”?

paragraphs.text: From there, the knowledge moved west with merchants and scholars. By about 800 CE, Baghdad had paper mills, and its scholars used paper to copy books on mathematics, medicine, and astronomy. Papermaking then spread across North Africa and reached Spain, where Europe's first paper mill operated by the 1100s.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering historical events from an informational text”?

paragraphs.text: Several centuries later, in the 1450s, Johannes Gutenberg's printing press in Germany depended on a steady supply of cheap paper. Without the long journey that began in China, the printing revolution might never have happened.

paragraphs.text: Amara Okoye was nine years old the first time she walked the beach near her grandmother's house in Lagos and counted bottle caps instead of seashells. She stopped at two hundred. "I thought the ocean was making them," she remembers. "I didn't understand that they came from us."
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice”?

paragraphs.text: Amara's beach is not unusual. Scientists estimate that about 11 million metric tons of plastic enter the ocean every year, roughly a garbage truck's worth every minute. Unlike paper or food waste, most plastic does not break down. Instead, sunlight and waves crack it into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics, which fish and seabirds mistake for food.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice”?

paragraphs.text: Much of this plastic is used only once. A water bottle may be used for ten minutes, but it can remain in the ocean for hundreds of years. Researchers say the most effective solutions start on land: reducing single-use packaging, improving trash collection in fast-growing cities, and designing products that are easier to recycle.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice”?

paragraphs.text: Today, Amara is fifteen and leads a youth cleanup group that has removed more than two tons of trash from Lagos beaches. But she says cleanups are not enough. "We can pick up plastic every Saturday," she says, "but if we keep making it this fast, the ocean will always win."
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice”?

activities.skill: Analyzing the purpose of an author's structural choice
activities.prompt: Why does the author most likely begin and end the article with Amara's story?

choices.text: To prove that Lagos has the most plastic pollution in the world
To explain how microplastics are formed by sunlight and waves
To argue that beach cleanups are the best solution to ocean plastic, because cleanups remove every single piece of trash from the sand and the sea.
To make a global problem feel personal and to frame the main message in a real person's words

activities.rationale: Exactly. Amara's story makes huge numbers feel human, and her final quote delivers the article's main idea: we must make less plastic, not just pick it up.

paragraphs.text: More than 900 school districts in the United States have switched to a four-day school week, usually by adding about an hour to each school day and closing on Fridays or Mondays. paragraphs.text: Second, longer school days are hard on younger students. By the last hour of a longer day, many students are tired and learn less. paragraphs.text: Some families argue that a day off each week makes it easier to schedule appointments and gives students time to rest. This is a fair point. paragraphs.text: Text 1 — from a teacher's blog: Homework is practice, and practice is how skills become automatic. A musician does not learn a song only during lessons; she plays it at home until her fingers know it. In the same way, twenty minutes of math practice at night helps students remember what they learned in class. Homework also teaches responsibility, because students must manage their time without a teacher watching. When students skip practice, small gaps grow into big ones, and by the next unit they are lost. A short, focused assignment each night keeps those gaps from forming.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing two authors' perspectives on one topic”?

paragraphs.text: Text 2 — from a student newspaper: Homework is supposed to help students learn, but for many of us it mostly measures what is happening at home. Students who have a quiet room, a computer, and a parent who can help finish quickly. Students who care for younger siblings or share one phone for the whole family often cannot. A worksheet that takes one student fifteen minutes can take another student an hour, and the grade does not show the difference. If homework is given, it should be short, and students should be able to finish it during a study period at school, where everyone has the same quiet space, the same tools, and a teacher who can help.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing two authors' perspectives on one topic”?

choices.text: Text 1 sees homework as useful practice that builds responsibility, while Text 2 worries that homework is unfair because home situations differ.

Both authors believe homework should take at least an hour each night, and both agree the teacher should grade every single assignment.
Text 1 focuses on music lessons and practice time, while Text 2 focuses on computers, tablets, and the screen time that students need to limit.

activities.rationale: Right. The teacher compares homework to music practice and says it teaches responsibility; the student argues homework measures home resources, so it should be short or done at school.

paragraphs.text: A wetland is an area of land that is covered with shallow water for much of the year, and marshes, swamps, and bogs are all examples. For a long time, people drained wetlands to build farms and towns because they believed the land was useless, but scientists now know that wetlands do important work by cleaning the water that flows through them.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using cause-and-effect structure and a table to explain a process”?

paragraphs.text: Wetlands clean water in several steps. First, thick grasses and reeds slow the water down, and because it moves slowly, heavy bits of soil called sediment sink to the bottom. Next, the roots of plants absorb nutrients such as nitrogen, which can make algae grow too fast in lakes and rivers. Finally, tiny organisms in the mud break down some harmful chemicals.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using cause-and-effect structure and a table to explain a process”?

paragraphs.text: A seventh-grade class built a model wetland in a plastic tub to test these ideas. They poured muddy water into one end, filled the middle of the tub with reeds, and planted water plants at the far end. Then they measured how cloudy the water was at three places. A higher number means muddier water. Their results are shown in the table.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “using cause-and-effect structure and a table to explain a process”?

table.caption: Cloudiness of the water in the model wetland
rows: Middle of the tub (after the reeds)

choices.text: The water plants removed more cloudiness than the reeds did.
The reeds caused the biggest drop in cloudiness, from 80 to 35 units.

Wetlands matter because they are covered with shallow water.

activities.rationale: Right. The reeds lowered cloudiness by 45 units (80 to 35), more than the plants did (35 to 12). The passage explains why: slow water lets sediment sink.

paragraphs.text: In the 1700s, scurvy killed more sailors than battles did. On long voyages, sailors became weak, their gums bled, and old wounds opened again. Nobody knew the cause, and doctors argued about cures.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering events in a history-of-science text”?

paragraphs.text: In May 1747, a Royal Navy surgeon named James Lind decided to test the cures instead of arguing about them. On the ship HMS Salisbury, he chose twelve sailors who all had scurvy. He put them in six pairs and gave each pair a different treatment: cider, vinegar, seawater, a spice paste, a medicine mixture, or two oranges and a lemon each day. He kept everything else, such as meals and sleeping space, as similar as he could.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering events in a history-of-science text”?

paragraphs.text: After six days, the two sailors who ate the fruit were nearly well. One was ready to return to duty, and the other was strong enough to nurse the rest of the sick. The other pairs were still ill.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering events in a history-of-science text”?

paragraphs.text: Lind published his results in 1753 in a book about scurvy. However, the navy did not order lemon juice for its sailors until 1795, and scientists did not discover that vitamin C was the reason the fruit worked until the twentieth century. Lind's trial still matters today because it was an early example of a fair test: the same conditions for everyone, and one thing changed.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “ordering events in a history-of-science text”?

paragraphs.text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter about a quarter of all ocean species. Reefs also protect coastlines from waves and provide food and jobs for millions of people. But coral reefs are in danger, because warming oceans are causing a harmful change called bleaching.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “identifying the sentence that states the central idea of a science text”?

paragraphs.text: Corals are tiny animals, not plants, and each one has algae living inside its body. The algae make food from sunlight and give the coral its bright color. In return, the coral gives the algae a safe home. This partnership, in which both partners benefit, keeps the reef alive.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “identifying the sentence that states the central idea of a science text”?

paragraphs.text: When the ocean stays too warm for several weeks, the coral becomes stressed and pushes the algae out, and without the algae, the coral turns white. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If the water cools quickly, the algae can return and the coral can recover. If the heat lasts too long, the coral dies.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “identifying the sentence that states the central idea of a science text”?

paragraphs.text: Scientists are working to protect reefs by reducing pollution, limiting fishing near reefs, and searching for heat-resistant corals. Reefs that are healthy before a heat wave are more likely to recover afterward.

paragraphs.text: Text 1 (a letter from a merchant in Buffalo, New York, 1826): "Dear Brother, two years ago I paid nearly a hundred dollars to haul one ton of flour by wagon from Buffalo to New York City. This year I sent the same ton by canal boat for about ten dollars. The boats glide along behind patient mules, day and night, and the cargo arrives without a scratch. Farmers who once could not sell their crops now ship them to the city with ease, and every town on the canal is growing. People laughed at 'Clinton's Ditch,' but nobody is laughing now. It is the greatest work our country has ever built!"
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing how two texts present the same event”?

paragraphs.text: Text 2 (from a modern history book): The Erie Canal opened in 1825 and stretched 363 miles from Albany to Buffalo. It cut the cost of shipping a ton of freight from about $100 to about $10, and it helped New York City become the nation's busiest port. Towns such as Rochester and Syracuse grew quickly along its banks. However, the canal had costs, too. Thousands of workers, many of them immigrants from Ireland, dug much of it by hand in dangerous conditions. The canal's success also encouraged settlers to move west, which put more pressure on Native nations in New York to give up their land.

activities.rationale: Right. The merchant writes only praise, while the historian gives both benefits (cheaper shipping, growing towns) and costs (dangerous work, pressure on Native nations).

paragraphs.text: Mansa Musa became the ruler of the Mali Empire in West Africa around 1312. Mali controlled some of the richest gold mines of its time, and its traders also sold salt, which people needed to preserve food. Under Musa, the empire grew into one of the largest of its time.

paragraphs.text: In 1324, Musa traveled from Mali to Mecca, in present-day Saudi Arabia, as part of the hajj, a religious pilgrimage. He was followed by a very large caravan, and many camels carried gold. When he stopped in Cairo, Egypt, he spent and gave away so much gold that its value dropped in the city for years.

paragraphs.text: No other ruler of his time was as wise or as generous as Mansa Musa. When he returned home, he brought back scholars and architects, and he ordered new mosques to be built in Timbuktu. Timbuktu soon became a famous center of learning, with libraries full of handwritten books.

paragraphs.text: Look at a classroom world map and you may notice something odd: Greenland seems as large as Africa. In reality, Africa is about fourteen times larger. The reason is a mapmaking choice made more than four hundred years ago.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “choosing conclusions that a geography text supports”?

paragraphs.text: In 1569, the Flemish mapmaker Gerardus Mercator created a map for sailors. A globe is round, but a map is flat, so every flat map must stretch some part of Earth. Mercator stretched his map in a special way so that a ship's compass direction would appear as a straight line. A captain could draw a line between two ports, follow one compass heading, and arrive. For navigation, this was a huge advantage.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “choosing conclusions that a geography text supports”?

paragraphs.text: The stretching has a cost. The farther a place is from the equator, the more the Mercator map enlarges it. Greenland, Canada, and Russia look enormous, while places near the equator, such as Africa and South America, look smaller than they really are. Today, many atlases use other kinds of projections that show sizes more accurately, but those maps cannot keep every compass direction straight. Mapmakers explain that no flat map can be perfect; each one is designed for a purpose.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “choosing conclusions that a geography text supports”?

activities.skill: Choosing conclusions that a geography text supports

choices.text: Greenland is really about as large as Africa.

Mercator wanted to make Africa look small on purpose.
Places near the equator look smaller than they really are on his map.
A map that shows sizes accurately is the best choice for sailors.

activities.rationale: Strong reading. The passage says Mercator made a map "for sailors" and that places near the equator look smaller. It never says he wanted Africa to look small, and accurate-size maps cannot keep compass lines straight.

paragraphs.text: Grocery stores often sell the same product in more than one size, and a larger package usually costs more money. However, the total price does not tell you whether a package is a better deal. To compare fairly, shoppers use the unit price, which is the price for one unit of measure, such as one ounce. To find it, divide the price by the number of units.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing unit rates from a text and a table”?

paragraphs.text: Marisol is shopping for apple juice for her family's lunches. The store sells three bottle sizes, shown in the table. The 12-ounce bottle is the easiest to carry, but a small size often has a higher unit price than a large one. Marisol also knows that her family drinks about 64 ounces of juice each week, so a large bottle will not spoil before they finish it.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing unit rates from a text and a table”?

paragraphs.text: Unit price is only one part of a smart decision, because a lower unit price helps only if the food is actually used. If a family buys an enormous package and throws half of it away, they have wasted money. Marisol must therefore compare the unit prices and also consider how much her family will realistically use.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “comparing unit rates from a text and a table”?

activities.prompt: Which bottle gives Marisol the lowest price per ounce, and why?

choices.text: The 64-ounce bottle, because it costs $0.12 per ounce
The 12-ounce bottle, because it has the lowest total price
The 32-ounce bottle, because $0.125 is less than $0.12
The 12-ounce bottle, because it costs $0.15 per ounce

paragraphs.text: The Green Team made two plans. First, they will place a sharing table in the cafeteria where students can leave unopened food for others to take. Second, they will ask the cafeteria to replace paper trays with reusable trays, which can be washed and used many times. Together, they hope these changes will lower the weekly total by one fifth.

segments.text: "See?" she said. "Nothing in this room has changed. Only the light." Her voice was so
that my breathing slowed. We sat close together and listened to the storm while she told me about the hurricane she had lived through as a girl, when her whole village
three days without electricity. "People helped each other," she said. "We shared food and told stories, and the dark became less frightening." The storm weakened
, hour by hour, until only a soft drizzle remained. By then I felt
. When the lights finally hummed back on, I was almost
to see them, because the lantern's glow had made the room feel like a secret.

paragraphs.text: Last month, Westbrook Middle School banned cell phones during lunch. Principal Davis announced the rule in early September, saying that students were spending lunch on their screens instead of talking with each other. The ban began the following Monday.

paragraphs.text: This rule is unfair and unnecessary. In a survey by the student council, 70 percent of the 410 students who answered said they use their phones at lunch to contact family or finish homework. A lunch period is the one time of day when students can relax, and phones help many of us feel calm.

paragraphs.text: The school should let students use phones in the cafeteria for the first fifteen minutes of lunch. Teachers could ask for phones to stay away during the last fifteen minutes to protect conversation. Please sign the student council petition outside the library before Friday. Then come to the school board meeting on Thursday and speak up.

paragraphs.text: The Maple Grove Town Council is deciding whether to open the public library on Sundays. Right now, the library closes at 5 p.m. on Saturday and does not open again until Monday morning. Library director Ms. Reyes says Sunday hours would cost the town about $14,000 a year to pay staff and keep the building lit and heated.

paragraphs.text: To learn what residents think, the council asked three groups to answer a short survey. The results are shown in the table. Supporters say that students and working parents often cannot visit during the week and need a quiet place to study, use computers, and borrow books. Opponents argue that the money should go to repairing the library's roof, and some residents worry about traffic and parking near the building.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What detail in this section connects to “writing a short evidence-based response from a civic text and a table”?

paragraphs.text: Council member Torres says the survey is useful but not final. "Numbers tell us what people want," she said, "but we also have to decide what the town can afford." The council will vote next month.

lessons.summary: Follow a student team as it studies runoff, tests a rain garden, and explains what its measurements can—and cannot—show.

objectives.content: Analyze cause and effect in a schoolyard water investigation.
objectives.language: Build a qualified explanation or argument using precise vocabulary, relevant evidence, and a stated limitation.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can readers decide what the evidence supports about can a schoolyard hold the rain?
beforeReading.background: Preview the title and identify what you already know and what you would still need to verify.
beforeReading.hook: As you read, track how each section adds evidence, a qualification, or a new question.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to investigate cause and effect in a schoolyard water investigation and distinguish a supported conclusion from an overstatement.

vocabulary.definition: water that flows over the ground instead of soaking in
vocabulary.example: In this fictional schoolyard investigation, water crosses a paved courtyard after heavy rain and collects beside the library door. The science club wonders whether a planted rain garden could slow that flow. Their question is specific: would a shallow, planted basin collect water from one section of the courtyard, and how quickly would the water level fall? They do not begin by claiming that a garden would prevent every flood. They first need to describe the site and decide what evidence could answer their question.

vocabulary.definition: to pass into or through a material
vocabulary.example: In this fictional schoolyard investigation, water crosses a paved courtyard after heavy rain and collects beside the library door. The science club wonders whether a planted rain garden could slow that flow. Their question is specific: would a shallow, planted basin collect water from one section of the courtyard, and how quickly would the water level fall? They do not begin by claiming that a garden would prevent every flood. They first need to describe the site and decide what evidence could answer their question.

vocabulary.definition: a factor that can change in an investigation
vocabulary.example: In this fictional schoolyard investigation, water crosses a paved courtyard after heavy rain and collects beside the library door. The science club wonders whether a planted rain garden could slow that flow. Their question is specific: would a shallow, planted basin collect water from one section of the courtyard, and how quickly would the water level fall? They do not begin by claiming that a garden would prevent every flood. They first need to describe the site and decide what evidence could answer their question.

vocabulary.definition: information used to support or question an idea
vocabulary.example: In this fictional schoolyard investigation, water crosses a paved courtyard after heavy rain and collects beside the library door. The science club wonders whether a planted rain garden could slow that flow. Their question is specific: would a shallow, planted basin collect water from one section of the courtyard, and how quickly would the water level fall? They do not begin by claiming that a garden would prevent every flood. They first need to describe the site and decide what evidence could answer their question.

paragraphs.text: In this fictional schoolyard investigation, water crosses a paved courtyard after heavy rain and collects beside the library door. The science club wonders whether a planted rain garden could slow that flow. Their question is specific: would a shallow, planted basin collect water from one section of the courtyard, and how quickly would the water level fall? They do not begin by claiming that a garden would prevent every flood. They first need to describe the site and decide what evidence could answer their question.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question or decision frames the reading?

paragraphs.text: The students mapped the courtyard into three areas. The roof drained through a downspout, the paved walkway sloped toward the door, and a narrow planting strip sat downhill from both. They measured the planting strip and marked a small test basin inside it. Their design included a shallow depression, a layer of gravel, and soil chosen for the school’s planting plan. They recorded the starting water level after each rain. A ruler at the basin edge made the measurement repeatable, while a notebook kept observations together.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: For the first two storms, the team checked the basin at the same time after rainfall ended. The water level was lower at the second check than at the first. On the third storm, however, the level fell more slowly. A student noticed that the ground was already damp before the rain began. The group added that observation to its record. It did not erase the unusual result or call it a mistake. Soil that is already wet may have less space for additional water, so the starting condition could help explain the difference.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The team also compared the basin with a nearby patch of compacted soil. Water remained on the compacted patch longer during their observation, but the two areas were not identical in size or slope. That comparison suggested a useful question; it did not prove that soil type alone caused every difference. Rain amount, slope, plant roots, and the time of each check could also matter. The students learned that a fair comparison requires careful measurement and a clear account of what changed and what stayed the same.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: At the next meeting, the club proposed measuring the same locations after several storms and recording rainfall, soil condition, and water depth. They would also check whether water reached the library door. Their evidence could help the school decide whether to adjust the basin or add another planting area. The rain garden was a practical response, but the investigation was still in progress. By separating observations from explanations, the students could make a careful claim: in the storms they measured, the planted basin held water temporarily, and more consistent comparisons were needed to understand why the results varied.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What conclusion is justified, and what remains uncertain?

activities.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the students’ investigation so far?

choices.text: The basin held water temporarily during the storms measured, but more comparable observations are needed.
The basin prevented all flooding because one water level decreased.
The compacted soil proves that every planted area absorbs water at the same rate.

activities.rationale: The final paragraph limits the claim to the storms observed and calls for more consistent comparisons.

vocabulary.definition: something considered more important to address first
vocabulary.example: In this fictional school, the student council has enough funding to add trees beside one walking route this year. The East Route passes the bus stop and library entrance. The South Route connects the gym, cafeteria, and outdoor courts. Both routes are used every day, and both have long sections with little shade. The council asks students to recommend where the first trees should go. The choice is about which route to address first, not whether one group of students matters more.

vocabulary.definition: a set of questions used to collect responses
vocabulary.example: Maya argues for the East Route. In a one-week survey, 42 of 60 students who responded said they used it at least three days a week. The route also has a waiting area near the bus stop. Maya says shade there could help students who arrive early and people walking to the library. She acknowledges that the survey did not ask how long people waited. Her proposal is to plant near the bus stop first, then review how the area is used before choosing a second location.

vocabulary.definition: a limit that affects a decision
vocabulary.example: At the meeting, students suggest combining the proposals: plant the first trees at a location that can be reached from the bus stop and the cafeteria crossing, if the site is suitable. Others warn that a shared location may not shade either route well. The council decides to visit both areas, check underground utility constraints, and ask students who did not complete the survey. It will compare shade, safety, foot traffic, and planting space before voting. The disagreement helps the group make a stronger decision because each proposal reveals a different need—and the evidence still has gaps.

paragraphs.text: The survey numbers are useful but incomplete. Students chose whether to respond, and the two routes did not receive exactly the same number of responses. The survey therefore describes the responding students’ reported use; it does not prove which route has the greatest need. The council could gather additional evidence by observing both routes at several times and mapping their existing shade.

vocabulary.definition: an object made or used by people in the past
vocabulary.example: A local history museum is preparing an exhibit about a train station that served a growing town. The exhibit team finds a metal lunch tin with a scratched name, a dated station timetable, and two short accounts written many years later. The sources are part of a fictional classroom case; they are designed to practice historical reasoning. The tin is an artifact, but it cannot explain its own story. Historians ask what an object can show, what other records might help, and which questions remain open.

vocabulary.definition: an explanation of what evidence may mean
vocabulary.example: The exhibit team chooses Label B and adds a question card: “Who used this tin, and how could we find out?” Visitors can inspect the timetable and see which claims it supports. The label is less dramatic than Label A, yet it models how evidence and interpretation differ. Careful historical writing does not avoid interpretation. It makes the reasoning visible, identifies the limits of the sources, and leaves room for new evidence to change an explanation.

vocabulary.definition: to check a claim against another source
vocabulary.example: The curator’s note adds another source: a later oral history in which a former resident remembers that “many families used the station platform as a meeting place.” The speaker does not mention the tin or Asha Patel. The account may offer context about how residents used the station, but memory recorded later can be incomplete. A researcher could compare the account with employment records, photographs, or additional interviews. If another source identifies Asha as a station worker, that would corroborate part of Label A; it still would not prove what was inside the tin.

paragraphs.text: Label A reads: “Asha Patel carried this tin to her station job every morning. She kept letters inside it and shared lunch with coworkers.” The label gives a vivid story, but the evidence file only shows that the name A. Patel is scratched into the tin. The timetable lists train departures; it does not identify workers. Asha may have owned the tin, but the evidence described so far does not establish her job, routine, or what she stored inside it.

paragraphs.text: Label B reads: “A tin marked A. Patel was found near the station. A timetable from the same period shows frequent departures. These objects suggest that the station was part of a busy town, but they do not identify the tin’s owner.” This label makes a narrower claim. It connects two pieces of evidence while acknowledging that the objects do not answer every question. A reader may still ask whether the tin was left at the station, brought there by a visitor, or moved later.

vocabulary.definition: how easily people can reach and use a service
vocabulary.example: During a week of unusually hot weather, a city council considers opening two public libraries as daytime cooling centers. Supporters argue that libraries are familiar, accessible public spaces where residents can rest, drink water, and find information. Critics ask whether the buildings can remain open longer without reducing other services or overloading staff. The policy question is not simply whether libraries are useful. It is how the city can provide a dependable service while accounting for location, hours, capacity, transportation, and the needs of people who may not already use a library.

vocabulary.definition: the amount a place or system can serve
vocabulary.example: During a week of unusually hot weather, a city council considers opening two public libraries as daytime cooling centers. Supporters argue that libraries are familiar, accessible public spaces where residents can rest, drink water, and find information. Critics ask whether the buildings can remain open longer without reducing other services or overloading staff. The policy question is not simply whether libraries are useful. It is how the city can provide a dependable service while accounting for location, hours, capacity, transportation, and the needs of people who may not already use a library.

vocabulary.definition: a condition that limits available choices
vocabulary.example: Staff members describe practical constraints. The branches have limited seating, and some rooms are already reserved for tutoring. Extending hours would require a schedule for staff, cleaning, and water supplies. A library manager warns that a crowded room could become uncomfortable even if the building is cool. A neighborhood group suggests a shuttle from areas farther away. That idea could improve access but would require a driver, a route, and funding. Each proposal changes both the likely benefit and the resources needed to deliver it.

vocabulary.definition: a benefit gained by accepting a cost or limitation
vocabulary.example: During a week of unusually hot weather, a city council considers opening two public libraries as daytime cooling centers. Supporters argue that libraries are familiar, accessible public spaces where residents can rest, drink water, and find information. Critics ask whether the buildings can remain open longer without reducing other services or overloading staff. The policy question is not simply whether libraries are useful. It is how the city can provide a dependable service while accounting for location, hours, capacity, transportation, and the needs of people who may not already use a library.

paragraphs.text: During a week of unusually hot weather, a city council considers opening two public libraries as daytime cooling centers. Supporters argue that libraries are familiar, accessible public spaces where residents can rest, drink water, and find information. Critics ask whether the buildings can remain open longer without reducing other services or overloading staff. The policy question is not simply whether libraries are useful. It is how the city can provide a dependable service while accounting for location, hours, capacity, transportation, and the needs of people who may not already use a library.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question or decision frames the reading?

paragraphs.text: A planning team reviews an illustrative one-week pilot at two branches. The north branch recorded 84 visits and the south branch 53. The north branch is beside a bus transfer point; the south branch is near several apartment buildings. The counts are visits, not unique people, and the pilot did not record how many residents needed a place but could not reach either branch. A larger count may reflect greater need, easier access, repeat visits, or some combination. The numbers can guide questions, but they cannot by themselves identify everyone who would benefit.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: Staff members describe practical constraints. The branches have limited seating, and some rooms are already reserved for tutoring. Extending hours would require a schedule for staff, cleaning, and water supplies. A library manager warns that a crowded room could become uncomfortable even if the building is cool. A neighborhood group suggests a shuttle from areas farther away. That idea could improve access but would require a driver, a route, and funding. Each proposal changes both the likely benefit and the resources needed to deliver it.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The council compares three possible plans: open both branches for regular hours with water and public information; extend hours at the north branch while testing a shuttle; or rotate extended hours between the branches. The first plan is easier to organize but may not reach residents who cannot travel during the day. The second uses the pilot’s higher visit count but risks treating visits as a complete measure of need. The rotating plan shares staff and operating costs, yet its changing schedule may make the service harder to remember. A clear public schedule would matter under any option.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: A responsible recommendation would state what the pilot supports and what remains uncertain. For example, the visit counts show that residents used both branches during the pilot, but they do not show whether either site met community need. The council could begin with a limited schedule, publish transportation and capacity information, and collect anonymous counts of time, location, and unmet requests. It could also ask community organizations to share information about residents who were unable to attend. After several weeks, the council could compare access and operating data before deciding whether to expand the service.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The debate illustrates a broader policy principle: public services are shaped by design choices as well as by their existence. A building may be open and still be out of reach for someone without transportation, a flexible work schedule, or a comfortable place to wait. A pilot can reveal patterns, but its measures should match the question decision makers need to answer. The strongest policy argument combines evidence, practical constraints, and a plan to learn from results without presenting a short trial as proof that every community member has been served.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What conclusion is justified, and what remains uncertain?

vocabulary.definition: an order assigned to items using selected rules
vocabulary.example: The team runs a short trial with two versions of the feed. Version A places the newest stories first. Version B uses a ranking rule based on each reader’s earlier clicks. In the trial, readers open more stories in Version B. The result supports a narrow claim: during this trial, the click-based version was associated with more story opens. It does not establish that readers learned more, trusted the app more, or encountered a wider range of ideas. Those outcomes were not measured.

vocabulary.definition: an action that signals interaction, such as opening or replying
vocabulary.example: The case shows why digital media analysis begins with definitions. A platform may call an increase in clicks “better engagement,” but the phrase does not automatically mean deeper learning or a healthier information diet. Readers and designers should ask what was counted, who participated, how items were ordered, and which outcomes were left out. A result is more useful when its limits are stated alongside it. Careful interpretation keeps a measurable behavior from standing in for a broader conclusion it cannot support.

vocabulary.definition: a defined way to observe or count something
vocabulary.example: A fictional student news app changes the order of stories in each reader’s feed. The design team says a ranked feed can help readers find articles they are likely to open. A student group asks a different question: does seeing more opened stories mean readers understand more? These questions sound similar, but they require different evidence. Opening a story is an observable action. Understanding a story is a learning outcome that would need a separate measure, such as an explanation that accurately uses the article’s evidence.

paragraphs.text: A student researcher proposes that earlier clicks may help the app surface relevant topics. Another student points out that the rule might repeatedly place familiar topics near the top, reducing the chance that a reader sees something unexpected. Both explanations could fit the same increase in opens. To distinguish them, the team would need to define relevance and variety, decide how to measure each, and examine what appears lower in the feed as well as what readers open.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The trial also has limits. It is short, uses a fictional app with a small group of volunteers, and compares only two ordering rules. A reader who opens several stories may not read each one carefully. A story appearing near the top has a greater chance to be noticed, so position itself can affect the result. If the team wants to study learning, it could ask readers to summarize a story and identify supporting evidence. If it wants to study variety, it could classify topics and compare how many distinct ones appear in each feed.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The students recommend that the app label its goal clearly and test more than one outcome before describing the ranking as successful. They suggest reporting story opens separately from comprehension and topic variety. They also ask whether readers can switch to a newest-first view. Their recommendation does not assume that ranking is always harmful or always helpful. Instead, it treats a design choice as a question that can be examined with measures suited to the claim.

beforeReading.background: Preview the title and identify what you already know and what you would still need to verify.

vocabulary.definition: a measure that can provide evidence about a larger condition
vocabulary.example: This fictional project report describes a coastal community restoring a small wetland beside a walking path. Before work begins, the project team records water depth, plant cover, and the number of bird visits observed during scheduled checks. These measures are indicators: each can reveal something about the site, but none alone defines a healthy wetland. The team also marks a nearby area where no restoration work is planned. Comparing the two places over time may help researchers interpret change, although the sites can differ in ways that affect the results.

vocabulary.definition: a starting point used for comparison
vocabulary.example: This fictional project report describes a coastal community restoring a small wetland beside a walking path. Before work begins, the project team records water depth, plant cover, and the number of bird visits observed during scheduled checks. These measures are indicators: each can reveal something about the site, but none alone defines a healthy wetland. The team also marks a nearby area where no restoration work is planned. Comparing the two places over time may help researchers interpret change, although the sites can differ in ways that affect the results.

vocabulary.definition: a return toward a healthier or more functional condition
vocabulary.example: This fictional project report describes a coastal community restoring a small wetland beside a walking path. Before work begins, the project team records water depth, plant cover, and the number of bird visits observed during scheduled checks. These measures are indicators: each can reveal something about the site, but none alone defines a healthy wetland. The team also marks a nearby area where no restoration work is planned. Comparing the two places over time may help researchers interpret change, although the sites can differ in ways that affect the results.

vocabulary.definition: to observe or measure over time
vocabulary.example: The team proposes a monitoring plan for the next three years. It will repeat the same measurements in both areas, record rainfall and season, and add a simple assessment of plant survival. Community volunteers can help observe the path, while trained staff check water levels using a consistent method. The plan does not make the project successful in advance. It makes future conclusions more informative because the measures, comparison, and limits are stated clearly.

paragraphs.text: This fictional project report describes a coastal community restoring a small wetland beside a walking path. Before work begins, the project team records water depth, plant cover, and the number of bird visits observed during scheduled checks. These measures are indicators: each can reveal something about the site, but none alone defines a healthy wetland. The team also marks a nearby area where no restoration work is planned. Comparing the two places over time may help researchers interpret change, although the sites can differ in ways that affect the results.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question or decision frames the reading?

paragraphs.text: The restoration team removes a barrier that had altered the flow of water into one section. It also plants native vegetation selected for the site. In the first month, plant cover increases in the restored area. Bird visits vary from one check to the next. The project manager cautions that a quick increase in cover does not prove the wetland has recovered. New plants may need time to establish, and bird counts can change with weather, season, observer timing, or the availability of food elsewhere.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: A year later, the team finds that water depth changes across more parts of the restored site, and plant cover remains higher than at the initial check. The nearby comparison area shows little change in plant cover during the same period. Those patterns are consistent with a positive response at the restored site. They are not a complete explanation of cause. Rainfall differed between the two years, and the team did not measure every feature of habitat quality. The comparison helps, but it cannot control for all environmental differences.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: Some residents define success as more wildlife near the path. Others focus on whether the site can hold water during storms. The project team explains that these goals are related but not interchangeable. A change in water movement may influence plants and habitat, but a single year of observation may be too short to identify long-term effects. The team needs to connect each goal to a measure and explain how often it will be checked. It should also report uncertainty instead of turning a promising pattern into a guarantee.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The team proposes a monitoring plan for the next three years. It will repeat the same measurements in both areas, record rainfall and season, and add a simple assessment of plant survival. Community volunteers can help observe the path, while trained staff check water levels using a consistent method. The plan does not make the project successful in advance. It makes future conclusions more informative because the measures, comparison, and limits are stated clearly.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: A careful report might conclude that the restored area showed increased plant cover and broader water-depth variation during the first year, while bird observations remained inconsistent. The team can say these early indicators are encouraging, but additional monitoring is needed to assess durability and broader habitat outcomes. That conclusion answers the current evidence without pretending to answer every question. In environmental science, success is often evaluated through several connected indicators over time, with attention to what each one can and cannot reveal.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What conclusion is justified, and what remains uncertain?

beforeReading.background: Preview the title and identify what you already know and what you would still need to verify.

vocabulary.definition: a rule or plan that guides decisions
vocabulary.example: In this fictional school, a student advisory group is reviewing the phone policy. During class, phones are expected to remain away unless a teacher asks students to use them for a learning task. Some students want the rule to continue; others want a designated break-time option. The group reads two short arguments and reviews an illustrative survey summary. The assignment is not to decide whether technology is good or bad in general. It is to judge which policy would address the concerns in this school and what evidence is still missing.

vocabulary.definition: a position that challenges or qualifies a claim
vocabulary.example: Argument A supports the current rule. Its authors say that putting phones away during lessons can reduce interruptions and make it easier to follow discussions. They also note that a consistent rule gives teachers a predictable way to begin class. The authors acknowledge a counterclaim: students may need to contact family or check an important message. They propose that the office remain available for urgent communication and that teachers approve phones when a lesson requires a device. Their argument emphasizes a shared classroom routine, but it does not provide direct measures of attention or learning.

vocabulary.definition: reflecting the range of people or views in a larger group
vocabulary.example: In this fictional school, a student advisory group is reviewing the phone policy. During class, phones are expected to remain away unless a teacher asks students to use them for a learning task. Some students want the rule to continue; others want a designated break-time option. The group reads two short arguments and reviews an illustrative survey summary. The assignment is not to decide whether technology is good or bad in general. It is to judge which policy would address the concerns in this school and what evidence is still missing.

vocabulary.definition: the way a rule or plan is put into practice
vocabulary.example: In this fictional school, a student advisory group is reviewing the phone policy. During class, phones are expected to remain away unless a teacher asks students to use them for a learning task. Some students want the rule to continue; others want a designated break-time option. The group reads two short arguments and reviews an illustrative survey summary. The assignment is not to decide whether technology is good or bad in general. During class, phones are expected to remain away unless a teacher asks students to use them for a learning task. Some students want the rule to continue; others want a designated break-time option. The group reads two short arguments and reviews an illustrative survey summary. The assignment is not to decide whether technology is good or bad in general. It is to judge which policy would address the concerns in this school and what evidence is still missing.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question or decision frames the reading?

paragraphs.text: Argument A supports the current rule. Its authors say that putting phones away during lessons can reduce interruptions and make it easier to follow discussions. They also note that a consistent rule gives teachers a predictable way to begin class. The authors acknowledge a counterclaim: students may need to contact family or check an important message. They propose that the office remain available for urgent communication and that teachers approve phones when a lesson requires a device. Their argument emphasizes a shared classroom routine, but it does not provide direct measures of attention or learning.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: Argument B proposes a supervised phone break at lunch. Its authors say a clearly defined time could recognize students’ need to communicate without changing the expectation during instruction. They also point out that some students use a phone to coordinate transportation or care responsibilities. The proposal has a cost: staff would need to explain and supervise the routine, and students might disagree about whether a message is urgent. The authors suggest a trial period and a review of classroom interruptions, but they do not specify how those interruptions would be counted.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The survey summary reports that 126 students responded: 71 support the current rule, 39 want a lunch option, and 16 are undecided. The survey was shared through two advisory classes, and participation was optional. The summary does not say how many students received it, whether grade levels responded at similar rates, or how students who were absent could share a view. The results describe the respondents, but they may not represent every student. A larger count does not fix a sampling gap if the same groups are still missing.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: The advisory group identifies evidence it would need before recommending a change. It could use the same brief observation routine across several classes, ask students from every grade to respond, and collect anonymous comments about urgent communication. The group should define an interruption consistently rather than counting only incidents a teacher happens to notice. It could also compare the time needed to teach and supervise a lunch option with the value students report. Those measures would not answer every question, but they would make the discussion more specific.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What new evidence, perspective, or limitation does this section add?

paragraphs.text: At the next meeting, students draft a conditional recommendation: keep phones away during instruction, clarify how students can reach family in an urgent situation, and test a supervised lunch option only if staff can manage it safely. They propose reviewing the trial after a set period using student responses and the same classroom observation method. Another student argues that the school should keep the current policy without a trial. The group records that disagreement and the evidence each side wants. A useful policy statement makes its reasoning visible and names how the school will revisit the decision.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What conclusion is justified, and what remains uncertain?

lessons.title: How a Map Shrinks the World
lessons.summary: Learn how a map scale turns a distance on paper into a distance on the ground.
lessons.subject: Math and social studies
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how a ratio connects a map distance to a real distance.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how a map scale is a ratio that changes a map distance into a real distance.
objectives.language: Use ratio vocabulary and sequence words to explain a calculation from a text.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can a small drawing tell us about a very large place?
beforeReading.background: Think about a map you have used. How could you tell how far away a place was?
beforeReading.hook: A paper map is only a few centimeters across, but the land it shows can be hundreds of kilometers wide.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what a scale is and how readers use it to find a real distance.

vocabulary.definition: the ratio that compares a map distance with a real distance
vocabulary.example: The scale on the map is 1 centimeter to 5 kilometers.

vocabulary.definition: how far one place is from another
vocabulary.example: The distance from school to the museum is 20 kilometers.

vocabulary.definition: a comparison of two quantities
vocabulary.example: The ratio of centimeters to kilometers stays the same.

vocabulary.definition: a small piece of information
vocabulary.example: A bus map shows many small details.

paragraphs.text: A map cannot be the same size as the land it shows. Instead, mapmakers shrink everything by the same amount. The scale tells readers how much the map has been shrunk. On one school field-trip map, the scale is 1 centimeter to 5 kilometers. That means every centimeter on the paper stands for 5 kilometers on the ground.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does a scale tell the reader?

paragraphs.text: Suppose the map shows the science museum 4 centimeters from the school. To find the real distance, multiply 4 by 5. The museum is 20 kilometers away. Notice that the calculation uses a ratio: 1 centimeter is to 5 kilometers as 4 centimeters is to 20 kilometers. Both ratios describe the same relationship.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the writer find the real distance?

paragraphs.text: A scale can also be written without units, such as 1:500,000. This form works with any unit of length. The scale of 1 centimeter to 5 kilometers is the same as 1:500,000, because 5 kilometers equals 500,000 centimeters. However, most people find the numbers easier to understand when the units are kilometers or miles.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why can a scale be written without units?

paragraphs.text: Mapmakers choose a scale to fit the purpose of the map. A city bus map uses a small distance for each centimeter so that streets and stops are easy to see. A map of a whole country uses a much larger distance, so it can show fewer small details. Neither map is wrong. Each one is designed for a different job.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why do mapmakers use different scales?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what does a map scale tell readers?

choices.text: How many places the mapmaker decided to put on the map.
choices.why: The scale is about size, not about the number of places; the text says it tells how much the map has been shrunk.

choices.text: How much the real distances were shrunk to fit on the map.
How many kilometers a person can walk in one hour.
choices.why: Walking speed is not mentioned in the passage; the scale compares a distance on paper with a distance on the ground.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the scale tells readers how much the map has been shrunk, so each centimeter stands for a set distance on the ground.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 1, mapmakers “shrink everything by the same amount.” What does shrink mean?

choices.text: make something smaller
make something clearer
choices.why: The map has to fit on paper, but nothing in the sentence says the map becomes easier to see; it becomes smaller.

choices.text: move something farther
choices.why: The land does not move; the sentence is about the map being a smaller copy of the land.

activities.rationale: A map cannot be the same size as the land, so shrinking the land means making its picture smaller.

activities.prompt: Another map uses the same scale as the passage. The library is 6 centimeters from the school on that map. How far away is the library?

choices.text: 11 kilometers
choices.why: That adds 5 to 6, but the scale tells you to multiply each centimeter by 5 kilometers.

choices.text: 6 kilometers
choices.why: Six centimeters on the paper is not 6 kilometers; each centimeter stands for 5 kilometers.

choices.text: 30 kilometers

activities.rationale: Each centimeter stands for 5 kilometers, so 6 centimeters stands for 6 times 5, which is 30 kilometers.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that shows how to turn a map distance into a real distance.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives the worked example: multiply 4 centimeters by 5 to get 20 kilometers.

activities.prompt: How does paragraph 2 connect to paragraph 1?

choices.text: It disagrees with the scale that paragraph 1 introduced.
choices.why: Paragraph 2 uses the same scale, 1 centimeter to 5 kilometers, so it supports paragraph 1 and does not disagree.

choices.text: It gives a worked example that uses the scale explained in paragraph 1.
It begins a new topic that has nothing to do with the scale.
choices.why: Paragraph 2 keeps the same scale and the same map, so the topic is the same as paragraph 1.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 applies the scale from paragraph 1 to a real example, the museum that is 4 centimeters away.

activities.prompt: Map X has a scale of 1 centimeter to 1 kilometer. Map Y has a scale of 1 centimeter to 5 kilometers. Which statement does paragraph 4 support?

choices.text: Map X can show more small details because each centimeter covers less land.
Map Y can show more small details because each centimeter covers more land.
choices.why: A centimeter on Map Y covers more land, which leaves less room for small details, according to paragraph 4.

choices.text: Both maps show exactly the same details because both have a scale.
choices.why: Having a scale does not make maps show the same details; paragraph 4 says the scale is chosen for a purpose.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says a smaller distance for each centimeter makes small details easy to see, so Map X can show more of them.

activities.prompt: Explain why neither the city bus map nor the country map is wrong. Use one detail from paragraph 4.
lookFor: A clear claim that both maps can be correct
One accurate detail about scale or purpose from paragraph 4
A reason that connects the detail to the claim
rubric: States that each map has a different purpose
Uses an accurate detail from the text
Explains how the scale fits the purpose
activities.frame: Neither map is wrong because ___. For example, the bus map ___, while the country map ___.
activities.model: Neither map is wrong because each one has a different job. The bus map uses a small distance for each centimeter, so streets and stops are easy to see, while the country map uses a larger distance and shows fewer small details.

activities.prompt: A scale drawing of a classroom uses 1 centimeter for every 50 centimeters of the real room. A desk is 3 centimeters long on the drawing. Explain how to find its real length and what that number means.
lookFor: Multiplies 3 by 50 to get 150 centimeters
Says that each drawing centimeter stands for 50 real centimeters
Names the unit in the answer
rubric: Says that each drawing centimeter stands for 50 real centimeters
Names the unit in the answer
activities.frame: I multiply ___ by ___ because every centimeter on the drawing stands for ___. The desk is ___ long.

teacherGuide.miniLesson: Model the calculation in paragraph 2 on the board as a ratio table: 1 cm to 5 km, 4 cm to 20 km. Ask students what stays the same in each row.

teacherGuide.misconception: Students may add the scale number to the map distance instead of multiplying; a ratio table shows that every row is multiplied by the same number.

scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 3: 6 times 5 equals 30 kilometers; adding gives 11, a common error.
Question 6: the smaller the distance per centimeter, the more detail a map can show.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: Neither map is wrong because each is designed for a different job. A bus map shows small details with a small distance per centimeter, and a country map covers much more land with a larger distance per centimeter.
