lessons.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
lessons.summary: Follow a scientific explanation of why the sky looks blue, why it is not violet, and why sunsets are red.
lessons.subject: Science (light and waves)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain a natural phenomenon using cause and effect.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain why the sky looks blue and why sunsets look red using the scattering of light.
objectives.language: Use because, therefore and as a result to connect causes and effects.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can one process explain both a blue sky and a red sunset?
beforeReading.background: Think about what color the sky is at noon and at sunset.
beforeReading.hook: Sunlight looks white, but the sky does not. Where does the blue come from?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn how air changes the color of sunlight and why the sky is not violet.

vocabulary.definition: the distance between two peaks of a wave
vocabulary.example: Blue light has a short wavelength.

vocabulary.definition: to send in many directions
vocabulary.example: Air molecules scatter blue light.

vocabulary.definition: the layer of gases around Earth
vocabulary.example: Sunlight enters the atmosphere.

vocabulary.definition: a tiny particle of a substance
vocabulary.example: Nitrogen molecules scatter light.

paragraphs.text: On a clear day the sky looks blue, but sunlight itself looks white. White light is actually a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow. Each color travels as a wave, and different colors have different wavelengths. Violet and blue have short wavelengths, while orange and red have longer ones.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is white light made of?

paragraphs.text: As sunlight enters the atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules such as nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter light in many directions. Short-wavelength light scatters much more than long-wavelength light. Therefore, blue light is scattered all across the sky, and some of it reaches your eyes from every direction.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happens to light in the atmosphere?

paragraphs.text: If violet light is scattered even more than blue, why isn't the sky violet? There are several reasons. The Sun gives off less violet light than blue light, the upper atmosphere absorbs some of the violet, and human eyes are less sensitive to violet than to blue. Together, these effects make blue the color we see.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why is the sky not violet?

paragraphs.text: The same process explains red sunsets. When the Sun is low, its light travels through much more air before reaching you. Most of the blue light is scattered out of the direct beam along the way, leaving the longer red and orange wavelengths to reach your eyes.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are sunsets red?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is white light?

choices.text: a single color with a very long wavelength
choices.why: Paragraph 1 says different colors have different wavelengths, so white light is not a single color.

choices.text: a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow
a color that only appears at sunset
choices.why: Sunset color is explained in paragraph 4 and is not the same as white light.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says white light is a mixture of all the colors of the rainbow.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, molecules “scatter” light. What does scatter mean?

choices.text: send it in many directions
stop it from moving at all
choices.why: The text says some blue light still reaches your eyes, so the light is not stopped completely.

choices.text: make it move much faster
choices.why: The text never says the light speeds up; it says the light is sent in different directions.

activities.rationale: The passage says molecules scatter light in many directions.

activities.prompt: On a planet with no atmosphere, what would the daytime sky most likely look like from the ground?

choices.text: blue, because the sunlight itself is white all day
choices.why: Blue light is scattered by gas molecules, and without an atmosphere there are none.

choices.text: dark, because nothing would scatter the sunlight
red, because the Sun would always be low in the sky
choices.why: Red skies happen when a low Sun's light passes through a lot of air, and there would be no air.

activities.rationale: The sky is blue because molecules scatter blue light, so without molecules there is nothing to scatter it.

activities.prompt: What question does paragraph 3 answer?

choices.text: Why is the sky not violet if violet scatters more?
Why is white light made of many different colors?
choices.why: The color mixture of white light is explained in paragraph 1.

choices.text: Why does the Sun look so red at the end of the day?
choices.why: The red sunset is explained in paragraph 4.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 begins with the question about why the sky is not violet.

activities.prompt: Why does the author ask a question at the start of paragraph 3?

choices.text: To show that scientists still do not know the answer
choices.why: The paragraph goes on to give three reasons, so scientists do have an answer.

choices.text: To introduce a brand new topic about the Moon's light
choices.why: The paragraph stays on sky color; the Moon is never mentioned.

choices.text: To address a question a thoughtful reader might already have

activities.rationale: The question anticipates the reader's objection that violet should look brighter than blue.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that explains why sunsets look red.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says the low Sun's light travels through more air, so most blue light is scattered away, leaving red and orange.

activities.prompt: Explain why the sky looks blue and not violet. Use two reasons from the text.
lookFor: Says blue light is scattered across the sky
Gives at least two reasons from paragraph 3
Connects the reasons to what we see
rubric: Connects causes to the color we see
activities.frame: The sky looks blue because ___. It is not violet because ___ and ___.
activities.model: The sky looks blue because air molecules scatter short-wavelength blue light across the sky. It is not violet because the Sun gives off less violet light than blue and our eyes are less sensitive to violet.

activities.prompt: At noon the Sun's light passes through less air than at sunset. Use that fact to explain why the noon sky is blue and the sunset is red.
lookFor: Says blue light scatters across the sky at noon
Says at sunset the light passes through more air so blue is scattered away
Uses because, therefore or as a result
rubric: Says blue light scatters across the sky at noon
Says at sunset the light passes through more air so blue is scattered away
Uses because, therefore or as a result
activities.frame: At noon, ___ because ___. At sunset, ___ because ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: At noon the Sun's light passes through less air than at sunset. Use that fact to explain why the noon sky is blue and the sunset is red.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Explain why the sky looks blue and why sunsets look red using the scattering of light.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use because, therefore and as a result to connect causes and effects.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Use a prism or a diagram to show white light splitting into colors. Ask students to predict which colors air will scatter most before reading paragraph 2.
discussion: Why does a short wavelength scatter more?
How is a red sunset like looking through more air?
What other everyday observations depend on light scattering?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think the sky reflects the ocean; the passage explains that the color comes from scattered sunlight.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 3: with no atmosphere there are no molecules to scatter light.
Question 5: the author asks the question the reader is likely to think.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The sky looks blue because air molecules scatter blue light across the sky. It is not violet because the Sun gives off less violet and our eyes are less sensitive to it.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.en: Read one paragraph at a time. Ask your student to explain in their own words why sunsets are red. You can talk in any language, then ask for one sentence in English.
directions.es: Lean un párrafo a la vez. Pida a su estudiante que explique con sus propias palabras por qué los atardeceres son rojos. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What does the air do to sunlight?
Why is the sunset red?
familySupport.noEnglishRequired: Family discussion can happen in any language; the student can practice explaining one idea in English afterward.

connections.speak: Explain the blue sky aloud using scatter.
connections.listen: Listen to a science talk about light.

lessons.title: Pages per Day: Finding a Unit Rate
lessons.summary: Two friends read different numbers of pages in different numbers of days, and a unit rate shows how their reading compares.
lessons.subject: Math (ratios and rates)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how to find a unit rate and what it means.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain that a unit rate tells how much there is for one unit, found by dividing.
objectives.language: Use per, for each and sequence words to explain a rate.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can one number help us compare two different amounts?
beforeReading.background: Think about how many pages you could read in one day.
beforeReading.hook: Sam read 24 pages and Ana read 30 pages. Who reads more each day?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what a unit rate is and how to find one.

vocabulary.definition: a comparison of two different kinds of things
vocabulary.example: Sam's rate compares pages with days.

vocabulary.definition: a rate that tells how much there is for 1 of something
vocabulary.example: The unit rate is 6 pages for 1 day.

vocabulary.definition: for each, or for every one
vocabulary.example: Six pages per day means 6 pages for each day.

vocabulary.definition: to split an amount into equal groups
vocabulary.example: Divide 24 pages by 4 days to find the unit rate.

paragraphs.text: Sam belongs to a reading club, and on his own he reads 24 pages in 4 days. He wants to figure out how many pages he reads during each single day.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Sam want to find out?

paragraphs.text: A rate is a comparison of two different kinds of things, and in this story the rate compares pages with days. Sam's rate is 24 pages for 4 days. A unit rate tells how much there is for just 1 of something, and we find it by dividing. When we divide 24 by 4, we get 6, so Sam's unit rate is 6 pages per day.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do you find a unit rate?

paragraphs.text: The word per means for each. Six pages per day means that for each day, Sam reads 6 pages. Knowing the unit rate helps Sam make a plan, because if he keeps reading 6 pages every day, he will finish 12 pages in 2 days and 18 pages in 3 days.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does per mean?

paragraphs.text: Sam's friend Ana reads 30 pages in 5 days. Her unit rate is also 6 pages per day, because 30 divided by 5 is 6. Even though the two friends have different totals, they read the same number of pages during each day.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How are Sam and Ana alike?

activities.prompt: How many pages does Sam read in 4 days?

choices.text: 24 pages
6 pages
choices.why: Six is how many pages Sam reads in one day, which is the unit rate and not the total for 4 days.

choices.text: 4 pages
choices.why: Four is the number of days, not the number of pages he read.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says Sam reads 24 pages in 4 days.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, the word “per” is used. What does per mean?

choices.text: added to
choices.why: Adding is a different operation; the text says per tells how much there is for each day.

choices.text: for each
out of all
choices.why: Out of all describes a whole group, but per describes one single day or one single unit.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says that per means for each, so 6 pages per day means 6 pages for each day.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding a unit rate in the correct order.

items.text: Say the unit rate with per: 6 pages per day.
Write the two amounts: 24 pages and 4 days.
Divide the pages by the number of days.
Read the answer, which is 6.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 names the two amounts first, then says to divide, and then states the unit rate with per.

activities.prompt: Mia reads 20 pages in 5 days. What is her unit rate?

choices.text: 25 pages per day
choices.why: That adds the pages and the days, but a unit rate comes from dividing the pages by the days.

choices.text: 15 pages per day
choices.why: That subtracts the days from the pages; the text says the way to find a unit rate is to divide.

choices.text: 4 pages per day

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says to divide, and 20 divided by 5 is 4, so Mia reads 4 pages per day.

activities.prompt: What does paragraph 4 show about Sam and Ana?

choices.text: Ana reads more pages each day because her total is bigger.
choices.why: A bigger total does not mean a bigger unit rate; Ana also read for more days.

choices.text: Sam reads fewer pages each day because he read for fewer days.
choices.why: Fewer days does not mean fewer pages each day; Sam's unit rate is the same as Ana's.

choices.text: They read the same number of pages each day.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says both friends have a unit rate of 6 pages per day, even though their totals are different.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that tells what a unit rate is.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says that a unit rate tells how much there is for just 1 of something.

activities.prompt: Explain how to find the unit rate when someone reads 30 pages in 5 days.
lookFor: Divides 30 by 5
States the unit rate as 6 pages per day
Uses a sequence word such as first or then
rubric: Gives the correct unit rate with units
activities.frame: First, I divide ___ by ___. Then I see that the unit rate is ___ pages per day.
activities.model: First, I divide 30 pages by 5 days. Then I see that the unit rate is 6 pages per day, which means the person reads 6 pages for each day.

activities.prompt: A store sells 3 notebooks for 12 dollars. Explain how to find the cost of 1 notebook and say what the unit rate means.
lookFor: Divides 12 by 3
States 4 dollars per notebook
Says that one notebook costs 4 dollars
rubric: Says that one notebook costs 4 dollars
activities.frame: I divide ___ by ___. The unit rate is ___ dollars per notebook, which means ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: A store sells 3 notebooks for 12 dollars. Explain how to find the cost of 1 notebook and say what the unit rate means.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Explain that a unit rate tells how much there is for one unit, found by dividing.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use per, for each and sequence words to explain a rate.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Draw 4 boxes on the board and place 24 counters in them equally. Ask how many are in each box, then connect the picture to dividing 24 by 4 and to the phrase 6 per box.
discussion: How is a unit rate different from a total?
Why did Sam and Ana have the same unit rate when their totals were different?
What other unit rates do you see at home or at school, such as cost per item?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may add or subtract the two numbers instead of dividing; acting out equal groups shows why a unit rate comes from division.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 4: 20 divided by 5 is 4, so Mia reads 4 pages per day. Adding gives 25 and subtracting gives 15.
Question 5: Sam and Ana both read 6 pages per day, because 24 divided by 4 and 30 divided by 5 both equal 6.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: First, I divide 30 pages by 5 days. The unit rate is 6 pages per day, so the person reads 6 pages for each day.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.en: Read one paragraph at a time. Ask your student to explain how 24 pages in 4 days becomes 6 pages per day. You can talk in any language, then ask for one sentence in English.
directions.es: Lean un párrafo a la vez. Pida a su estudiante que explique cómo 24 páginas en 4 días se convierten en 6 páginas por día. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What does the word per mean?
How do you find how much there is for one day?
familySupport.noEnglishRequired: Family discussion can happen in any language; the student can practice explaining one idea in English afterward.

connections.speak: Explain aloud how Sam's 24 pages in 4 days became 6 pages per day.
connections.listen: Listen to a talk about ratios and rates and find the unit rate.

lessons.title: Below Zero: Negative Numbers on a Thermometer
lessons.summary: A class tracks winter temperatures and uses a number line to compare numbers above and below zero.
lessons.subject: Math (integers)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how negative numbers are ordered on a number line.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain that negative numbers are below zero and that farther below zero means smaller.
objectives.language: Use colder than, warmer than and below zero to compare numbers.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can numbers show amounts that are less than zero?
beforeReading.background: Think about a very cold day. How could a number show how cold it is?
beforeReading.hook: A thermometer can show a number with a minus sign. What does it mean?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what negative numbers mean and how to put them in order.

vocabulary.definition: a number that is less than zero
vocabulary.example: Negative four is a negative number.

vocabulary.definition: a number that is greater than zero
vocabulary.example: Three degrees is a positive number.

vocabulary.definition: a tool that measures temperature
vocabulary.example: Lena read the thermometer outside her window.

vocabulary.definition: a unit for measuring temperature
vocabulary.example: Water freezes at zero degrees Celsius.

paragraphs.text: On a cold winter morning, Lena looked at the thermometer outside her window. It showed -4 degrees Celsius. The number was below zero, so it has a negative sign. Zero degrees is the point where water freezes.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did Lena's thermometer show?

paragraphs.text: A thermometer is like a vertical number line. Numbers above zero are positive. Numbers below zero are negative. The farther below zero a number is, the colder it is. So -8 degrees is colder than -4 degrees.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How is a thermometer like a number line?

paragraphs.text: Lena's class recorded the morning temperature for four days. On Monday it was 3 degrees. On Tuesday it was 0 degrees. On Wednesday it was -2 degrees, and on Thursday it was -5 degrees. The class used the number line to put the numbers in order. The coldest day was Thursday. The warmest day was Monday.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did the class put the temperatures in order?

paragraphs.text: The class also found how much the temperature changed. From Tuesday at 0 to Wednesday at -2, the temperature went down 2 degrees. From Wednesday at -2 to Thursday at -5, it went down 3 degrees.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did the temperature change?

activities.prompt: What temperature did Lena's thermometer show in paragraph 1?

choices.text: 4 degrees Celsius
choices.why: A plain 4 leaves out the negative sign, so it would mean above zero instead of below zero.

choices.text: -4 degrees Celsius
-8 degrees Celsius
choices.why: Negative eight is the colder example from paragraph 2, not the number on Lena's thermometer.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the thermometer showed -4 degrees Celsius.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, a thermometer is like a “vertical” number line. What does vertical mean?

choices.text: going up and down
going side to side
choices.why: A thermometer does not lie sideways; its numbers rise and fall along a tall tube.

choices.text: going around in a circle
choices.why: A number line is straight, so it does not curve around in a circle.

activities.rationale: A thermometer's numbers go up and down, so a vertical number line goes up and down.

activities.prompt: Sort each temperature as positive, negative, or zero.

items.text: 0 degrees
-5 degrees
7 degrees
3 degrees
-2 degrees

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says numbers above zero are positive and numbers below zero are negative, so zero, which is neither above nor below zero, goes in its own group.

activities.prompt: Put the temperatures in order from coldest to warmest.

items.text: 0 degrees on Tuesday
3 degrees on Monday
-5 degrees on Thursday
-2 degrees on Wednesday

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says Thursday was the coldest day and Monday was the warmest, and the number line puts -5, -2, 0 and 3 in that order.

activities.prompt: Why is -8 degrees colder than -4 degrees?

choices.text: It is closer to zero on the number line, so it is colder.
choices.why: A number that is closer to zero is warmer, not colder, when both numbers are below zero.

choices.text: It is farther below zero on the number line.
It has more degrees of heat above the freezing point.
choices.why: Heat above freezing belongs to positive numbers, and both of these numbers are below zero.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the farther below zero a number is, the colder it is.

activities.prompt: How does paragraph 3 use the idea from paragraph 2?

choices.text: It uses the number line to put four temperatures in order.
It compares thermometers with other kinds of measuring tools.
choices.why: The paragraph is about Lena's class and its temperatures, not about other measuring tools.

choices.text: It explains why water freezes at zero degrees Celsius.
choices.why: The freezing point is mentioned in paragraph 1, and paragraph 3 does not explain it.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says the class used the number line to put the temperatures in order.

activities.prompt: A student says that -2 degrees is warmer than -5 degrees. Is the student right? Explain using the number line.
lookFor: States that the student is right
Says -2 is closer to zero or farther above -5
Uses evidence such as Wednesday and Thursday from the text
rubric: Uses the number line idea correctly
Connects the idea to the days in the text
activities.frame: The student is ___ because -2 is ___ to zero than -5. On the number line, ___ is farther below zero.
activities.model: The student is right because -2 is closer to zero than -5. On the number line, -5 is farther below zero, and Thursday at -5 degrees was colder than Wednesday at -2 degrees.

activities.prompt: On a mountain, the temperature was 2 degrees in the afternoon and -6 degrees at night. Explain which temperature is colder and how far the temperature went down.
lookFor: States that -6 degrees is colder
Says -6 is farther below zero
Finds a drop of 8 degrees
activities.frame: The colder temperature is ___ because ___. The temperature went down ___ degrees.

lessons.transferPrompt: On a mountain, the temperature was 2 degrees in the afternoon and -6 degrees at night. Explain which temperature is colder and how far the temperature went down.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Explain that negative numbers are below zero and that farther below zero means smaller.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use colder than, warmer than and below zero to compare numbers.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Draw a vertical number line from 8 down to -8 on the board. Mark the four temperatures from paragraph 3 and ask students to read them from top to bottom.
discussion: What does the negative sign tell us about a number?
Why is -5 colder than -2 even though 5 is greater than 2?
Where else do we use numbers below zero, such as money owed or floors below ground?

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: What causes the seasons to change?
beforeReading.background: Think about how the weather changes through the year where you live.
beforeReading.hook: When students in Chicago wear winter coats, students in Chile can be at the beach.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what really causes the seasons.

vocabulary.definition: one of the four parts of the year, such as summer or winter
vocabulary.example: Winter is the coldest season in the north.

vocabulary.definition: the imaginary line that Earth spins around
vocabulary.example: Earth's axis goes through the North and South Poles.

vocabulary.definition: to lean to one side

vocabulary.definition: to travel in a path around something

paragraphs.text: Many people think summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun. That idea is not correct. In fact, Earth is a little closer to the Sun in January, when it is winter in the northern half of the world.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What wrong idea does the writer correct?

paragraphs.text: Seasons happen because Earth is tilted. Earth's axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. The axis leans about 23.5 degrees. As Earth orbits the Sun, which takes one year, the axis keeps pointing the same way in space.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What causes the seasons?

paragraphs.text: When the northern half of Earth leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly, and the days are longer. This makes the northern half warmer, so it is summer there. At the same time, the southern half leans away from the Sun, so it is winter there.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happens when the north leans toward the Sun?

paragraphs.text: Six months later, Earth is on the other side of the Sun. Now the southern half leans toward the Sun. It has summer, and the north has winter. So when students in Chicago wear winter coats in January, students in Santiago, Chile are enjoying summer.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happens six months later?

lessons.title: Favorite Pets: Reading a Bar Graph

objectives.content: Read a bar graph and its data table to compare amounts and check a total.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can a picture of data help us compare groups?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time your class voted on something.
beforeReading.hook: Twenty-four students voted for a favorite pet. Which pet won?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how a bar graph shows data and how to use it.

vocabulary.definition: a graph that uses bars to show amounts
vocabulary.example: The bar graph shows how many students chose each pet.

vocabulary.definition: to look at how things are alike and different
vocabulary.example: The class used the bars to compare the votes.

vocabulary.definition: the amount you get when you add everything together
vocabulary.example: The total number of votes is 24.

vocabulary.definition: a choice that a person makes in a group
vocabulary.example: Each student made one vote.

paragraphs.text: Mr. Silva's class voted for their favorite kind of pet, and each of the 24 students voted only once. Mr. Silva wrote the votes in the table. Then he drew a bar graph so that the whole class could see the results at the same time.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did Mr. Silva do with the votes?

paragraphs.text: A bar graph uses bars to show amounts, and each bar stands for one kind of pet. The taller the bar, the more votes it shows. The bar for dogs goes up to 9, because 9 students chose dogs, and the bar for fish goes up to 5.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do the bars show the votes?

paragraphs.text: The class used the bars to compare the pets. Dogs got the most votes, and birds got the fewest votes. Dogs got 5 more votes than birds, because 9 minus 4 is 5. Cats got 6 votes, so cats came in second place.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did the class find by comparing the bars?

paragraphs.text: A bar graph also helps us check a total. When we add all of the bars, 9 plus 6 plus 5 plus 4 is 24. That number matches the number of students in the class, so everyone knows that every vote was counted.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why did the class add the bars?

table.description: A table of votes from 24 students. Dogs got 9 votes, cats got 6, fish got 5 and birds got 4.

activities.prompt: How many students chose fish?

choices.text: 6 students
choices.why: Six is the number of votes for cats, which is the pet in second place.

choices.text: 4 students
choices.why: Four is the number of votes for birds, which got the fewest votes.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the bar for fish goes up to 5, and the table also shows 5 votes for fish.

activities.rationale: The class looked at the bars to see which pet had more votes and which had fewer, so compare means to see how they are the same or different.

lessons.title: Two Ways to Find the Area of an L-Shaped Room
lessons.summary: Two students find the area of an L-shaped living room by adding rectangles and by subtracting a missing corner.
lessons.subject: Math (area and composite figures)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain two different methods for solving one problem.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how to find the area of an L-shaped figure by adding or subtracting rectangles.
objectives.language: Use first, next, then and but to compare two methods.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can we find the area of a shape that is not a rectangle?
beforeReading.background: Think about a room or a table that is not a simple rectangle.
beforeReading.hook: The room is shaped like the letter L, so length times width will not work by itself.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out two ways to find the area of an L-shaped room.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of flat space inside a shape
vocabulary.example: The area of the floor is 52 square meters.

vocabulary.definition: a shape with four sides and four square corners
vocabulary.example: The room can be cut into two rectangles.

vocabulary.definition: a unit for area; a square that is 1 meter on each side
vocabulary.example: The flooring covers 2 square meters in each box.

vocabulary.definition: to take one amount away from another
vocabulary.example: Eli will subtract the missing corner from the big square.

paragraphs.text: Dani's family is planning to put new flooring in their living room. Because the room is shaped like the letter L, Dani cannot simply multiply one length by one width, so she must find the area in a different way. Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape, and it is measured in square units.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why can Dani not just multiply one length by one width?

paragraphs.text: Dani's first method is to cut the L into two rectangles. The bigger rectangle is 8 meters long and 5 meters wide, so its area is 8 times 5, which is 40 square meters. The smaller rectangle is 4 meters long and 3 meters wide, so its area is 4 times 3, which is 12 square meters. When she adds the two areas, she finds that 40 plus 12 is 52 square meters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is Dani's first method?

paragraphs.text: Dani's brother, Eli, tries a different method. He imagines the L inside a large square that measures 8 meters on each side, and that square has an area of 8 times 8, or 64 square meters. However, the corner that is missing from the L measures 4 meters by 3 meters, so its area is 12 square meters. Eli subtracts the missing corner from the square, and 64 minus 12 is 52 square meters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How is Eli's method different?

paragraphs.text: Both methods give the same answer, which is a good sign, because Dani and Eli have checked each other's work. The flooring comes in boxes that each cover 2 square meters, so the family divides 52 by 2 and discovers that they need 26 boxes.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How many boxes does the family need?

activities.prompt: In Dani's first method, what is the area of the smaller rectangle?

choices.text: 40 square meters
choices.why: Forty square meters is the area of the bigger rectangle, not the smaller one.

choices.text: 7 square meters
choices.why: Seven comes from adding 4 and 3, but area comes from multiplying length by width.

choices.text: 12 square meters

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the smaller rectangle is 4 meters by 3 meters, so its area is 12 square meters.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, Eli “imagines” the L inside a large square. What does imagines mean?

choices.text: builds it out of wooden boards
choices.why: The text does not say Eli builds anything; he is thinking about a square that is not really there.

choices.text: pictures it in his mind
draws it on the living room floor
choices.why: Nothing in the paragraph says Eli draws on the floor; the square is only an idea.

activities.rationale: The large square is not part of the room, so Eli imagines it, which means he pictures it in his mind.

activities.prompt: Put the steps of the problem in the order the text gives them.

items.text: Add the two areas together.
Divide by 2 to find the number of boxes.
Cut the L into two rectangles.
Find the area of each rectangle.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 cuts the L into rectangles, finds each area and adds, and paragraph 4 divides by 2 to find the boxes.

activities.prompt: A different L-shaped room fits inside a square that is 10 meters on each side. The missing corner measures 4 meters by 5 meters. Using Eli's method, what is the area of the room?

choices.text: 120 square meters
choices.why: That adds the area of the missing corner to the square, but Eli's method takes it away.

choices.text: 80 square meters
20 square meters
choices.why: Twenty is the area of the missing corner alone, not the area of the room.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 shows the method: the square is 10 times 10, which is 100, and the corner is 4 times 5, which is 20, so 100 minus 20 is 80.

activities.prompt: Why is it a good sign that Dani and Eli both get 52 square meters?

choices.text: It suggests that the area of 52 square meters is correct.
It shows that every L-shaped room has an area of 52.
choices.why: The answer belongs only to this room; other L-shaped rooms can have different measurements.

choices.text: It proves that adding and subtracting are the same step.
choices.why: Adding and subtracting are different operations, and the two methods use them in different places.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says Dani and Eli checked each other's work, because two different methods reached the same area.

activities.prompt: Why does the author describe two different methods for the same room?

choices.text: To explain why one method is correct and the other is wrong.
choices.why: Both methods give 52 square meters, so neither one is wrong.

choices.text: To prove that Eli is better at math than his sister Dani.
choices.why: The text does not compare the two students' skill; it treats their work as equal.

choices.text: To show that one problem can be solved in more than one way.

activities.rationale: Paragraphs 2 and 3 show two methods that both give 52 square meters, and paragraph 4 says they checked each other.

lookFor: Multiplies 6 by 4 to get 24
Multiplies 2 by 3 to get 6
Adds to get 30 square meters

lessons.title: Solving an Equation Like a Balanced Scale
lessons.summary: A balanced scale with marbles shows why you must do the same thing to both sides of an equation.
lessons.subject: Math (equations)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain the steps for solving an equation and why they work.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain that an equation stays balanced when the same operation is done to both sides.
objectives.language: Use first, next, so and because to explain a procedure.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why must we do the same thing to both sides of an equation?
beforeReading.background: Think about a seesaw or a scale. What happens if one side gets heavier?
beforeReading.hook: A bag of marbles hides a secret number. How can a balanced scale help us find it?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how to solve an equation and how to check the answer.

vocabulary.definition: a math sentence that says two amounts are equal
vocabulary.example: The equation x + 3 = 11 describes the scale.

vocabulary.definition: a letter that stands for a number we do not know
vocabulary.example: The variable x stands for the marbles in the bag.

vocabulary.definition: having equal amounts on both sides
vocabulary.example: The scale is balanced, so both sides are equal.

vocabulary.definition: to test an answer to see if it is correct
vocabulary.example: We check the answer by putting 8 in place of x.

paragraphs.text: An equation is a math sentence that says two amounts are equal. You can think of an equation as a balanced scale, because the amount on the left side has the same value as the amount on the right side. Letters called variables stand for numbers that we do not know yet.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is an equation?

paragraphs.text: Imagine a scale with a bag on the left pan. The bag holds an unknown number of marbles, and we call that number x. Next to the bag are 3 loose marbles, and on the right pan are 11 marbles. Because the scale is balanced, we can write the equation x + 3 = 11.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the scale show?

paragraphs.text: To find x, we need to get the bag by itself, so we remove 3 marbles from the left pan. Now the scale would tip, so we must remove 3 marbles from the right pan too. That leaves x on one side and 8 on the other side. Therefore x = 8, which means the bag holds 8 marbles.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do we find x?

paragraphs.text: This is the key rule: whatever you do to one side of an equation, you must also do to the other side. The rule works for multiplication and division as well. Suppose 3 bags of the same size balance 18 marbles, which we write as 3x = 18. If we divide both sides by 3, then x = 6, so each bag holds 6 marbles.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the key rule?

paragraphs.text: Finally, we check the answer. In the first equation, we put 8 in place of x and get 8 + 3 = 11. That is true, so the answer is correct.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do we check an answer?

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, how many marbles are on the right pan?

choices.text: 3 marbles
choices.why: Three is the number of loose marbles on the left pan, next to the bag.

choices.text: 11 marbles
8 marbles
choices.why: Eight is the answer for the bag, which is found later in paragraph 3.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says that 11 marbles are on the right pan.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 1, “variables” stand for numbers “we do not know yet.” What is a variable?

choices.text: a letter that stands for an unknown number
a number that changes from day to day
choices.why: A variable does not change by the day; it stands for one number we have not found yet.

choices.text: a sign that shows two amounts are equal
choices.why: The equal sign is the symbol that shows equal amounts, and a variable is a letter.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says letters called variables stand for numbers that we do not know yet.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for solving x + 3 = 11 in the order the text gives them.

items.text: Read the value of x, which is 8.
Put 8 in place of x to check the answer.
Write an equation that matches the balanced scale.
Take 3 away from both sides.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 writes the equation, paragraph 3 removes 3 from both sides and reads x, and paragraph 5 checks the answer.

activities.prompt: A bag and 5 loose marbles balance 12 marbles, so x + 5 = 12. What is x?

choices.text: 7 marbles
17 marbles
choices.why: That adds 5 to 12, but the text says to remove the loose marbles from both sides.

choices.text: 60 marbles
choices.why: That multiplies 5 by 12, but nothing in the equation tells you to multiply.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 shows how to remove the loose marbles from both sides, and 12 minus 5 is 7.

activities.prompt: Why must 3 marbles also be removed from the right pan in paragraph 3?

choices.text: The right pan is heavier than the left pan at the start.
choices.why: The scale starts out balanced, so neither pan is heavier at the beginning.

choices.text: The rule says to take marbles only from the larger side.
choices.why: Paragraph 4 says to do the same thing to both sides, not to the larger side only.

choices.text: Removing marbles from one side only would make the scale tip.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says that removing 3 from the left alone would tip the scale, so the same amount must come off the right.

activities.prompt: How does paragraph 5 fit with the rest of the text?

choices.text: It starts a new problem that has a different variable.
choices.why: Paragraph 5 uses the same equation, x + 3 = 11, and the same variable, x.

choices.text: It repeats the key rule from paragraph 4 in new words.
choices.why: The key rule is in paragraph 4, and paragraph 5 does something different with it.

choices.text: It shows how to test the answer found in the earlier steps.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 puts 8 in place of x in the first equation to see that 8 + 3 equals 11.

activities.model: I divide both sides by 4. Then x = 5. To check, I put 5 in place of x, and 4 times 5 is 20, so the answer is correct.

objectives.content: Explain how reflecting, absorbing and trapping heat make a solar oven work, and use data as evidence.
objectives.language: Use because, so that and compared with to explain a design and its data.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can sunlight be used to heat food?
beforeReading.background: Think about how hot a car can get when it sits in the sun.
beforeReading.hook: A cardboard box can warm food with no electricity and no fire. How?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how each part of a solar oven works and what the test showed.

vocabulary.definition: to bounce light back instead of letting it pass through
vocabulary.example: Shiny foil reflects sunlight into the box.

vocabulary.definition: to take in light or heat
vocabulary.example: Black paper absorbs light and changes it to heat.

vocabulary.definition: to keep something from escaping
vocabulary.example: Plastic wrap traps warm air inside the box.

vocabulary.definition: coming from the Sun
vocabulary.example: A solar oven uses energy from the Sun.

paragraphs.text: A solar oven cooks food using only energy from the Sun. A group of students built one from a pizza box. Their goal was to warm a snack without using electricity or fire.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What was the students' goal?

paragraphs.text: The students cut a flap in the lid and covered the inside of the flap with aluminum foil. Foil is shiny, so it reflects sunlight. They propped the flap open so the foil bounced extra light into the box. Inside the box, they taped a sheet of black paper to the bottom. Dark colors absorb light and change it into heat.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do the foil and the black paper do?

paragraphs.text: Next, the students covered the opening with clear plastic wrap. The wrap lets sunlight in, but it traps warm air inside, like the windows of a car on a sunny day. Without the plastic, the warm air would blow away.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the plastic wrap do?

paragraphs.text: To test the design, the students set the oven in the sun with a thermometer inside. The air started at 22 degrees Celsius. After one hour, it measured 68 degrees. They also tested a second box that had no foil flap. In the same hour, that box reached only 54 degrees. The foil oven was 14 degrees warmer.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did the test show?

paragraphs.text: The data supported the students' idea that reflecting more light makes the oven hotter. Still, they wondered what else they could change. A bigger flap or a darker bottom might raise the temperature even more, but they would have to test one change at a time.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did the students want to do next?

activities.prompt: What was the air temperature inside the foil oven after one hour?

choices.text: 68 degrees Celsius
22 degrees Celsius
choices.why: Twenty-two degrees is where the air started, before the oven sat in the sun for an hour.

choices.text: 54 degrees Celsius
choices.why: Fifty-four degrees is the temperature of the box with no foil flap, not the foil oven.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says that after one hour the air in the foil oven measured 68 degrees.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, foil “reflects” sunlight. What does reflects mean?

choices.text: soaks the light inside itself
choices.why: Soaking light in is what the black paper does, which the text calls absorbing.

choices.text: bounces the light back
turns the light into sound
choices.why: Nothing in the text says light becomes sound; the foil sends the light somewhere else.

activities.rationale: The foil is shiny and bounces extra light into the box, so reflects means bounces the light back.

activities.prompt: Sort each part of the oven by the job it does.

A dark surface that turns light into heat
A cover that keeps warm air from blowing away

choices.text: 22 degrees

choices.text: 14 degrees

It describes how the students built the pizza box oven.

lessons.title: Mean or Median? Two Bike Shops Compared
lessons.summary: A shopper compares used-bike prices at two shops and learns when an outlier makes the median a better measure of center than the mean.
lessons.subject: Math (statistics)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Compare two measures of center and justify a choice with evidence.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how an outlier affects the mean and the median and choose the better measure of center.
objectives.language: Use because, however and whereas to justify a choice with data.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How do we choose the best number to describe a whole data set?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time one very high or very low number changed an average.
beforeReading.hook: One expensive bike can change a shop's average price, but does it change the typical price?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how the mean and the median respond to an outlier.

vocabulary.definition: the sum of the values divided by the number of values
vocabulary.example: The mean price at Corner Bikes is $200.

vocabulary.definition: the middle value when the data are in order
vocabulary.example: The median price at Corner Bikes is $140.

vocabulary.definition: a value that is far away from the other values
vocabulary.example: The $460 bike is an outlier.

vocabulary.definition: the highest value minus the lowest value
vocabulary.example: The range at Park Cycles is $40.

vocabulary.definition: one number that describes the middle or typical value of a data set
vocabulary.example: The mean and the median are measures of center.

paragraphs.text: Two bike shops, Corner Bikes and Park Cycles, each have five used bicycles for sale. A shopper named Priya wants to compare their prices, so she calculates two measures of center, the mean and the median. A measure of center is a single number that describes the middle or typical value of a data set.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Priya want to compare?

paragraphs.text: The mean is the sum of all the values divided by the number of values. At Corner Bikes, the five prices add up to $1,000, and when 1,000 is divided by 5, the mean is $200. The median is the middle value after the data have been arranged in order, and at Corner Bikes the middle price is $140. Although both numbers are supposed to describe the center, they disagree by $60.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How are the mean and the median found?

paragraphs.text: To understand the disagreement, Priya examines the data more carefully. One bicycle at Corner Bikes costs $460, which is much higher than every other price in the shop. A value that is far away from the rest of the data is called an outlier. An outlier pulls the mean upward, because the mean depends on every value in the data set, whereas the median depends only on the middle position. For this shop, the median of $140 describes a typical bicycle better than the mean of $200 does, since four of the five bicycles cost $150 or less.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why do the mean and the median differ at Corner Bikes?

paragraphs.text: Park Cycles has no outlier. Its prices are $160, $170, $180, $190 and $200, so the mean and the median are both $180. When the data are spread evenly in this way, either measure describes the center well. Priya also considers the range, which is the highest price minus the lowest price. The range at Park Cycles is only $40, while the range at Corner Bikes is $340, which means the prices at Park Cycles are much closer together.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How is Park Cycles different?

paragraphs.text: Priya concludes that a single number never tells the whole story about a data set. She will use the median to describe the typical price, the range to describe how much the prices vary, and the mean only when no outlier is present.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Priya decide?

activities.rationale: The outlier is a very high price, so it moves the mean toward a higher value, which makes the mean $200 instead of $140.

activities.prompt: Suppose Corner Bikes sells the $460 bike. The other four prices are $120, $130, $140 and $150. What is the new mean?

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives the method: 120 + 130 + 140 + 150 is 540, and 540 divided by 4 is $135.

lessons.title: Is the Spinner Fair? Probability and Equal Chances
lessons.summary: Two friends use probability to find out why their spinner game is unfair and how to change the rules.
lessons.subject: Math (probability)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain why a game is fair or unfair using probability.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain that probability compares favorable outcomes with all equally likely outcomes, and that a fair game gives equal chances.
objectives.language: Use because, so and out of to explain probability.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can numbers tell us whether a game is fair?
beforeReading.background: Think about a game of chance, such as a spinner or a number cube.
beforeReading.hook: One player has 3 chances out of 8 and the other has 5 chances out of 8. Is that fair?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how probability shows whether a game is fair.

vocabulary.definition: a number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is
vocabulary.example: The probability of landing on red is 3/8.

vocabulary.definition: something that may or may not happen
vocabulary.example: Landing on blue is an event.

vocabulary.definition: giving every player an equal chance
vocabulary.example: Noor changed the rules to make the game fair.

vocabulary.definition: having the same chance of happening
vocabulary.example: Sections of the same size are equally likely.

paragraphs.text: Probability is a number from 0 to 1 that tells how likely an event is to happen. An event that is impossible has a probability of 0, and an event that is certain has a probability of 1. An event that is just as likely to happen as not to happen has a probability of 1/2.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does probability tell us?

paragraphs.text: Noor and Ben are playing a game with a spinner. The spinner has 8 sections that are all the same size. Three sections are red, two are blue, two are green, and one is yellow. Because every section is equally likely, the probability of landing on red is 3/8.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the probability of landing on red?

paragraphs.text: At first, Noor scores a point when the spinner lands on red, and Ben scores a point when it lands on any other color. Ben has 5 sections out of 8, so his probability is 5/8, while Noor has only 3/8. The game is not fair, because the two players do not have equal chances of winning.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why is the first game not fair?

paragraphs.text: Noor decides to change the rules. Now she scores on red or yellow, which covers 4 sections, and Ben scores on blue or green, which also covers 4 sections. Each player now has a probability of 4/8, or 1/2, so the game is fair.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does Noor make the game fair?

paragraphs.text: To test the new rules, they spin the spinner 40 times. Noor's colors come up 18 times, and Ben's colors come up 22 times. These results are not exactly equal, but that is normal. Experimental results usually come close to the theoretical probability, and the more times they spin, the closer the results tend to get.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are the results from 40 spins not exactly equal?

activities.prompt: How many sections of the spinner are blue or green?

choices.why: Two is the number of blue sections alone, so it leaves out the green sections.

choices.text: 5 sections
choices.why: Five is the number of sections that Ben had in the first game, which are not red.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says two sections are blue and two are green, and paragraph 4 says blue or green covers 4 sections.

choices.why: Results can come out even by luck, but the text judges the game by the sections on the spinner, not by the results.

choices.why: Both players follow the rules in paragraph 3, yet the game is still called not fair.

lessons.title: Finding Points on a Park Map: The Coordinate Plane
lessons.summary: A park map on a coordinate plane shows how to plot ordered pairs, name quadrants and find distances.
lessons.subject: Math (the coordinate plane)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how to plot a point and name its location.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how an ordered pair locates a point, which quadrant it is in and how to find a distance between points.
objectives.language: Use first, then, left, right, up and down to give directions.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can two numbers tell us exactly where something is?
beforeReading.background: Think about a map with letters and numbers on the edges.
beforeReading.hook: Two numbers can name any spot in a park. How does that work?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how to plot points on a coordinate plane and name their quadrants.

vocabulary.definition: a flat grid made by a horizontal and a vertical number line
vocabulary.example: The park map is drawn on a coordinate plane.

vocabulary.definition: the point (0, 0) where the two axes meet
vocabulary.example: Every plotted point starts from the origin.

vocabulary.definition: two numbers in order that name a point, such as (3, 2)
vocabulary.example: The ordered pair (3, 2) names the playground.

vocabulary.definition: one of the four sections of a coordinate plane
vocabulary.example: The pond is in Quadrant II.

vocabulary.definition: the horizontal or vertical number line of a coordinate plane
vocabulary.example: The x-axis is the horizontal axis.

paragraphs.text: A coordinate plane is a flat grid formed by two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is called the x-axis, and the vertical line is called the y-axis. They meet at a point called the origin, which is written (0, 0), and the axes divide the plane into four sections called quadrants.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is a coordinate plane?

paragraphs.text: Every point on the plane has an ordered pair, such as (3, 2), and the order of the two numbers matters. The first number tells how far to move left or right from the origin, and the second number tells how far to move up or down. To plot (3, 2), start at the origin, move 3 units to the right, and then move 2 units up.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do you plot an ordered pair?

paragraphs.text: Negative numbers tell us to move in the opposite direction. A negative x-coordinate means left, and a negative y-coordinate means down. Imagine a park map in which the playground is at (3, 2), the pond is at (-4, 1), the picnic area is at (-2, -3), and the bike rack is at (5, -1).
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do negative coordinates mean?

paragraphs.text: The signs of the coordinates tell us which quadrant a point is in. The playground has two positive numbers, so it is in Quadrant I, at the top right. The pond has a negative x and a positive y, so it is in Quadrant II, at the top left. The picnic area has two negative numbers, so it is in Quadrant III, at the bottom left, and the bike rack is in Quadrant IV, at the bottom right.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do the signs tell us the quadrant?

paragraphs.text: Points that share one coordinate are easy to compare. The fountain is at (3, -4), directly below the playground, and both points have an x-coordinate of 3. To find the distance, count the vertical units: 2 units down to the x-axis plus 4 more units gives 6 units. If each unit stands for 50 meters, the fountain is 300 meters from the playground.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How far is the fountain from the playground?

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, what does the first number in an ordered pair tell you?

choices.text: how far to move up or down
choices.why: Moving up or down is told by the second number, not by the first number.

choices.text: which quadrant the point is in
choices.why: The quadrant depends on the signs of both numbers, and the first number alone does not name it.

choices.text: how far to move left or right

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the first number tells how far to move left or right from the origin.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 1, the axes cross at “right angles.” What does that mean?

choices.text: They meet only at the top of the grid.
choices.why: The axes meet at the origin, which is in the middle of the grid and not at the top.

choices.text: They run beside each other and never meet.
choices.why: Lines that never meet would not cross at the origin, but paragraph 1 says the axes meet there.

choices.text: They meet and form square corners.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the axes cross and meet at the origin, and a right angle is a square corner.

(2, 3) and (3, 2) are always in two different quadrants.

lessons.title: How Much Water Fills the Tank? Volume of a Prism
lessons.summary: A class finds the volume of a fish tank, changes cubic centimeters to liters and thinks about water height.
lessons.subject: Math (volume)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how to find volume and why the units are cubic.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how to find the volume of a rectangular prism by multiplying base area by height and how to convert units.
objectives.language: Use first, then, because and so to explain a calculation.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How do we measure the space inside an object?
beforeReading.background: Think about how much water a bucket or a bathtub can hold.
beforeReading.hook: A tank is 50 centimeters long. How can the class know how much water it holds?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how to calculate the volume of a tank and what the units mean.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of space inside a three-dimensional shape
vocabulary.example: The volume of the tank is 60,000 cubic centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: a solid shape with six rectangular faces
vocabulary.example: The fish tank is a rectangular prism.

vocabulary.definition: a unit for volume; a cube that is 1 centimeter on every edge
vocabulary.example: The tank holds 60,000 cubic centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: a unit for liquids that equals 1,000 cubic centimeters
vocabulary.example: The tank holds 60 liters of water.

paragraphs.text: Volume is the amount of space inside a three-dimensional shape. Ms. Torres's class wants to buy a fish tank shaped like a rectangular prism, and before they buy it, they need to know how much water it can hold.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the class want to know?

paragraphs.text: The tank is 50 centimeters long, 30 centimeters wide, and 40 centimeters tall. To find the volume of a rectangular prism, multiply the length by the width by the height. First, the class multiplies 50 by 30 to get the area of the base, which is 1,500 square centimeters. Then they multiply 1,500 by the height of 40, and the volume is 60,000 cubic centimeters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the class find the volume?

paragraphs.text: Volume is measured in cubic units because it counts cubes. One cubic centimeter is a cube that is 1 centimeter long on every edge, so the tank holds 60,000 of these small cubes. That number is hard to picture, so the class converts it to liters. One liter of water takes up 1,000 cubic centimeters, and 60,000 divided by 1,000 gives 60 liters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are the units cubic?

paragraphs.text: However, a fish tank is never filled to the very top. The class decides to fill the water to a height of 30 centimeters, so the water forms a smaller prism. It has the same base of 1,500 square centimeters but a height of only 30 centimeters, so its volume is 1,500 times 30, which is 45,000 cubic centimeters, or 45 liters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How much water will the class use?

paragraphs.text: Ms. Torres reminds the students that the height of the water matters, not just the height of the tank. If the water level were 10 centimeters lower, the volume would drop by 1,500 times 10, or 15,000 cubic centimeters, which is 15 liters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why does the height of the water matter?

activities.prompt: What is the volume of the whole tank?

choices.text: 45,000 cubic centimeters
choices.why: Forty-five thousand is the volume of the water when it only reaches 30 centimeters, not the whole tank.

choices.text: 1,500 cubic centimeters
choices.why: Fifteen hundred is the area of the base in square centimeters, so it is not a volume.

choices.text: 60,000 cubic centimeters

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the volume of the tank is 60,000 cubic centimeters.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, the class “converts” the volume to liters. What does converts mean?

choices.text: makes the number much larger
choices.why: The number becomes smaller, 60 instead of 60,000, so converting is not about making it bigger.

choices.text: changes it into a different unit
checks it against a second tank
choices.why: The class does not use a second tank; it writes the same volume in a unit that is easier to picture.

activities.rationale: The class writes 60,000 cubic centimeters as 60 liters, so converts means changes it into a different unit.

activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding the volume of the tank in the order the text gives them.

items.text: Write the answer in cubic units.
Divide by 1,000 to change cubic centimeters to liters.
Multiply the length by the width to get the base area.
Multiply the base area by the height.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 multiplies length by width and then by height, and paragraph 3 gives cubic units and divides by 1,000 to find liters.

choices.why: That adds the three measurements, but paragraph 2 says to multiply them.

choices.text: 30,000 cubic centimeters
1,000 cubic centimeters

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives the method: 40 times 25 is 1,000, and 1,000 times 30 is 30,000 cubic centimeters.

activities.prompt: Why does the class use a height of 30 centimeters in paragraph 4 instead of 40?

choices.why: Paragraph 2 says the tank is 40 centimeters tall, so 30 centimeters is not the height of the tank.

choices.text: Adding water makes the base of the tank smaller than it was.
choices.why: The base of the tank stays the same, 1,500 square centimeters, no matter how much water is added.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 begins by saying a fish tank is never filled to the very top, so the water forms a smaller prism with a height of 30 centimeters.

choices.text: a switch to a unit that replaces the liter

lessons.summary: A table of percentages shows how one city's electricity changed over five years, and the text explains shares, percentage points and energy sources.

objectives.content: Describe how a city's energy sources changed using percent shares from a table, and explain the difference between a share and an amount.
objectives.language: Use increased, decreased and percentage points to describe change.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can data show a change in the way we make energy?
beforeReading.background: Think about where the electricity at your school comes from.
beforeReading.hook: In five years, one city's coal use dropped from 32 percent to 10 percent. What replaced it?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how the sources of Riverton's electricity changed and how to read the data.

vocabulary.definition: able to be supplied again and again by nature
vocabulary.example: Sunlight and wind are renewable sources of energy.

vocabulary.definition: a fuel such as coal or natural gas that formed from ancient living things
vocabulary.example: Coal is a fossil fuel.

vocabulary.definition: one unit of difference between two percents
vocabulary.example: Coal fell by 22 percentage points.

vocabulary.definition: the part of a whole that one thing makes up
vocabulary.example: Solar's share of the electricity was 22 percent.

vocabulary.definition: the place or thing that something comes from
vocabulary.example: Wind is a source of electricity.

paragraphs.text: Every light, phone charger and refrigerator in the city of Riverton runs on electricity, but that electricity is made in different ways. The table shows how much of Riverton's electricity came from each source five years ago and this year. Each column adds up to 100 percent.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the table show?

paragraphs.text: Sources of electricity fall into two groups. Fossil fuels, such as coal and natural gas, are burned to make electricity, and burning them releases carbon dioxide, which traps heat in the atmosphere. Renewable sources, such as sunlight, wind and moving water, are replaced naturally and do not release carbon dioxide while making electricity.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What are the two groups of sources?

paragraphs.text: The table shows a big shift. Five years ago, coal and natural gas together supplied 72 percent of Riverton's electricity, but this year they supply 48 percent. Over the same period, renewable sources grew from 28 percent to 52 percent, which is an increase of 24 percentage points. Renewable sources now supply more than half of the city's electricity.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did the two groups change?

paragraphs.text: Coal changed the most, falling from 32 percent to 10 percent, a drop of 22 percentage points. Solar power grew the most, rising from 8 percent to 22 percent, an increase of 14 percentage points. Wind rose by 6 points and hydropower rose by 4 points, while natural gas fell by only 2 points.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Which sources changed the most?

paragraphs.text: Percentages describe shares, not amounts. Suppose Riverton used 500 million kilowatt-hours of electricity this year. Solar's share of 22 percent means 0.22 times 500, or 110 million kilowatt-hours. Because a share is a percent of a total, readers should always ask whether the total itself has also changed.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the difference between a share and an amount?

lessons.title: How Much Paper Wraps the Box? Surface Area

objectives.content: Explain how to find surface area by adding the areas of all faces and how it differs from volume.
objectives.language: Use first, next, finally, whereas and in contrast to explain a procedure and compare ideas.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How do we measure the outside of a three-dimensional shape?
beforeReading.background: Think about wrapping a present. How do you know how much paper to use?
beforeReading.hook: A box has six faces. How much paper does it take to cover all of them?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how to find surface area and how it differs from volume.

vocabulary.definition: the total area of all the faces of a three-dimensional shape
vocabulary.example: The surface area of Hana's box is 392 square centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: a flat surface of a solid shape
vocabulary.example: A rectangular prism has six faces.

vocabulary.definition: a flat pattern that folds into a three-dimensional shape
vocabulary.example: Hana drew a net of the box.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of space inside a three-dimensional shape
vocabulary.example: The volume of the box is 480 cubic centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: a solid shape with six rectangular faces
vocabulary.example: The gift box is a rectangular prism.

paragraphs.text: Hana wants to wrap a gift in a box that is 12 centimeters long, 8 centimeters wide, and 5 centimeters tall. Before she cuts the wrapping paper, she needs to know the surface area of the box. Surface area is the total area of all the faces of a three-dimensional shape.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Hana need to know first?

paragraphs.text: A rectangular prism has six faces, and they come in three pairs of matching rectangles. The top and bottom are each 12 by 8, so each has an area of 96 square centimeters. The front and back are each 12 by 5, so each has an area of 60 square centimeters. The two sides are each 8 by 5, so each has an area of 40 square centimeters.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What are the faces of the box?

paragraphs.text: Hana adds the areas of all six faces, and 96 + 96 + 60 + 60 + 40 + 40 equals 392. The surface area is 392 square centimeters. She can also use a shorter way by doubling the area of each pair of faces: 2 times 96 plus 2 times 60 plus 2 times 40 gives 192 plus 120 plus 80, which is also 392.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does Hana find the surface area?

paragraphs.text: Many students confuse surface area with volume. Surface area measures the outside of the box in square units, because it covers flat faces. Volume measures the space inside the box in cubic units. Hana's box has a volume of 12 times 8 times 5, which is 480 cubic centimeters, but the paper she needs depends on the surface area.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How is surface area different from volume?

paragraphs.text: A net can help. A net is a flat pattern that folds into a three-dimensional shape. If Hana drew the net of her box, she would see all six rectangles laid out, and she could check that no face was left out or counted twice. In real life, she should cut the paper a little larger than 392 square centimeters, because the edges must overlap and fold.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How can a net help Hana?

choices.text: eight faces

activities.rationale: The paragraph then explains that the two measures are different, so confuse means to mix up two different ideas.

lessons.title: How Many Tickets Can We Buy? Inequalities in Real Life
lessons.summary: A class with a budget writes and solves an inequality, then reads the solutions on a number line.
lessons.subject: Math (inequalities)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how to write and solve an inequality for a real situation.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how to write, solve and graph an inequality for a real situation with a limit.
objectives.language: Use at most, at least, fewer than and more than to describe limits.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How do we show a limit with math?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time you had a budget or a maximum number of something.
beforeReading.hook: A class has 120 dollars. How many tickets can it buy?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how an inequality shows a limit and how to solve one.

vocabulary.definition: a math sentence that compares two amounts that may not be equal
vocabulary.example: The inequality 8t + 24 ≤ 120 shows the budget limit.

vocabulary.definition: a number that makes an equation or inequality true
vocabulary.example: The number 12 is a solution of the inequality.

vocabulary.definition: no more than a given amount
vocabulary.example: The class can spend at most 120 dollars.

vocabulary.definition: no less than a given amount
vocabulary.example: At least 15 students must sign up.

vocabulary.definition: staying the same no matter how many items there are
vocabulary.example: The bus costs a fixed 24 dollars.

paragraphs.text: An equation says that two amounts are equal, but many real situations have limits instead. When a problem says that something can be at most, at least, fewer than or more than a certain amount, we use an inequality. The symbols are < for less than, > for greater than, ≤ for less than or equal to, and ≥ for greater than or equal to.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: When do we use an inequality?

paragraphs.text: Ms. Okafor's class has a budget of 120 dollars for a museum trip. The bus costs a fixed 24 dollars, and each ticket costs 8 dollars. The class can spend at most 120 dollars, so the total cost must be less than or equal to 120. If t stands for the number of tickets, the inequality is 8t + 24 ≤ 120.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the class write the problem?

paragraphs.text: To solve it, the class uses the same steps as for an equation. First, they subtract 24 from both sides to get 8t ≤ 96. Then they divide both sides by 8 to get t ≤ 12. This means the class can buy 12 tickets or fewer. Dividing by a positive number does not change the direction of the inequality sign.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the class solve the inequality?

paragraphs.text: A solution of an inequality is any number that makes it true. Many numbers work here: 5, 9 and 12 all make 8t + 24 ≤ 120 true, but 13 does not, because 8 times 13 plus 24 is 128, which is more than 120. Since tickets come in whole numbers and cannot be negative, the real solutions are 0, 1, 2 and so on up to 12.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is a solution of an inequality?

paragraphs.text: On a number line, the solutions to t ≤ 12 are drawn with a closed circle at 12 and an arrow pointing left. The closed circle shows that 12 itself is included. If the inequality were t < 12, the circle would be open, because 12 would not be a solution.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do we graph the solutions?

activities.prompt: What is the fixed cost of the bus in paragraph 2?

choices.text: 8 dollars
choices.why: Eight dollars is the cost of one ticket, which changes with the number of tickets.

choices.text: 24 dollars
120 dollars
choices.why: One hundred twenty dollars is the whole budget for the trip, not the cost of the bus.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the bus costs a fixed 24 dollars.

repaired after it has broken down
choices.why: Nothing in the text says the bus was broken or repaired; fixed describes a price that does not change.

choices.text: picked by the students before the trip
choices.why: The text does not say who chose the price; it says the bus cost is 24 dollars in every case.

lessons.title: Which Soil Helps Bean Plants Grow? A Fair Test
lessons.summary: A science club designs a fair test, uses means to compare plant growth and thinks about the limits of its claim.

lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
