objectives.content: Explain how a fair test controls variables and how mean heights from a table support a claim with limits.
objectives.language: Use because, the data show and might to explain evidence and limits.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can a fair test help us answer a science question?
beforeReading.background: Think about a plant you have seen growing in different places.
beforeReading.hook: Three cups, three kinds of soil, and one question about which plants grow tallest.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how the club made its test fair and what the data show.

vocabulary.definition: something in a test that can change
vocabulary.example: The type of soil was the variable that the club changed.

vocabulary.definition: kept the same on purpose during a test
vocabulary.example: The amount of water was a controlled variable.

vocabulary.definition: a substance that living things need to grow
vocabulary.example: Potting soil contains nutrients that help roots.

vocabulary.definition: the sum of the values divided by the number of values
vocabulary.example: The mean height for potting soil was 12 centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: a careful study that is designed to answer a question
vocabulary.example: The club planned an investigation of soil.

paragraphs.text: Plants need water, light, air and nutrients to grow. A seventh-grade science club wanted to find out whether the type of soil changes how tall bean plants grow. A good scientific investigation changes only one thing at a time, so the club designed a fair test.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question did the club want to answer?

paragraphs.text: The club planted bean seeds in three kinds of soil: potting soil, garden soil and sand. The type of soil was the variable that the club changed on purpose. Everything else stayed the same. Each cup was the same size, held the same amount of soil, received 50 milliliters of water every other day and sat on the same sunny windowsill. Variables that stay the same in a test are called controlled variables.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did the club make the test fair?

paragraphs.text: Each kind of soil had four cups, with one seed in every cup. Using four cups instead of one helped the club avoid being fooled by a single seed that grew badly or unusually well. After 14 days, the club measured the height of every plant in centimeters and found the mean for each kind of soil. The table shows the results.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why did the club use four cups of each soil?

paragraphs.text: The data show a clear pattern. Plants in potting soil had a mean height of 12 centimeters, which is 3 centimeters taller than the mean for garden soil and 9 centimeters taller than the mean for sand. The club's explanation was that potting soil holds water and contains nutrients. Sand drains quickly and holds few nutrients, so roots have less to use.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What pattern do the data show?

paragraphs.text: The club was careful about its claim. The results support the idea that potting soil is best for bean plants in this test, but the club tested only one kind of plant for 14 days. To be more certain, they could repeat the test, add more cups or measure the plants for a longer time.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why was the club careful about its claim?

table.description: A table of bean plant heights after 14 days in three kinds of soil. Potting soil plants measured 11, 12, 13 and 12 centimeters, with a mean of 12. Garden soil plants measured 8, 9, 10 and 9, with a mean of 9. Sand plants measured 2, 3, 4 and 3, with a mean of 3.

objectives.content: Explain how the Nile flood created three farming seasons in ancient Egypt.
objectives.language: Use sequence words and because to describe a yearly cycle.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can a river decide the way people live?
beforeReading.background: Think about a place where the weather or the water changes during the year. How do people there plan their work?
beforeReading.hook: Egypt is mostly desert, yet farmers there fed a great civilization.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how the Nile created three seasons and why the flood had to be the right size.

vocabulary.definition: water that rises and covers land that is usually dry
vocabulary.example: The flood covered the fields every year.

vocabulary.definition: the top layer of earth where plants grow
vocabulary.example: The river left dark, rich soil on the land.

vocabulary.definition: to gather a crop when it is ready

vocabulary.definition: a channel dug to carry water

paragraphs.text: Egypt is mostly desert, but people have farmed there for thousands of years. The reason is the Nile River. Each year the Nile rose and spilled over its banks. When the water went down, it left a layer of dark, rich soil. Egyptians called the farmland the Black Land. They called the dry desert beyond it the Red Land.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why was the Nile important to farmers?

paragraphs.text: Egyptians divided the year into three seasons that followed the river. Akhet was the flood season. Farmers could not plant, so they fixed tools and repaired canals. Peret was the season when the water went down. Farmers plowed the wet soil and planted wheat and barley. Shemu was the harvest season. Farmers cut the grain and stored it.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happened in each of the three seasons?

paragraphs.text: The system worked only when the flood was the right size. If the river rose too little, crops were small and families had less food. If it rose too high, it could wash away homes. So officials measured the river with a tool called a nilometer. The marks on it helped them guess how big the harvest would be.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why did officials measure the river?

lessons.title: Three Branches, Three Jobs
lessons.summary: See how the United States divides power among Congress, the President and the courts, and how each one checks the others.
lessons.subject: Social studies (civics)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain who does which job in a government and why power is shared.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 3 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Describe the three branches of the national government and give one example of a check.
objectives.language: Use because, so and each to explain why power is divided.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do people share power instead of giving it to one person?
beforeReading.background: Think about a group project. What can go wrong if one person makes every decision?
beforeReading.hook: The people who wrote the Constitution did not want any one person to have all the power.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn the job of each branch and how the branches limit one another.

vocabulary.definition: one main part of a larger group
vocabulary.example: Congress is one branch of the government.

vocabulary.definition: a rule that everyone in a country must follow
vocabulary.example: A new law set the speed limit near the school.

vocabulary.definition: to say no to a bill so that it cannot become a law
vocabulary.example: The President can veto a bill.

vocabulary.definition: a fair share of power so no side is too strong
vocabulary.example: Three branches keep a balance of power.

paragraphs.text: The writers of the Constitution had a worry. They did not want one person or one group to hold all the power. So they divided the national government into three parts, called branches. Each branch has its own job, and each one can limit the others.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are there three branches?

paragraphs.text: The legislative branch is Congress. It has two parts, the Senate and the House of Representatives. Members of Congress make the laws. The executive branch carries out the laws. The President leads this branch, with help from the Vice President and many agencies. The judicial branch is made up of courts. Judges decide what laws mean and whether a law follows the Constitution.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does each branch do?

paragraphs.text: The branches check one another. Suppose Congress passes a bill. The President can veto it, which means saying no. Congress can override the veto if two-thirds of its members vote again for the bill. Later, a court can decide that a law does not follow the Constitution. Because of these checks, no branch can act alone, and the power stays in balance.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How do the branches check one another?

rows: Congress: the Senate and the House of Representatives
The President, the Vice President and many agencies
The Supreme Court and other federal courts
table.description: A table with three rows for the legislative, executive and judicial branches. Each row names who is in the branch and its main job.

lessons.title: How the Maya Wrote Numbers with Dots and Bars
lessons.summary: Learn how the Maya used a dot, a bar and a shell to write any number, and how place value works in base 20.
lessons.genre: Informational text with math and a table
lessons.subject: Social studies and math (ancient Maya)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how a number system works and why zero matters.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how the Maya number system uses place value and zero.
objectives.language: Use first, then, so and because to explain a calculation.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can a few symbols write any number?
beforeReading.background: Think about our own numbers. Why does the 2 in 20 mean something different from the 2 in 2?
beforeReading.hook: The ancient Maya wrote every number they needed with only three symbols.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn what each symbol means and how to read a Maya number with two levels.

vocabulary.definition: a mark or picture that stands for something
vocabulary.example: A dot is a symbol for the number 1.

vocabulary.definition: the idea that where a digit sits changes its value
vocabulary.example: In place value, a dot in the top level is worth 20.

vocabulary.definition: a person whose job was to write and keep records
vocabulary.example: A Maya scribe wrote numbers on bark paper.

vocabulary.definition: placed one on top of another
vocabulary.example: The Maya stacked the symbols in levels.

paragraphs.text: The Maya built cities, studied the stars and kept careful calendars in southern Mexico and Central America. To track days and trade goods, their scribes needed a way to write numbers. They invented a system that used only three symbols: a dot, a bar and a shell.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why did the Maya need numbers?

paragraphs.text: A dot stands for 1. A bar stands for 5. A shell shape stands for 0. To write 7, a scribe drew one bar and two dots, because 5 plus 2 equals 7. The symbols were stacked, with the dots above the bars. Three bars and four dots made 19, the largest number that one level could show.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does each symbol mean?

paragraphs.text: To write larger numbers, the Maya stacked levels one above another. The bottom level shows ones. The level above it shows twenties, not tens. So a dot in the second level means 1 times 20, which is 20. A system in which the position of a symbol changes its value is called a place-value system. Our own system works this way too, but ours is built on groups of ten.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the second level show?

paragraphs.text: Here is an example. Suppose the top level has two dots, and the bottom level has one bar and three dots. The top level is worth 2 times 20, which is 40. The bottom level is worth 5 plus 3, which is 8. Add the two levels: 40 plus 8 equals 48.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How is 48 found?

paragraphs.text: The shell mattered because it marked an empty place. Without it, a reader could not tell the difference between 1, one dot alone, and 20, a dot above a shell. The Maya were among the first peoples in history to use a symbol for zero.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why was the shell important?

table.description: A table with six rows that shows how the Maya drew the numbers 0, 1, 5, 7, 13 and 19 with dots, bars and a shell, and how to read each one.

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what does one bar stand for?

choices.why: One dot stands for 1; a bar is worth more than a dot.
Twenty is the value of a dot in the second level, not the value of a bar.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says a dot stands for 1, a bar stands for 5 and a shell stands for 0.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, the symbols were stacked. What does stacked mean?

choices.text: placed one on top of another
spread out in one long line
choices.why: The text says the dots were above the bars, so the symbols were not in one long line.

choices.text: crossed out and written again
choices.why: Nothing in the paragraph says the scribes made mistakes or wrote symbols again.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the dots were above the bars, and paragraph 3 says the levels were stacked one above another.

activities.prompt: Use the table. Which number did the Maya draw with two bars and three dots?

choices.why: Twenty-three would need a dot in the second level; the table row shows only one level.
Eight is one bar and three dots; two bars are worth 10, so the total is larger.

activities.rationale: The row for 13 in the table shows two bars and three dots, which is 10 plus 3.

activities.prompt: A scribe draws one dot in the top level and a shell in the bottom level. Which number is it?

choices.why: One dot alone is 1, but the shell tells you the dot is in the second level, which is worth 20.
Twenty-one would need a dot in the bottom level too; the shell means that level is empty.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says a dot in the second level means 20, and paragraph 5 says the shell marks an empty bottom level.

activities.prompt: Why would a number system need a symbol for zero?

choices.text: to show that a number is too large for a scribe to write
choices.why: Large numbers are written with more levels, so zero is not used to mean a number is too large.

choices.text: to show that a calendar day has ended and a new day begins
choices.why: The shell is part of the number system; the text does not connect it to the end of a day.

choices.text: to show that a place is empty so numbers are not confused

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 says that without the shell, a reader could not tell 1 from 20.

activities.prompt: What is the main job of paragraph 4?

choices.text: It argues that the Maya system is better than ours.
choices.why: The paragraph never compares the two systems; it just finds the value of one number.

choices.text: It describes how scribes learned to write numbers.
choices.why: The paragraph is about a calculation, not about how scribes were taught.

choices.text: It shows a worked example of the idea in paragraph 3.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 begins with Here is an example and uses the two levels explained in paragraph 3 to find 48.

activities.prompt: A Maya number has one dot in the top level and one bar and two dots in the bottom level. Explain how to find its value.

Says the bottom level is 5 plus 2, or 7
Adds the levels to get 27

Finds the value of the bottom level
Adds the two levels and states 27

activities.model: The top level is worth 20 because one dot in the second level means 1 times 20. The bottom level is worth 7 because a bar is 5 and two dots add 2. I add them to get 27.

Says position changes the value of a symbol
Compares our groups of ten with the Maya groups of twenty
rubric: Says the 3 in 30 is worth 30, or three tens
Says position changes the value of a symbol
Compares our groups of ten with the Maya groups of twenty

teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use first, then, so and because to explain a calculation.

teacherGuide.misconception: Students may read the second level as tens. The text says it shows twenties, so one dot there is 20, not 10.

scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 4: one dot in the top level is 20 and a shell in the bottom level adds 0, so the number is 20.
Question 7: 1 times 20 is 20, 5 plus 2 is 7 and 20 plus 7 is 27.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The top dot is worth 20 and the bottom bar and two dots are worth 7, so the number is 27.

lessons.title: A Clerk's Letter from Philadelphia, 1787 (an invented letter)
lessons.summary: Read an invented letter from a young clerk to learn how the delegates solved a big argument about how states would be represented.
lessons.subject: Social studies (United States history)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Retell events from one person's point of view and explain a compromise.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain the compromise that created the House and the Senate.
objectives.language: Use past tense and because to retell a disagreement and its solution.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How do people with different needs reach an agreement?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time when two groups wanted different things. How did you decide?
beforeReading.hook: This letter is invented for this lesson. It is not a real document, but the argument it describes really happened.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what the states argued about and how the delegates solved the problem.

vocabulary.definition: a person chosen to speak and vote for a group
vocabulary.example: Each state sent delegates to Philadelphia.

vocabulary.definition: the number of people who live in a place
vocabulary.example: A state with a large population has many people.

vocabulary.definition: an agreement in which each side gives up something
vocabulary.example: The two sides reached a compromise.

vocabulary.definition: a person whose job is to write, copy and carry papers
vocabulary.example: The clerk carried papers up the stairs.

paragraphs.text: This letter is invented for this lesson. Its writer, Marcus Hale, is a made-up young clerk who helps a delegate in the summer of 1787. Leaders from the states met in Philadelphia that summer to talk about how to improve the nation's government.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Is this letter a real document?

paragraphs.text: Philadelphia, July 30, 1787. Dear Lena, The State House is so hot that I can hardly hold my pen. The delegates keep the windows shut so that no one outside can hear. They want to speak freely, and they have promised to keep their talk secret. I carry papers up and down the stairs all day, but I cannot tell you what is written on them.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are the windows shut?

paragraphs.text: I can tell you what the big quarrel was about, since everyone in town knows it. The large states wanted each state to have votes in Congress based on its number of people. The small states were afraid that no one would listen to them. They wanted every state to have the same number of votes. For weeks the men argued, and a few of them talked of going home.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What was the quarrel about?

paragraphs.text: Two weeks ago they found a compromise. One part of Congress, the House of Representatives, will count the people of each state. The other part, the Senate, will give every state two members. Nobody was fully happy, but both sides gave up something, and the work goes on. Your loving brother, Marcus.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What was the compromise?

paragraphs.text: Marcus is invented, but the compromise was real. The delegates were all men. No women, no Black Americans and no Native nations were in the room, so many people had no voice in these decisions. Historians study letters like this one to learn how people lived, and they also ask whose voices are missing.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Whose voices are missing?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what did the large states want?

choices.text: Votes in Congress based on the number of people in each state.
The same number of votes in Congress for every state.
choices.why: The same number of votes for every state is what the small states wanted, not the large states.

choices.text: A secret meeting held in a different city for the delegates.
choices.why: The meeting place was not part of the argument; the quarrel was about votes in Congress.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says the large states wanted votes based on each state's number of people.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 4, the delegates found a compromise. What is a compromise?

choices.text: a vote in which the larger side wins everything
choices.why: The paragraph says both sides gave up something, so the larger side did not win everything.

choices.text: an agreement in which each side gives up something
a promise that no one will ever talk about the topic
choices.why: The delegates did keep their talks secret, but a compromise is the agreement they reached.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says nobody was fully happy, but both sides gave up something to reach the agreement.

activities.prompt: Why do the delegates keep the windows shut even though the room is very hot?

choices.text: They want to talk freely without being heard outside.
They want the papers to stay cool and dry inside.
choices.why: The heat is the writer's complaint, but nothing says the papers need to stay cool.

choices.text: They want the clerks to stay close to the desks.
choices.why: Nothing in the letter says the clerks must stay near the desks; the writer moves around all day.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says the shut windows keep outsiders from hearing, since the delegates want to speak freely.

activities.prompt: Why might the author tell these events through a clerk's letter to his sister?

choices.text: A personal letter lets the author list every law that was passed.
choices.why: The letter names only one compromise, so it does not list every law.

choices.text: A personal letter lets the author argue against the delegates.
choices.why: Marcus does not argue against anyone; he reports what he saw and heard.

choices.text: A personal letter lets readers see events through one person's eyes.

activities.rationale: Marcus describes the heat, the stairs and the quarrel in his own voice, which shows how a person in the room might have seen events.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that explains how the delegates solved the quarrel.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 explains that the House would count people and the Senate would give each state two members.

activities.prompt: Explain how the compromise gave something to both large states and small states. Use details from paragraph 4.
lookFor: Says the House counts people, which helps large states
Says the Senate gives each state two members, which helps small states
Says each side gave up something
rubric: Explains what the large states received
Explains what the small states received
Connects both ideas to the word compromise
activities.frame: The large states got ___ because the House ___. The small states got ___ because the Senate ___.
activities.model: The large states got more power in the House because it counts the people of each state. The small states got an equal voice in the Senate because every state has two members. Both sides gave up something, so it was a compromise.

activities.prompt: Two groups in your class want different things for a class party. Explain a compromise that gives each group something, and say what each group gives up.
lookFor: Names the two groups and what each wants
Describes a fair compromise
Says what each group gives up
rubric: Names the two groups and what each wants
Says what each group gives up
activities.frame: One group wants ___, and the other wants ___. A compromise could be ___. Each group gives up ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Two groups in your class want different things for a class party. Explain a compromise that gives each group something, and say what each group gives up.

teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use past tense and because to retell a disagreement and its solution.

scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 1: the large states wanted votes based on population.
Question 6: the House helps large states and the Senate helps small states.

lessons.title: Too Many Buyers, Too Few Tickets: Supply and Demand
lessons.summary: Use a price table for a town festival to see how supply, demand and price work together.
lessons.genre: Informational text with a data table
lessons.subject: Social studies (economics) and math
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how price changes what people buy and what sellers offer.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how supply, demand and price are connected, using a data table.
objectives.language: Use as, so and when to explain a cause-and-effect pattern with numbers.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How does price help decide who gets what?
beforeReading.background: Think about something people really want, such as a popular toy. What happens to its price?
beforeReading.hook: A fictional town festival has only 200 tickets, and many more people want one.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn what supply and demand mean and to find the price where they match.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of something that is for sale
vocabulary.example: The supply of tickets is 200.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of something that people want to buy at a price
vocabulary.example: Demand is high when the price is low.

vocabulary.definition: not enough of something to meet what people want
vocabulary.example: A shortage means some people go without.

vocabulary.definition: more of something than people want to buy
vocabulary.example: A surplus leaves tickets unsold.

paragraphs.text: In the fictional town of Lantern Bay, a winter festival will fill the park with lights. The park can hold only 200 people, so only 200 tickets can be sold. This number is the supply, the amount that is for sale. The festival committee wants to choose a fair price.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the supply of tickets?

paragraphs.text: People do not all want a ticket at every price. Demand is the number of tickets people want to buy at a certain price. The table shows that at $4, people want 400 tickets. At $6, they want 300. At $8, they want 200. As the price goes up, fewer people want to buy.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does demand change as the price rises?

paragraphs.text: Compare demand with supply. At $4, 400 people want tickets, but only 200 tickets exist. That is a shortage of 200, so many families would be turned away. At $10, only 120 people want tickets, but 200 tickets are for sale. That is a surplus of 80 tickets that nobody buys.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happens at $4 and at $10?

paragraphs.text: At $8, the number of people who want tickets is exactly 200, the same as the supply. There is no shortage and no surplus. Economists call this the balance point. Notice that the demand fell from 400 to 200 when the price rose from $4 to $8. That is a drop of half, or 50%. The committee can use the balance point as a guide, but it may also think about what families can afford.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why is $8 the balance point?

table.description: A table with four rows. Each row gives a ticket price, how many tickets people want to buy at that price and the 200 tickets that are available.

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why is the supply of tickets only 200?

choices.text: The committee wants to raise a lot of money.
choices.why: Raising money is not mentioned; the limit comes from how many people fit in the park.

choices.text: The park can hold only 200 people.
Most people in Lantern Bay do not want tickets.
choices.why: The table shows many more people want tickets at some prices, so the limit is not about interest.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the park can hold only 200 people, so only 200 tickets can be sold.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, there is a shortage of 200 tickets. What is a shortage?

choices.text: not enough of something to meet what people want
more of something than people want to buy
choices.why: That describes a surplus, which the paragraph shows at the $10 price.

choices.text: a lower price that is set for a few days
choices.why: The paragraph is about numbers of tickets, not about lowering the price.

activities.rationale: At $4, 400 people want tickets but only 200 exist, so there are not enough for everyone who wants one.

activities.prompt: Use the table. How many tickets do people want to buy at $6?

choices.why: Two hundred is the number of tickets available, and it is also the demand at $8.
Four hundred is the number people want at $4, one price lower.

activities.rationale: The $6 row of the table shows 300 tickets people want to buy.

activities.prompt: Use the table. At $10, how many of the 200 tickets would be left over?

choices.text: 120 tickets
choices.why: One hundred twenty is the number of tickets people want, not the number left over.

choices.text: 200 tickets
choices.why: Two hundred is the whole supply, but 120 of those tickets would be sold.

choices.text: 80 tickets

activities.rationale: At $10 the supply is 200 and the demand is 120, and 200 minus 120 equals 80 tickets left over.

activities.prompt: What can the reader infer about the committee choosing a price of $4?

choices.text: The committee would have too many tickets left unsold.
choices.why: Unsold tickets appear at $10, not at $4, where demand is larger than supply.

choices.text: Many families who want tickets would not be able to get one.
The park would be less crowded than it would at $10.
choices.why: At $4 the demand is 400, so all 200 tickets would sell and the park would be full.

activities.rationale: At $4 the demand is 400 but the supply is 200, so there would be a shortage of 200 tickets.

activities.prompt: How does the writer organize paragraphs 2, 3 and 4?

lessons.title: From Idea to Law: How a Bill Moves Through Congress
lessons.summary: Follow a bill through committees, two chambers and the President's desk, and see why the path is long on purpose.
lessons.subject: Social studies (civics)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain a multi-step process and evaluate why it is designed that way.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain the steps by which a bill becomes law and the purpose of each check.
objectives.language: Use first, next, however and as a result to explain a long process.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why is it hard to make a national law?
beforeReading.background: Think about a rule in your school. Who had to agree before it began?
beforeReading.hook: Most bills never become laws, and that is not an accident.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn the steps a bill follows and why the process is slow and careful.

vocabulary.definition: a written idea for a law that members of Congress vote on
vocabulary.example: The bill was introduced in the Senate.

vocabulary.definition: a small group of members who study one subject
vocabulary.example: The education committee studied the bill.

vocabulary.definition: to pass a bill again after a veto, by a larger vote
vocabulary.example: Congress needs two-thirds to override a veto.

vocabulary.definition: done carefully and on purpose
vocabulary.example: The slow process is deliberate.

paragraphs.text: Every law that governs the United States began as an idea. The idea might come from a citizen, a group, the President or a member of Congress. However, only a member of Congress can formally introduce it. Once a member presents the idea in writing, it is called a bill.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Who can introduce a bill?

paragraphs.text: The bill first goes to a committee, a small group of members who study one subject, such as education or transportation. The committee may hold hearings, listen to experts, change the wording or vote to set the bill aside. Many bills end here. In fact, most bills never become law.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What can a committee do?

paragraphs.text: If the committee approves, the bill goes to the full chamber, either the House of Representatives or the Senate, where members debate and vote. Usually a simple majority is needed to pass. Then the bill moves to the other chamber, which repeats the steps. If the two chambers pass different versions, members from both meet to settle the differences, and each chamber must vote again on the same final text.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happens after a chamber passes a bill?

paragraphs.text: Finally, the bill reaches the President. The President can sign it, which makes it a law, or veto it, which sends it back with objections. Congress can override a veto, but that requires a two-thirds vote in both chambers. Such votes are difficult to win, so a veto is a strong check on Congress.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What can the President do with a bill?

paragraphs.text: This long path is deliberate. Each step gives people a chance to question, improve or stop a bill, which makes it harder for any single group to pass a law carelessly. The cost is that progress can be slow, and critics sometimes argue that important problems wait too long for solutions.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What are the benefit and the cost of the long path?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, who can formally introduce a bill?

choices.text: A member of Congress

choices.why: Citizens can have ideas, but the paragraph says only a member of Congress can formally introduce one.

choices.text: The President acting on their own
choices.why: The President can suggest an idea, but the paragraph says a member of Congress must present it.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says that ideas may come from many people, but only a member of Congress can formally introduce a bill.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 5, the long path is deliberate. What does deliberate mean?

choices.text: done in secret and without notice
choices.why: The steps are public, with hearings and debates, so nothing in the text suggests secrecy.

choices.text: done by accident and without a plan
choices.why: The paragraph says each step has a purpose, so the path was planned and not an accident.

choices.text: done carefully and on purpose

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 says each step gives people a chance to question or stop a bill, so the long path was planned on purpose.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the order in which a bill follows them.

choices.text: Committees write every bill that Congress will vote on.
choices.why: A member of Congress writes and introduces a bill; the committee only studies and changes it.

choices.text: Committees decide that many bills never reach a full vote.

choices.why: Making a law takes the full chambers and the President, not a committee alone.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says a committee can set a bill aside and that most bills never become law, so many stop at this step.

choices.why: Hearings are part of a committee's study; they do not show the two branches limiting each other.

choices.text: Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote.

choices.why: Settling differences happens between the two chambers of Congress, not between Congress and the President.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 describes the veto and the override, the two ways the President and Congress check each other.

lessons.title: Two Views: Should 16-Year-Olds Vote in Local Elections?
lessons.summary: Compare two arguments, each with a claim, evidence and a response to the other side, and decide how well each one is supported.
lessons.subject: Social studies (civics)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Identify a claim, evidence and a counterclaim in an argument.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Identify and compare two arguments by their claims, evidence and counterclaims.
objectives.language: Use claim, evidence, however and although to compare two sides.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can two people care about the same community and still disagree?
beforeReading.background: Think about a decision in your town or school. Who should help decide it?
beforeReading.hook: Two invented writers, Dana and Omar, give their views on a real question that some towns have faced.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find each writer's claim, evidence and answer to the other side.

vocabulary.definition: a statement that a writer wants readers to accept
vocabulary.example: Dana's claim is that 16-year-olds should vote.

vocabulary.definition: facts and reasons that support a claim
vocabulary.example: Her evidence is that teens use the buses.

vocabulary.definition: a point from the other side that a writer answers
vocabulary.example: Omar answers with a counterclaim about youth councils.

vocabulary.definition: to think about how strong or important each point is
vocabulary.example: Readers should weigh the evidence before they decide.

paragraphs.text: In most of the United States, a person must be 18 to vote. A few cities, such as Takoma Park, Maryland, let 16-year-olds vote in city elections. Should more towns do the same? Here are two arguments from invented writers, Dana and Omar.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What question do the writers answer?

paragraphs.text: Dana says yes. Her claim is that local decisions affect 16-year-olds every day. Cities decide bus routes, park hours and how safe the streets near school are. Teenagers ride the buses and use the parks, and many already have jobs and pay sales taxes. Dana also believes that voting is a habit. A person who votes for the first time at 16, while still living with family, may be more likely to keep voting for life.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is Dana's claim and evidence?

paragraphs.text: Omar says no. His claim is that 18 is a clear and fair line for adult responsibilities. At 18, a person can serve on a jury, sign a contract and live independently. He also worries that younger voters have less time to learn about candidates and might simply copy the opinions of parents or friends.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is Omar's claim and evidence?

paragraphs.text: Each writer answers the other side. Dana admits that any age line is somewhat arbitrary, but she points out that 16-year-olds already take on adult duties, such as driving and working. Omar admits that local issues matter to teenagers, but he argues that they can speak at public meetings and join youth councils without a vote.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does each writer answer the other side?

paragraphs.text: Both writers care about young people and good government. Readers must weigh the evidence. How much do local decisions change teenagers' lives, and is 18 the right moment to start voting? A strong argument does not ignore the other side; it explains why its own evidence matters more.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What should readers do with the evidence?

activities.prompt: What is Dana's main claim in paragraph 2?

choices.text: Eighteen is a clear and fair age to vote.
choices.why: That is Omar's claim in paragraph 3, not Dana's claim.

choices.text: Youth councils give teens enough of a voice.
choices.why: Youth councils are part of Omar's answer to Dana in paragraph 4, not Dana's own claim.

choices.text: Local decisions affect 16-year-olds every day.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says Dana's claim is that local decisions affect 16-year-olds every day.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 5, readers must weigh the evidence. What does weigh mean here?

choices.text: measure how heavy each piece of paper is
choices.why: The word is used about ideas, not about objects that have a weight on a scale.

choices.text: count how many writers agree with a view
choices.why: The text says there are only two writers, and the point is how strong the evidence is, not how many agree.

choices.text: think about how strong each point is

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 asks readers to decide how much local decisions change teenagers' lives, which means judging how strong the points are.

activities.prompt: Which two details does Dana use as evidence for her claim?

choices.text: At 18, a person can serve on a jury.
choices.why: Jury service at 18 is Omar's evidence that 18 is a clear line for adult duties.

choices.text: Teenagers ride the buses and use the parks.
Younger voters might copy their parents or friends.
choices.why: Copying parents or friends is Omar's worry about younger voters, not Dana's evidence.

choices.text: Many teenagers already have jobs and pay sales taxes.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives Dana's evidence: teenagers use buses and parks, and many already work and pay sales taxes.

activities.prompt: Sort each point under the writer who makes it.

items.text: Teenagers use city buses and parks

activities.rationale: Paragraphs 2 to 4 give each writer's points: Dana argues from daily effects and habit, and Omar argues from a clear line and other ways to be heard.

activities.prompt: Which statement can the reader infer about both writers?

choices.text: They both believe that the voting age should not change.
choices.why: Dana wants a lower voting age, so the two writers do not agree about the age.

choices.text: They want what they think is best for teenagers and the town.
They both think teenagers know less than adults do.
choices.why: Only Omar worries about how much teenagers know, and Dana disagrees with him.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 says both writers care about young people and good government, although they disagree about the age.

activities.prompt: Why does paragraph 4 show each writer answering the other?

choices.text: It shows that a strong argument deals with the other side's points.
It shows that the writers agree on all of the main facts.
choices.why: The writers still disagree at the end of paragraph 4, so they do not agree on every fact.

choices.text: It shows that one writer has given up on the argument.
choices.why: Neither writer gives up; each one admits a point and still keeps the original claim.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 gives each writer a counterclaim, and paragraph 5 says a strong argument explains why its own evidence matters more.

lessons.title: Reading a Census Table: Is Elm Creek Growing?
lessons.summary: Use a census table for a fictional town to compare amounts and percents and learn why a number alone can mislead.
lessons.genre: Informational text with a data table
lessons.subject: Social studies and math (population, percent)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Compare amounts and percents and explain what they show about a community.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Calculate a percent of a population and explain the difference between an amount and a rate of change.
objectives.language: Use however, while and because to compare two kinds of change.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do we need both numbers and percents to understand a change?
beforeReading.background: Think about how your school or neighborhood has changed. How could you measure the change?
beforeReading.hook: The fictional town of Elm Creek added 3,000 people twice, yet the two changes were not equal.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn how a census table shows growth and why percents tell a fuller story.

vocabulary.definition: an official count of the people who live in a place
vocabulary.example: The census shows how many people live in Elm Creek.

vocabulary.definition: the number of people who live in a place
vocabulary.example: The population of Elm Creek grew.

vocabulary.definition: a part out of 100 equal parts
vocabulary.example: Twenty percent means 20 out of every 100.

vocabulary.definition: a person who lives in a place
vocabulary.example: Every resident counts in the census.

paragraphs.text: Every ten years, the United States counts its people in a census. Local governments use these counts to plan schools, roads and services. In the fictional town of Elm Creek, a census table shows how the town has changed since the year 2000.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why does a town use a census?

paragraphs.text: The table shows steady growth. The population rose from 12,000 in 2000 to 15,000 in 2010, an increase of 3,000. It then rose from 15,000 to 18,000 in 2020, another increase of 3,000. At first glance, the two decades look equal.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did the population change?

paragraphs.text: Percent change tells a different story. The first increase of 3,000 was 25% of the 12,000 residents who lived in town in 2000, because 3,000 divided by 12,000 is 0.25. The second increase of 3,000 was only 20% of 15,000. The amount stayed the same, but the rate of growth slowed, because the same number of new people is a smaller part of a bigger town.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why are the two increases not equal?

paragraphs.text: The table also shows residents under 18. Their number grew from 3,600 to 4,500, so the schools probably needed more space. However, their share of the town shrank from 30% in 2000 to 25% in 2020, because adults grew in number more quickly than children did. Planners watch both kinds of numbers. Counts show how many classrooms or buses are needed, while percents show how the makeup of the community is changing.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do counts and percents each show?

paragraphs.text: Reading a table well takes two steps. First, find the numbers. Second, ask what they are being compared with. A number alone cannot say whether a change is large or small. A change of 3,000 people means more in a town of 12,000 than in a town of 150,000.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What are the two steps for reading a table?

table.description: A table with three rows for the years 2000, 2010 and 2020. Each row shows the town population, the increase from ten years earlier and the number of residents under 18.

activities.prompt: Use the table. What was the population of Elm Creek in 2010?

choices.why: Twelve thousand is the population in 2000, one row earlier.
Eighteen thousand is the population in 2020, one row later.

activities.rationale: The 2010 row of the table shows a population of 15,000.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 1, the census counts people. What is a census?

choices.text: a vote to choose the leaders of a town
choices.why: A vote chooses leaders, but the paragraph says the census is a count used for planning.

choices.text: an official count of the people in a place
a map that shows where roads and schools are
choices.why: A map could help a planner, but the text says the census counts the people, not places.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the United States counts its people every ten years in a census.

activities.skill: Calculate a percent from a table
activities.prompt: Use the table. What percent of Elm Creek residents were under 18 in 2010?

choices.why: Forty-two comes from copying digits of 4,200; divide 4,200 by the whole population of 15,000 instead.
Thirty-five does not match 4,200 out of 15,000; check the division carefully.

activities.rationale: In 2010, 4,200 of the 15,000 residents were under 18, and 4,200 divided by 15,000 is 0.28, or 28%.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer explain the 25% and 20% figures in paragraph 3?

choices.text: To show that the town lost people between 2010 and 2020.
choices.why: The table shows the population rising in each decade, so the town did not lose people.

choices.text: To show that an equal increase can be a different rate of growth.

lessons.title: Writing in Clay: Scribes of Mesopotamia
lessons.summary: Learn how people in Mesopotamia pressed marks into clay to keep records, and why some of their writing survives today.
lessons.subject: Social studies (ancient Mesopotamia)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do people invent writing?
beforeReading.background: Think about a list or a note you wrote this week. What did it help you remember?
beforeReading.hook: More than 5,000 years ago, people in Mesopotamia wrote with a reed on soft clay.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn how cuneiform was made, who learned it and why we can still read it.

vocabulary.definition: a person whose job was to write and keep records
vocabulary.example: A scribe wrote down how much grain the farmer sold.

vocabulary.definition: a flat piece of clay used for writing
vocabulary.example: The tablet dried in the sun.

vocabulary.definition: a sharp reed used to press marks into clay
vocabulary.example: The scribe pressed the stylus into the clay.

vocabulary.definition: a scientist who studies the past by digging up old objects
vocabulary.example: An archaeologist found a tablet in the ruins.

paragraphs.text: Mesopotamia means “the land between the rivers.” The rivers are the Tigris and the Euphrates, in what is now Iraq and nearby lands. More than 5,000 years ago, people there built some of the first cities. Farmers grew more grain than their own families needed, so the cities needed a way to keep records.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why did the cities need records?

paragraphs.text: In the south, in a land called Sumer, people wrote with a sharp reed called a stylus. They pressed it into soft, wet clay. Each press made a small wedge-shaped mark. Today this writing is called cuneiform, from a Latin word that means wedge. When the clay dried, the writing stayed.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How was cuneiform made?

paragraphs.text: At first, scribes used clay tablets to count goods, such as sacks of grain, jars of oil and sheep. Later they wrote letters, laws, prayers and stories. Learning cuneiform took years, because there were hundreds of signs. Most students were boys from families that could pay for the training.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did scribes write over time?

paragraphs.text: Clay lasts a very long time, so many thousands of tablets have survived. Archaeologists can still read them. The tablets tell us about the prices of goods, how people settled arguments, and even the practice work of students. Without them, we would know much less about life in the first cities.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why can we still learn from the tablets?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, why did the first cities need a way to keep records?

choices.text: The rivers flooded the cities during every season.
choices.why: The paragraph names two rivers, but it never says flooding was the reason for records.

choices.text: Farmers grew more grain than their families needed.
Rulers wanted to send letters to far-away lands.
choices.why: Letters are mentioned later in paragraph 3; paragraph 1 gives a different reason.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says farmers grew more grain than their own families needed, so the cities needed to keep records.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, people wrote with a stylus. What is a stylus?

choices.text: a sharp reed used to press marks into clay
a flat stone used to smooth wet clay
choices.why: The paragraph says the writing was pressed into the clay, not smoothed with a stone.

choices.text: a thin brush used to paint on tablets
choices.why: Nothing in the paragraph mentions paint; each mark was made by a press of the reed.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says people wrote with a sharp reed called a stylus and pressed it into soft, wet clay.

activities.prompt: How is paragraph 3 organized?

choices.text: It compares clay tablets with paper used in other lands.
choices.why: Paper is not mentioned in this text; the paragraph is about how clay tablets were used.

choices.text: It tells how tablets were used first and how their uses grew later.
It lists the rules that every student had to follow.
choices.why: The paragraph says students trained for years, but it does not list any rules.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 begins with At first, counting goods, and then says Later, scribes wrote letters, laws, prayers and stories.

activities.prompt: What can the reader infer about being a scribe in Sumer?

choices.text: It was a skilled job that few people were trained to do.
It was an easy job that most children learned at home.
choices.why: The text says learning took years and cost money, so it was not easy or learned by most children.

choices.text: It was a job that ended once paper was invented.
choices.why: Paper is never mentioned, so the text does not support a date when the job ended.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says learning took years because there were hundreds of signs, and most students were boys from families that could pay for the training.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How does a town decide how to spend its money?
beforeReading.background: Think about money in your family. How do people decide what to buy first?
beforeReading.hook: The fictional town of Riverton has $1,000,000 to spend this year, and everyone wants something different.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to learn what a budget is and how to find the dollars behind each percent.

vocabulary.definition: a plan for how money will be spent in one year
vocabulary.example: The town budget is $1,000,000.

vocabulary.definition: money that people pay to the government
vocabulary.example: Residents pay taxes to the town.

vocabulary.definition: work that the government does for the community
vocabulary.example: Trash pickup is a town service.

vocabulary.definition: the part of a whole that something receives
vocabulary.example: Police and fire teams get the largest share.

paragraphs.text: A town needs money to pay for services. Residents pay taxes, and the town uses that money to run police and fire teams, fix roads, pick up trash, and keep parks and libraries open. A budget is a plan for how the money will be spent in one year.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is a budget?

paragraphs.text: The leaders of Riverton, a fictional town, plan to spend $1,000,000 this year. The table shows where the money will go. Police and fire teams receive the largest share, 35%. Roads and trash pickup receive 25%. Parks and the library receive 20%, and town offices and other costs receive the last 20%.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Which service receives the largest share?

paragraphs.text: Every percent in the table is a part of the same whole. Together, the parts add up to 100%, or the whole $1,000,000. To find a part, multiply the whole by the percent. For example, 20% of $1,000,000 is $200,000.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How can you find the dollars for a percent?

paragraphs.text: Riverton holds a public meeting before leaders vote on the budget. Residents can speak. Some may ask for more money for the park, and others may ask for lower taxes. When the total is fixed, spending more in one place means spending less in another.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why is a budget about choices?

table.description: A table with four rows. Each row names a town service, the percent of the budget it receives and the dollars it receives, out of $1,000,000.

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what is a budget?

choices.text: a plan for how money will be spent in one year
a tax that every resident pays to the town each year
choices.why: A tax is money residents pay; the paragraph says a budget is a plan for spending it.

choices.text: a list of the services the town used in the past
choices.why: The paragraph looks ahead to one year of spending, not back at past services.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says a budget is a plan for how the money will be spent in one year.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, police and fire teams receive the largest share. What does share mean here?

choices.text: the act of giving a gift to a good friend
choices.why: The paragraph is about parts of one budget, not about gifts between friends.

choices.text: the part of a whole that something receives
the amount of money that a person earns
choices.why: The word describes how the town divides its money, not what any person earns.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives each service a percent of the $1,000,000, so a share is the part each one receives.

activities.prompt: Use the table. How many dollars are planned for roads and trash pickup?

choices.why: Three hundred fifty thousand dollars is the amount for police and fire teams.
Two hundred thousand dollars is the amount for parks and the library.

activities.rationale: The Roads and trash pickup row of the table shows 25%, which is $250,000.

activities.skill: Find a percent of a whole
activities.prompt: Riverton wants to add $50,000 to the library. What percent of the $1,000,000 budget is $50,000?

choices.why: Fifty percent would be $500,000, which is half of the budget.
Half of one percent would be only $5,000, much less than $50,000.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says 20% of $1,000,000 is $200,000, so 5%, which is one fourth of 20%, is $50,000.

activities.prompt: Riverton spends $50,000 more on parks and keeps the total at $1,000,000. What must happen?

choices.text: It must raise the total budget to $1,050,000.
choices.why: The question says the total stays at $1,000,000, so raising it is not allowed.

choices.text: It can spend more without changing anything.
choices.why: The total is fixed, so extra money for parks has to come from another service.

choices.text: It must spend $50,000 less somewhere else.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says that when the total is fixed, spending more in one place means spending less in another.

activities.prompt: What is the main job of paragraph 3?

choices.text: It lists the people who will vote on the town budget.
choices.why: The voting meeting is described in paragraph 4, and paragraph 3 is about calculating.

choices.text: It explains how to find a part of the budget, with an example.
It argues that the town should lower its taxes.
choices.why: No paragraph argues for lower taxes; paragraph 4 says only that some residents may ask for it.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 explains that you multiply the whole by the percent and gives 20% of $1,000,000 as an example.

activities.prompt: Explain what the table shows about Riverton's priorities. Use two percents from the table.

activities.model: The largest share, 35%, goes to police and fire teams. Compared with parks and the library, which get 20%, this shows that Riverton values safety services the most, although it still spends on other services.

lessons.title: The Grand Canal: Moving Grain Across China
lessons.summary: Learn why China's rulers joined rivers with a long canal, what it carried and what it cost the people who built it.
lessons.subject: Social studies (ancient and medieval China) and math
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain a problem, its solution and its costs and benefits.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain why the Grand Canal was built, what it did and what it cost, and use a rate to find a travel time.
objectives.language: Use because, so and however to explain benefits and costs.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do people build huge projects, and who pays the cost?
beforeReading.background: Think about a bridge, road or railroad near you. Why was it built?
beforeReading.hook: A canal about 1,800 kilometers long helped to feed a capital city far from the farms.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out why the canal was built, what it carried and what it cost people.

vocabulary.definition: a channel dug to carry boats or water
vocabulary.example: The canal joined two rivers.

vocabulary.definition: the seeds of plants such as rice and wheat
vocabulary.example: Boats carried grain north.

vocabulary.definition: a line of rulers from one family
vocabulary.example: The Sui dynasty ruled for a short time.

vocabulary.definition: to make something longer
vocabulary.example: Later rulers extended the canal to Beijing.

paragraphs.text: China's two longest rivers, the Yellow River and the Yangtze, both flow from west to east. A boat could travel along either river, but it could not go north or south from one to the other. For a country that stretches far in both directions, that was a problem.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What problem did the rivers cause?

paragraphs.text: To solve it, rulers dug canals that joined rivers and lakes. Some sections are about 2,500 years old. Around the year 600, during the Sui dynasty, workers linked many pieces into one long waterway, now called the Grand Canal. Later dynasties repaired it and extended it to reach Beijing. Today it is about 1,800 kilometers long.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How was the Grand Canal made?

paragraphs.text: The canal's main job was moving grain. The warm, wet south grew plenty of rice, while the north had a capital city and armies to feed. Boats carried rice north along the canal, along with salt, cloth and other goods. Moving goods by water cost less than carrying them by road, because one boat could hold as much as many carts.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did the canal carry, and why by water?

paragraphs.text: The canal also had a human cost. Historians say that millions of workers were called to dig it, and many were forced to work by the government. The heavy demands made people angry. The Sui dynasty lasted only about 37 years, and that anger is often named as one reason it fell.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What was the human cost?

paragraphs.text: Math helps show the size of the project. Suppose a loaded boat travels 30 kilometers each day. To cover 1,800 kilometers, it would need 1,800 divided by 30, or 60 days. Moving the same grain over land would have needed many more carts, animals and workers.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How long would the trip take?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what was the canal's main job?

choices.text: bringing water to farms in the far north
choices.why: The canal joined rivers for boats; the text does not say it watered northern farms.

choices.text: moving grain from the south to the north
keeping armies from crossing the rivers
choices.why: Armies are mentioned only as people who needed food, not as people the canal was meant to stop.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says the canal's main job was moving grain, since the south grew rice and the north needed to feed a capital and armies.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, later dynasties extended the canal. What does extended mean?

choices.text: made it longer
made it wider
choices.why: The text says it was extended to reach Beijing, which is about distance, not width.

choices.text: made it cleaner
choices.why: Nothing in the paragraph is about cleaning; the canal grew by reaching a new place.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says later dynasties extended it to reach Beijing, which means they made it longer.

activities.prompt: Another boat travels 20 kilometers each day. How many days would it need to cover 1,800 kilometers?

choices.text: 60 days
choices.why: Sixty days is the answer for 30 kilometers each day; a shorter daily distance needs more days.

choices.text: 1,780 days
choices.why: Subtracting 20 from 1,800 does not tell the days; divide the whole distance by the distance for one day.

choices.text: 90 days

activities.rationale: The passage divides the total distance by the daily distance, and 1,800 divided by 20 equals 90 days.

activities.prompt: What is the main job of paragraph 4?

choices.text: It explains how boats carried salt and cloth to the north.
choices.why: Salt and cloth are mentioned in paragraph 3, and paragraph 4 begins with the human cost.

choices.text: It describes how workers joined the rivers and lakes.
choices.why: Paragraph 2 describes how the pieces were joined; paragraph 4 is about the people who were called to work.

choices.text: It shows the cost of the project for the people who built it.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 begins with The canal also had a human cost and describes forced work and anger.

activities.prompt: Which statement is best supported by paragraphs 3 and 4 together?

choices.text: The canal was easy to build, so the government asked little of its workers.
choices.why: Paragraph 4 describes heavy demands and anger, so the work was not easy for people.

choices.text: The canal helped the government but also placed heavy demands on its people.
The canal was not useful, so later dynasties let it fall apart.
choices.why: Paragraph 2 says later dynasties repaired and extended it, so it was not left to fall apart.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 describes how the canal helped feed the capital, and paragraph 4 describes forced work and anger.

lessons.summary: Read two invented diary entries to follow a girl's arrival at Ellis Island and learn what newcomers experienced there.

objectives.content: Retell the order of events at Ellis Island and explain how a diary shows one person's experience.
objectives.language: Use first, next, then and at last to retell events in a diary.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: What is it like to arrive in a new country?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time you came to a new place. What did you see, feel and need to do?
beforeReading.hook: This diary is invented for this lesson. It is not a real diary, but Ellis Island was a real place where millions of newcomers arrived.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to follow the order of events and to notice how a diary shows feelings.

vocabulary.definition: a person who moves to a new country to live
vocabulary.example: Anya is an immigrant from Europe.

vocabulary.definition: a person whose job is to check people or things carefully
vocabulary.example: The inspector asked questions.

vocabulary.definition: a person who helps people who speak different languages understand each other
vocabulary.example: An interpreter repeated each question in Anya's language.

vocabulary.definition: a trip by ship
vocabulary.example: The passage across the ocean took twelve days.

paragraphs.text: This diary is invented for this lesson. It is not a real diary. It imagines a twelve-year-old girl named Anya, who sails to New York in March 1907 with her mother and her little brother. Her father is waiting for them in the city.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Is this diary real?

paragraphs.text: March 14. We have been on this ship for twelve days. We sleep far below the deck, where the air is warm and heavy. Today everyone ran to the rail. Through the mist I saw a huge green statue holding a torch. Mama cried, and so did many people around us.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did Anya see from the ship?

paragraphs.text: March 15. A ferry carried us to Ellis Island. We climbed a long staircase into a huge hall. Doctors watched us walk past. One doctor made a chalk mark on my brother's coat. Mama was frightened, but a second doctor looked at his eyes and said he was only tired. We were allowed to go on.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happened with the doctors?

paragraphs.text: Next, an inspector asked questions through an interpreter. What is your name? Can you work? Do you have someone waiting for you? Mama answered every question in a quiet voice. At last the inspector let us pass. Papa was standing at the gate, and my brother ran to him.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What happened at the end of the day?

paragraphs.text: Anya is invented, but Ellis Island was real. It opened in 1892 and closed in 1954. About twelve million people passed through it. Most were allowed to enter the country, although some were sent back, and some families waited a long time for an answer.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What parts of this text are real?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 3, what did one doctor do to Anya's brother's coat?

choices.text: He made a chalk mark on it.
He tore a small hole in it.
choices.why: Nothing in the paragraph says the coat was damaged; it only says it was marked.

choices.text: He wrote a name tag on it.
choices.why: A name tag is not mentioned; the mark was made with chalk and led to a second look.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says one doctor made a chalk mark on the coat, and a second doctor then looked at the boy's eyes.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 4, the inspector asked questions through an interpreter. What is an interpreter?

choices.text: a person who writes down each answer in a large record book kept by the island
choices.why: Writing answers is a different job, and the paragraph says the interpreter helped with the questions.

choices.text: a person who checks the health of newcomers and marks their coats with chalk
choices.why: Checking health was the doctors' job in paragraph 3, not the interpreter's.

choices.text: a person who helps people who speak different languages understand each other

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says the inspector asked questions through an interpreter, so the interpreter helped the inspector and Mama understand each other.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the diary in the order they happened.

items.text: The family meets Papa at the gate.

activities.rationale: Paragraphs 2 to 4 give the order: the statue on March 14, the ferry and doctors on March 15, then the inspector and Papa.

activities.prompt: Why did Mama cry when she saw the statue?

choices.text: The statue reminded her that the doctors would soon arrive.
choices.why: The diary does not connect the statue with the doctors; the doctors come on the next day.

choices.text: The statue showed that the long trip was almost over.
The statue meant that her husband had already left the city.
choices.why: Papa is waiting in New York, so the statue does not mean he had left.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says many people cried, and the family had been on the ship for twelve days, so the sight of land showed the trip was almost over.

choices.text: A diary lets readers see events and feelings through one person's eyes.
A diary lets readers learn every fact about Ellis Island in one place.
choices.why: A diary gives one person's day, so it cannot include every fact about the island.

choices.text: A diary lets readers compare Ellis Island with other ports in 1907.
choices.why: The diary does not mention other ports; paragraph 5 gives the facts about Ellis Island.

lessons.title: A Notice for a Free School, 1867 (an invented newspaper notice)
lessons.summary: Read an invented newspaper notice from Reconstruction to see how communities built schools and what the notice shows about their goals.
lessons.subject: Social studies (United States history)

objectives.content: Explain what an invented notice shows about the value people placed on education during Reconstruction.
objectives.language: Use because and for example to explain what a document shows.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: What can a short notice tell us about what people wanted?
beforeReading.background: Think about how a school in your community gets started. Who helps?
beforeReading.hook: This notice is invented for this lesson. It is not a real document, but it imitates the schools that communities really built after the Civil War.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what the notice says and what it suggests about the people who wrote it.

vocabulary.definition: the years after the Civil War when the nation worked to rebuild
vocabulary.example: Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877.

vocabulary.definition: a small group chosen to do a job
vocabulary.example: The committee planned the school.

vocabulary.definition: a change or addition to the Constitution
vocabulary.example: The 13th Amendment ended slavery.

vocabulary.definition: a short public message that tells people about something
vocabulary.example: The notice told people when the school would open.

paragraphs.text: Before the Civil War, many Southern states made it a crime to teach enslaved people to read. After the war ended in 1865, formerly enslaved people worked hard to start schools. The Freedmen's Bureau, a government agency, helped, and so did Black churches and neighbors. The notice below is invented for this lesson. It imitates the way a small-town newspaper might have announced a school.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Is the notice real?

paragraphs.text: NOTICE. A FREE SCHOOL will open on Monday, October 7, 1867, in the basement of Mount Hope Church in Spring Valley. Day classes are for children from five to fourteen years old. Night classes are for grown people who work in the fields and cannot come in daylight. Students will learn reading, writing and arithmetic. Bring a slate and pencil if you have them. If you have none, come anyway. There is no charge.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Who is the school for?

paragraphs.text: Teacher: Miss Ruth Allen. Committee: Mr. Samuel Brooks, Mrs. Hannah Freeman and Mr. Peter Lang. The committee asks neighbors for help. Families who can give a bench, a stove or firewood are asked to bring them. Those who can spare money may give it to Mr. Brooks, who will write each gift in a book that anyone may read.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the committee ask for help?

paragraphs.text: Notices like this one show how much people wanted education. This period is called Reconstruction, the years from 1865 to 1877 when the nation worked to rebuild after the war. The 13th Amendment ended slavery in 1865, and the 14th Amendment, in 1868, made all people born in the United States citizens. In 1877 Reconstruction ended. Soon many Southern states passed unfair laws that took away rights Black citizens had gained.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What was Reconstruction?

activities.prompt: According to paragraph 2, who are the night classes for?

choices.text: children from five to fourteen
choices.why: Children are the students of the day classes, which meet in daylight.

choices.text: the teacher and the committee
choices.why: The teacher and the committee organize the school; they are not the night students.

choices.text: grown people who work in the fields

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says night classes are for grown people who work in the fields and cannot come in daylight.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, the notice lists a committee. What is a committee?

choices.text: a large crowd that meets in a church
choices.why: A large crowd is not described; the notice names three people for the committee.

choices.text: a person who teaches reading and writing
choices.why: The teacher is named separately as Miss Ruth Allen; the committee is a different group.

choices.text: a small group chosen to do a job

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 names a teacher and then three people as the committee, who ask neighbors for help.

activities.prompt: Why does the notice say, “If you have none, come anyway”?

choices.text: It expected most of the students to forget to bring their pencils.
choices.why: The notice does not say students forget things; it speaks to people who do not own a slate or pencil.

choices.text: It wanted everyone to be able to learn, even without supplies.
It wanted every student to bring along a teacher from home.
choices.why: The notice names Miss Ruth Allen as the teacher, so students do not bring teachers.

activities.rationale: The sentence follows Bring a slate and pencil if you have them and the notice says there is no charge, so the goal is to include everyone.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that shows the community helped to pay for the school.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 asks for a bench, a stove, firewood and gifts of money that Mr. Brooks will record.

activities.prompt: Why does the author put paragraphs 1 and 4 before and after the notice?

choices.text: They repeat the words of the notice so that readers remember them.
choices.why: Paragraphs 1 and 4 add new information; they do not repeat the notice.

choices.text: They give background before the notice and meaning after it.
They argue that the notice should have been shorter.
