lessons.title: Two Ways to Share Power: Athens and Rome
lessons.summary: Compare how Athens and Rome governed themselves, who was included and what the United States borrowed from each.
lessons.subject: Social studies (ancient Greece and Rome)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Compare two systems and explain similarities, differences and limits.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Compare direct democracy in Athens with the republic in Rome and explain who was left out.
objectives.language: Use both, while, unlike and however to compare two systems.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Who gets to share power, and who decides?
beforeReading.background: Think about how your class makes a decision. Does everyone vote, or do some people speak for others?
beforeReading.hook: About 2,500 years ago, two cities tried new ways of sharing power, and their ideas still shape governments today.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to compare how decisions were made in Athens and Rome and to find who was left out.

vocabulary.definition: a government in which the people hold the power
vocabulary.example: Athens developed a democracy.

vocabulary.definition: a government in which citizens elect leaders to rule for them
vocabulary.example: Rome was a republic.

vocabulary.definition: a person who is chosen to speak and act for others
vocabulary.example: A representative votes for the people who elected her.

vocabulary.definition: a person who belongs to a country or city and has its rights
vocabulary.example: Only some people in Athens were citizens.

paragraphs.text: About 2,500 years ago, two cities in the Mediterranean world tried new ways of sharing power. Athens, in Greece, developed a democracy, a word from Greek that means rule by the people. Rome, in Italy, created a republic, in which citizens chose leaders to govern for them. Both ideas still shape governments today, including the government of the United States.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What two systems does the text compare?

paragraphs.text: In Athens, citizens made major decisions together. They gathered in an assembly, where any citizen could speak and vote on laws and on war. This is called direct democracy, because people vote on issues themselves instead of through representatives. Many officials were chosen by lottery, so ordinary citizens had a good chance to hold office.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did Athens make decisions?

paragraphs.text: Rome worked differently. After driving out its kings, Rome elected two consuls each year to lead the government, so that no one person could rule for long. A Senate of experienced leaders advised them. Citizens voted for officials in assemblies, but wealthy citizens had more influence in the voting. This was a representative system, since elected leaders acted for the people.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How did Rome make decisions?

paragraphs.text: Both systems left out many people. In Athens, only adult male citizens could take part. Women, enslaved people and foreigners could not vote. Rome also excluded women and enslaved people, and many people in conquered lands did not hold citizenship. For this reason, historians note that the word democracy meant something different then than it does today.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Who was left out?

paragraphs.text: The United States borrowed from both. Like Rome, it elects representatives and divides power among branches of government instead of holding a vote on every issue. Like Athens, it holds that political power comes from the citizens. Studying these cities shows that ideas about fairness change slowly, and that each generation decides again who is included.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What did the United States borrow?

rows: Citizens voted directly on laws in an assembly.
Citizens elected officials who led the government.
Many officials were chosen by lottery.
Two consuls were elected each year.
Adult male citizens, but wealthy men had more influence in voting.
Women, enslaved people and many people in conquered lands.

one ruler makes all the decisions alone

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 explains that elected leaders acted for the people, which is the meaning of a representative system.

It explains how the two systems began.
choices.why: Paragraph 1 introduces the systems; paragraph 4 describes who was left out.

choices.text: It argues that Rome was better than Athens.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 begins with Both systems left out many people and then names who was excluded in each city.

activities.prompt: Which statement does paragraph 5 best support?

choices.text: The United States copied Roman government exactly.
choices.why: The paragraph says the country borrowed, which is not the same as copying exactly, and it also mentions Athens.

choices.text: The United States rejected the ideas of ancient Greece.
choices.why: The paragraph says the United States holds that power comes from the citizens, an idea tied to Athens.

choices.text: The United States uses ideas from both Athens and Rome.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 says the United States elects representatives like Rome and holds that power comes from citizens like Athens.

activities.model: In Athens, citizens voted directly on laws in an assembly, while in Rome citizens elected officials such as consuls to lead for them. However, both cities left out women and enslaved people, so only some people shared power.

Gives a benefit of each
Gives a drawback of each

Why do historians say the word democracy meant something different in Athens?
Who is included in your community's decisions today, and who might still be missing?

Who was left out of voting in both cities?

lessons.title: Two Cousins, Two Choices, 1775 (two invented letters)
lessons.summary: Compare two invented letters from 1775, one from a Loyalist and one from a Patriot, and judge each writer's claim, evidence and response.
lessons.subject: Social studies (American Revolution)
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Identify claims, evidence and responses to the other side in two points of view.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original expanding text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Identify and compare two arguments from different points of view about the American Revolution.
objectives.language: Use claim, evidence, although and however to compare two arguments.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do people living through the same events disagree about what to do?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time when two people you know disagreed about a big decision. What did each one fear?
beforeReading.hook: Both letters are invented for this lesson. They are not real documents, but their arguments come from real debates in 1775.
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find each writer's claim and evidence and to decide how each answers the other.

vocabulary.definition: a colonist who wanted to resist British rule
vocabulary.example: A Patriot argued for liberty.

vocabulary.definition: a colonist who stayed loyal to the British king
vocabulary.example: A Loyalist feared war.

vocabulary.definition: a formal request signed and sent to leaders
vocabulary.example: The colonists sent a petition to the king.

vocabulary.definition: having someone speak and vote for you in a government
vocabulary.example: The colonists wanted representation in Parliament.

paragraphs.text: In 1775, colonists in North America disagreed about how to answer Britain's laws and taxes. Some, called Patriots, wanted to resist. Others, called Loyalists, wanted to stay loyal to the king. The two letters below are invented for this lesson, but their arguments come from real debates of the time. They were written by two made-up cousins, Caleb and Ruth Dalton.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Are the letters real?

paragraphs.text: Boston, June 1775. Dear Ruth, I cannot join you. Britain defended our towns and ports for many years, and that defense was expensive. It is fair that colonists help to pay for it. I also fear that war will bring ruin. Our trade would stop, our homes might burn and we would face the strongest navy in the world. We should send petitions and wait for the king to listen. Your cousin, Caleb.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is Caleb's claim and evidence?

paragraphs.text: Cambridge, June 1775. Dear Caleb, I understand your fear, but I cannot agree. The question is not whether we pay taxes. It is who decides. Parliament taxes us, yet no one in it speaks for us. We have sent petitions for years, and our complaints have not been answered. You say war will cost us everything, but obeying without a voice may cost us our liberty. In April, blood was already spilled at Lexington and Concord. Your cousin, Ruth.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is Ruth's claim, and how does she answer Caleb?

paragraphs.text: Notice how each writer uses a claim, evidence and an answer to the other side. Caleb's claim is that loyalty and patience are wiser. His evidence is the cost of past defense and the danger of war. Ruth's claim is that the real issue is representation. She answers Caleb's fear by saying that liberty is worth the risk. Neither writer was foolish, and each spoke from hopes and fears that were real. After the war, many Loyalists left the new nation, and families like the Daltons were divided.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the author say about the two writers?

activities.prompt: According to Caleb's letter, why is it fair for colonists to help pay for Britain's costs?

choices.text: Parliament has promised the colonists a vote in the future.
choices.why: Caleb never mentions a promise of a vote; Ruth is the one who raises the lack of representation.

choices.text: Britain defended the colonies for many years at great cost.
The king has answered every petition that colonists sent.
choices.why: Ruth says the petitions were not answered, and Caleb only suggests waiting for the king to listen.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 says Britain defended the towns and ports for many years and that the defense was expensive, so colonists should help pay.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, Caleb says colonists should send petitions. What is a petition?

choices.text: a formal request that is sent to leaders
a tax that is collected by a ruler
choices.why: A tax is the reason for the quarrel, but a petition is something colonists send to ask for change.

choices.text: a law that is passed by the colonists
choices.why: Colonists send petitions to the king; they do not pass them as laws.

activities.rationale: Caleb says to send petitions and wait for the king to listen, so a petition is a request sent to a leader.

activities.prompt: Sort each point under the writer who makes it.

items.text: War would stop trade and burn homes
The colonists should wait for the king to listen
No one in Parliament speaks for the colonists
Petitions have not been answered
Obeying without a voice may cost liberty
Britain paid to defend the colonies

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives Caleb's points about cost, risk and patience, and paragraph 3 gives Ruth's points about representation and liberty.

activities.prompt: Which statement can the reader infer about the two cousins?

choices.text: They disagree about what to do, but each writes honestly about a fear.
They agree about the problem, but they choose different words.
choices.why: They disagree about the problem itself, since Caleb accepts the taxes and Ruth questions who decides.

choices.text: They have stopped writing to each other after their quarrel.
choices.why: Ruth answers Caleb's letter in a friendly tone, so nothing shows that they stopped writing.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says each writer spoke from real hopes and fears, and Ruth begins her answer with I understand your fear.

activities.prompt: Why does the author write two letters instead of one?

choices.text: Two letters make the story of the war longer and more exciting.
choices.why: The letters are about a disagreement, and paragraph 4 says neither writer was foolish.

choices.text: Two letters prove that the Patriots were correct all along.
choices.why: Paragraph 4 gives each writer respectful treatment, so the author does not say one side was correct all along.

choices.text: Two voices let readers compare both sides of a real debate.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 explains that each writer uses a claim, evidence and an answer, so the two letters let readers compare both sides.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph in which a writer directly answers the other writer's fear.
activities.rationale: In paragraph 3, Ruth says that war may cost a lot but that obeying without a voice may cost liberty.

activities.prompt: Which writer gives the stronger reason? Use one piece of evidence from that writer and one point from the other writer.
lookFor: States clearly which writer is stronger
Uses accurate evidence from that writer's letter
Mentions a point from the other writer and responds to it
rubric: Supports it with evidence from the letters
Responds to the other writer's point
activities.frame: I think ___ gives the stronger reason because ___. Although ___ says ___, I think ___.
activities.model: I think Ruth gives the stronger reason because she says that no one in Parliament speaks for the colonists, so the problem is who decides. Although Caleb says Britain paid to defend the colonies, I think paying does not give a government the right to decide without a vote.

activities.prompt: Two students disagree about whether the school should add a longer lunch. Write two short sentences, one for each side, that each include a claim and one reason.
lookFor: States a claim for each side
Gives a reason for each side
Keeps each point fair and respectful
rubric: States a claim for each side
Gives a reason for each side
Keeps each point fair and respectful
activities.frame: One student believes ___ because ___. The other believes ___ because ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Two students disagree about whether the school should add a longer lunch. Write two short sentences, one for each side, that each include a claim and one reason.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Identify and compare two arguments from different points of view about the American Revolution.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use claim, evidence, although and however to compare two arguments.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Make a two-column chart with Caleb and Ruth. Fill in claim, evidence and response with phrases from the letters, then discuss which row is the most persuasive.
discussion: Which piece of evidence do you find most convincing, and why?
Why do you think the author wrote that neither writer was foolish?
How can a family stay close when its members disagree about a big decision?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think one side was always right because of what happened later. The text shows each writer reasoning from real hopes and fears in 1775.

scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 3: Caleb's points are the first three, and Ruth's are the last three.
Question 6: paragraph 3 shows Ruth responding directly to Caleb's fear of war.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: I think Ruth is stronger because she names the question of who decides. Although Caleb says Britain paid for defense, paying does not give the right to decide without a vote.

How does Ruth answer Caleb's fear of war?

lessons.title: Saturday at the Market: Two Voices
lessons.summary: Two siblings tell the same market trip, and a ten-dollar budget forces them to make a plan together.
lessons.subject: English language arts and math
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how two narrators show different feelings about the same events.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how two narrators give different views of the same events in a story.
objectives.language: Use first, then and finally to retell events, and use feeling words for each narrator.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How does the person telling a story change what we notice?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time you planned how to spend a small amount of money.
beforeReading.hook: Ana sees a total that is too big. Leo sees strawberries that smell like candy. Who is right?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how Ana and Leo see the same trip and how they solve the money problem.

vocabulary.definition: a unit of weight
vocabulary.example: The peaches cost two dollars a pound.

vocabulary.definition: the amount you get when you add everything together
vocabulary.example: The total was eleven dollars.

vocabulary.definition: to bend down and rest on your knees
vocabulary.example: Ana knelt beside her brother.

vocabulary.definition: the person who tells a story
vocabulary.example: Ana and Leo are both narrators.

paragraphs.text: Ana: Mom gave us ten dollars for the market. I held the money tightly in my pocket. I wanted peaches, which cost two dollars a pound, because I planned to bake a pie with three pounds. Leo kept tugging my sleeve. He is eight, and he treats every stand like a parade.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Ana want to buy, and why?

paragraphs.text: Leo: Ana was so serious! I found a basket of strawberries that smelled like candy. The sign said five dollars. “Can we buy them?” I asked. Ana stared at her fingers as if they were hiding a secret.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Leo notice?

paragraphs.text: Ana: I did the math in my head. Three pounds of peaches cost six dollars. One basket of strawberries costs five. The total was eleven dollars, and we only had ten. My cheeks felt warm. I did not want to tell Leo no.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What problem does Ana find?

paragraphs.text: Leo: I did not understand the numbers. I only knew Ana had gone quiet. Then she knelt down beside me. “What if we buy two pounds of peaches instead?” she asked. That would cost four dollars, and four plus five is nine. We would even have one dollar left!
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does Ana change the plan?

paragraphs.text: Ana: The pie would be a little smaller, but nobody would mind. Leo carried the strawberries home like treasure. At the door, I gave Mom the extra dollar, and she hugged us both.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the trip end?

activities.prompt: How much money did Mom give Ana and Leo?

choices.text: Ten dollars
Eleven dollars
choices.why: Eleven dollars is what the peaches and the strawberries would have cost together, not what Mom gave them.

choices.text: Nine dollars
choices.why: Nine dollars is what they spent in the end, after Ana changed the peach order.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says Mom gave them ten dollars for the market.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 4, Leo says Ana “knelt down beside me.” What does knelt mean?

choices.text: jumped up and moved away from him
choices.why: Jumping up and moving away would put Ana farther from Leo, but the sentence says she was beside him.

choices.text: bent down with her knees on the ground
stepped back and looked at the sign
choices.why: Stepping back would also leave space between them, and the text says she came down next to him.

activities.rationale: Ana comes down to Leo's level to talk to him, so knelt means she bent down with her knees on the ground.

activities.prompt: Why does the story switch between Ana and Leo as narrators?

choices.text: It lets readers see one trip through two different sets of feelings.
It teaches readers how to bake a peach pie for a family dinner.
choices.why: The pie is only part of Ana's plan; the story is about the trip and the money, not a recipe.

choices.text: It proves that the two narrators always agree about everything.
choices.why: Ana and Leo see the market differently, so the story does not show that they always agree.

activities.rationale: Ana thinks about prices and the total, while Leo notices the smell of strawberries and Ana's quiet face, so each voice shows a different feeling about the same moment.

activities.prompt: Ana buys two pounds of peaches and Leo gets one basket of strawberries. What is the total cost?

choices.text: Eleven dollars
choices.why: Eleven dollars is the cost of three pounds of peaches plus the basket, which Ana decided not to buy.

choices.text: Four dollars
choices.why: Four dollars is only the cost of the two pounds of peaches, and the strawberries cost extra.

choices.text: Nine dollars

activities.rationale: Two pounds of peaches cost 2 × 2 = 4 dollars, and 4 + 5 = 9 dollars, as paragraph 4 says.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen in the story.

items.text: Ana gives Mom the extra dollar.
Leo finds strawberries that cost five dollars.
Ana finds that the total is eleven dollars.
Ana suggests buying only two pounds of peaches.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 shows Leo finding the strawberries, paragraph 3 shows Ana finding the total, paragraph 4 shows her suggestion, and paragraph 5 ends with the extra dollar.

activities.prompt: What does Ana's question “What if we buy two pounds of peaches instead?” show about her?

choices.text: She has decided that Leo should not be allowed to choose.
choices.why: Ana's change keeps Leo's strawberries in the plan, so she is not refusing his choice.

choices.text: She is willing to give up part of her plan to include Leo.
She wants to spend all of the money on the strawberries.
choices.why: Ana still buys two pounds of peaches, so the money is not all spent on strawberries.

activities.rationale: Ana gives up one pound of peaches so that the strawberries fit in the budget, which shows she cares about Leo's wish.

activities.prompt: Why does the author use two narrators in this story? Use one detail from Ana's voice and one detail from Leo's voice.
lookFor: Says that two narrators show two points of view
Uses a detail from Ana's paragraphs, such as counting the total
Uses a detail from Leo's paragraphs, such as the strawberries or Ana going quiet
rubric: Explains why two voices help the reader
Uses one detail for each narrator
activities.frame: The author uses two narrators so that ___. Ana ___, while Leo ___.
activities.model: The author uses two narrators so that readers can see how one trip feels different to each person. Ana counts the total and worries about the money, while Leo notices the strawberries and Ana's quiet face.

activities.prompt: Write two short sentences about the same event, one from a person who is worried and one from a person who is excited. Use feeling words in each sentence.
lookFor: Describes the same event in both sentences
Uses a feeling word for the worried person and for the excited person
Shows a different thing that each person notices
rubric: Describes the same event in both sentences
Uses a feeling word for the worried person and for the excited person
Shows a different thing that each person notices
activities.frame: The worried person thinks ___. The excited person notices ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Write two short sentences about the same event, one from a person who is worried and one from a person who is excited. Use feeling words in each sentence.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Explain how two narrators give different views of the same events in a story.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use first, then and finally to retell events, and use feeling words for each narrator.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Read paragraph 1 aloud as Ana and paragraph 2 as Leo. Ask students to name one thing each narrator notices, then compare the two lists on the board.
discussion: What does Ana notice that Leo does not?
How would the story change if only Leo told it?
How does Ana solve the money problem without saying no to Leo?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think both narrators know the same things; point out that Leo says he did not understand the numbers.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 4: two pounds of peaches cost 4 dollars, and 4 + 5 = 9.
Question 3: each narrator notices different details, which shows a different point of view.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The author uses two narrators so that readers can see how one trip feels different to each person. Ana counts the total, while Leo notices the strawberries.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.en: Read one paragraph at a time and ask your student to say who is talking. Then ask how the same market trip feels different to Ana and to Leo. You can talk in any language, then ask for one sentence in English.
directions.es: Lean un párrafo a la vez y pida a su estudiante que diga quién está hablando. Luego pregunte cómo se siente el mismo viaje al mercado para Ana y para Leo. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What does Ana worry about?
What does Leo notice that Ana does not?
familySupport.noEnglishRequired: Family discussion can happen in any language; the student can practice explaining one idea in English afterward.

connections.write: Retell a shared experience from two different points of view.
connections.speak: Tell the market trip aloud first as Ana and then as Leo.
connections.listen: Listen to two people describe one event and compare what each notices.

lessons.title: Night Bus Home (a poem)
lessons.summary: A short original poem that uses similes, metaphors and a living bus to show how it feels to ride home at night.
lessons.subject: English language arts
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how comparisons help a poem show a feeling.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 4 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Identify similes and metaphors and explain how they build a mood and a theme.
objectives.language: Use the words like, is and shows to explain a comparison.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can comparisons make an ordinary ride feel special?
beforeReading.background: Think about riding home in a car or on a bus when it is dark outside.
beforeReading.hook: The poet says the bus sighs. How can a bus do that?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what the speaker sees on the bus and how the poet makes it feel calm.

vocabulary.definition: to let out a long, soft breath
vocabulary.example: The old bus seemed to sigh.

vocabulary.definition: to move with a deep, low sound
vocabulary.example: Trucks rumble down the street.

vocabulary.definition: a person you do not know
vocabulary.example: A stranger smiled at me.

vocabulary.definition: a thin rope or string
vocabulary.example: She pulled the cord to stop the bus.

paragraphs.text: The night bus sighs at the corner stop, a tired animal with glowing eyes. Its doors fold open like two big hands, and I step in from the cold. The seats are warm. The windows hum.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the bus like?

paragraphs.text: We rumble past the closed shops like a drum rolling down the street. Every window is a small gold screen: a stranger's kitchen, a cat on a sill, a blue television glowing in the dark.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the speaker see outside?

paragraphs.text: A woman holds a sleeping baby. A man reads, his lips moving with each word. Nobody talks, yet we all drift together down one slow river of light, carried toward our own front doors.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Who is on the bus?

paragraphs.text: My stop is next. I pull the cord. Ding! The bus sighs again, and I step out into the night. Home is a lamp in the window, and the whole dark city is a road that leads to it.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the poem end?

activities.prompt: Who is sleeping on the bus in stanza 3?

choices.text: a man holding a book
choices.why: The man is reading, so he is awake, and his lips move with each word.

choices.text: a baby held by a woman
a cat sitting on a sill
choices.why: The cat is one of the pictures seen through a window outside the bus, not a rider.

activities.rationale: Stanza 3 says a woman holds a sleeping baby.

activities.prompt: In stanza 2, the bus and its riders “rumble past the closed shops.” What does rumble mean?

choices.text: move with a deep, low sound
move without making any noise
choices.why: The poet compares the bus to a drum, so the bus makes a sound and is not silent.

choices.text: move with a sharp, high ringing
choices.why: A drum gives a deep sound, so a sharp, high ringing does not match the comparison.

activities.rationale: The poet says the bus is like a drum rolling down the street, which suggests a deep, low sound.

activities.prompt: In stanza 1, the poet says the night bus “sighs.” What does this show?

choices.text: The bus is broken and cannot start again.
choices.why: The poem says the bus rolls on and stops at corners, so it is not broken down.

choices.text: The driver is speaking to the riders aloud.
choices.why: A sigh belongs to the bus in the poem; no driver speaks to the riders at all.

choices.text: The bus seems tired, like a living thing.

activities.rationale: Giving the bus a sigh and calling it a tired animal makes it seem alive, which is personification.

activities.prompt: Sort each line from the poem by the kind of comparison it uses.

items.text: Every window is a small gold screen.
Home is a lamp in the window.
The whole dark city is a road that leads to home.
Its doors fold open like two big hands.
We rumble past the closed shops like a drum rolling down the street.

activities.rationale: A simile uses the word like, as in the doors and the drum. A metaphor says one thing is another, as in the windows, the lamp and the road.

activities.prompt: How does the poem move from stanza 1 to stanza 4?

choices.text: From a bright morning to a dark afternoon at school
choices.why: The poem happens at night from beginning to end, so it never shows a bright morning.

choices.text: From getting on the bus to getting ready to get off
From the speaker's home to a far-away city by train
choices.why: The speaker rides a bus and ends near home; no train or far-away city appears.

activities.rationale: Stanza 1 shows the speaker stepping in from the cold, and stanza 4 shows the speaker pulling the cord for the stop.

activities.prompt: What does the poet suggest about home?

choices.text: Home feels like a warm light that waits at the end of a trip.
Home is a faraway place that nobody can ever really find.
choices.why: The speaker is traveling toward home and calls it a lamp, so it is not hard to find.

choices.text: Home is a place we should leave behind when the night comes.
choices.why: The speaker is carried toward front doors and feels warm, so home is not something to leave behind.

activities.rationale: Stanza 4 says home is a lamp in the window and that the whole city is a road leading to it.

activities.prompt: How does the poet make the bus ride feel calm and warm? Use two details from the poem.
lookFor: Says the ride feels calm, warm or peaceful
Uses a detail such as the warm seats, the gold windows or the river of light
Explains how each detail creates the feeling
rubric: Connects each detail to the feeling
activities.frame: The ride feels ___ because the poet says ___ and ___.
activities.model: The ride feels calm and warm because the poet says the seats are warm and the riders drift down one slow river of light. These details make the bus feel like a safe place.

activities.prompt: Write one simile and one metaphor about a place you know at night, such as your street or your kitchen. Then circle the word that makes the simile.
lookFor: Writes a simile with like or as
Writes a metaphor that says one thing is another
Uses a sense detail such as light, sound or warmth
rubric: Writes a simile with like or as
Writes a metaphor that says one thing is another
Uses a sense detail such as light, sound or warmth
activities.frame: The ___ is like ___. The ___ is a ___.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Identify similes and metaphors and explain how they build a mood and a theme.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use the words like, is and shows to explain a comparison.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Read the poem aloud once with the lights lowered. Ask students to draw the picture from stanza 2, then discuss why the poet calls each window a screen.
discussion: Which comparison made the best picture in your mind?
What feeling do the words warm, hum and drift share?
What is the difference between a simile and a metaphor?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think a metaphor must use like or as; remind them that only a simile does, and a metaphor says one thing is another.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.

answerNotes: Question 4: the two lines with like are similes; the three lines that say something is something else are metaphors.
Question 6: the poem ends with home as a lamp in the window.

lessons.title: Safety Notice: Before, During and After a Science Lab
lessons.summary: Read a school safety notice, follow its steps in order and explain the reason behind its rules.
lessons.subject: English language arts and science
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain the order of steps and the reasons for safety rules.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Follow a set of safety instructions and explain how the notice is organized.
objectives.language: Use before, during and after to describe the order of steps.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why do instructions need to be clear and in the right order?
beforeReading.background: Think about a rule at school that keeps people safe.
beforeReading.hook: Some lab rules sound small, but each one protects somebody. Can you tell who?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what students must do before, during and after a science lab.

vocabulary.definition: to keep someone safe from harm
vocabulary.example: Goggles protect your eyes.

vocabulary.definition: tight glasses that cover your eyes
vocabulary.example: Put on your goggles before the lab.

vocabulary.definition: liquid that falls out of a container by accident
vocabulary.example: Tell your teacher about a spill.

vocabulary.definition: to hold or use something
vocabulary.example: Handle each tool with care.

paragraphs.text: Notice to all students: Please read this before your first science lab. Safety rules protect you, your classmates, and your teacher. Follow every rule, every time.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: Why do the rules exist?

paragraphs.text: Before the lab begins, put on your goggles. Tie back long hair. Tuck in loose sleeves, and keep your bag under the table so nobody trips over it.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do you do before the lab?

paragraphs.text: During the lab, handle each tool with care. Never taste anything. If you want to smell a chemical, do not put your nose near the cup. Instead, wave the smell toward you with your hand.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do you do during the lab?

paragraphs.text: If something spills, stop and tell your teacher right away. Do not wipe it up yourself. If glass breaks, do not touch the pieces. Your teacher will clean them up with the right tools.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do you do if there is an accident?

paragraphs.text: When the lab is over, wait until your teacher says you may clean up. Put the materials back on the tray. Wash your hands with soap and water, and scrub the backs of your hands and between your fingers. If you are ever unsure what to do, ask.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do you do after the lab?

activities.prompt: What should you do before the lab begins?

choices.text: Put on your goggles.
Taste the materials.
choices.why: The notice says to never taste anything, so this is a rule against tasting.

choices.text: Clean up the tray.
choices.why: Cleaning up comes at the end, after the teacher says that you may.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 begins with the first rule: before the lab begins, put on your goggles.

activities.prompt: Paragraph 3 says to “handle each tool with care.” What does handle mean?

choices.text: throw away in the bin
choices.why: The notice says to put materials back on the tray, so tools are kept and not thrown away.

choices.text: count out loud
choices.why: The sentence is about how to treat tools, and nothing in it is about counting.

choices.text: hold and use

activities.rationale: The notice tells students to treat each tool with care while they use it, so handle means to hold and use.

activities.prompt: Put these safety steps in the order the notice gives them.

items.text: Handle each tool with care.
Wait for your teacher to say you may clean up.
Wash your hands with soap and water.
Put on your goggles.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 gives the goggles step, paragraph 3 gives the tools step, and paragraph 5 gives the cleanup and hand-washing steps in that order.

activities.prompt: How is the notice organized?

choices.text: By tool: goggles, cups, trays and soap
choices.why: The notice does not go tool by tool; it groups rules by when each rule happens.

choices.text: By time: before, during and after the lab
By person: students first, then the teacher
choices.why: The notice speaks to students the whole time, and the teacher appears only as someone to tell.

activities.rationale: Paragraphs 2, 3 and 5 begin with Before the lab begins, During the lab, and When the lab is over.

activities.prompt: Select the paragraph that tells what to do if glass breaks.
activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says that if glass breaks, students should not touch the pieces because the teacher will clean them up.

activities.prompt: Why does the notice tell students not to wipe up a spill themselves?

choices.text: Wiping up a spill is the teacher's favorite part of every lab.
choices.why: The notice treats a spill as a safety matter, not as a job that one person enjoys.

choices.text: The spill may be unsafe to touch, so the teacher should check it.
Spills are always harmless, so nobody needs to fix them at all.
choices.why: The notice says to tell the teacher right away, so it does not treat spills as harmless.

activities.rationale: The spill rule sits among the safety rules and asks students to tell the teacher, which suggests the liquid might not be safe to touch.

activities.prompt: A student's cup tips over and water spreads across the table. Explain what the student should do and why. Use one detail from the notice.
lookFor: Says to stop and tell the teacher
Says not to wipe it up alone
Gives a reason such as keeping people safe
rubric: Gives a reason in a complete sentence
activities.frame: The student should ___ because ___. The notice says ___.
activities.model: The student should stop and tell the teacher right away because a spill could be unsafe. The notice says not to wipe it up yourself, so the teacher decides how to clean it.

activities.prompt: Write three safety steps for a place you know, such as a kitchen or a bike path. Put them in order and use the words before, during or after.
lookFor: Writes three steps that start with a command verb
Puts the steps in a logical order
Uses at least one time word
rubric: Writes three steps that start with a command verb
Puts the steps in a logical order
Uses at least one time word
activities.frame: Before ___, ___. During ___, ___. After ___, ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Write three safety steps for a place you know, such as a kitchen or a bike path. Put them in order and use the words before, during or after.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Follow a set of safety instructions and explain how the notice is organized.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use before, during and after to describe the order of steps.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Read the notice aloud and ask students to underline the first word of each rule. Point out that most rules begin with a command verb and a time word.
discussion: Which rule protects the person doing the lab, and which protects others?
Why is the order of the steps important?
What rule would you add to this notice?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think rules in a notice can be done in any order; ask what would go wrong if cleanup began before the lab ended.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 3: goggles, tools, wait for the teacher, and then wash hands.
Question 4: the notice is organized by time: before, during and after.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The student should stop and tell the teacher right away because a spill could be unsafe. The notice says not to wipe it up yourself.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.es: Lean el aviso juntos, un párrafo a la vez. Pida a su estudiante que diga cada paso en orden con las palabras antes, durante y después. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What do students do before the lab?
What should a student do after a spill?
familySupport.noEnglishRequired: Family discussion can happen in any language; the student can practice explaining one idea in English afterward.

connections.speak: Explain the steps of the notice aloud in order.
connections.listen: Listen to instructions and put the steps in order.

lessons.title: Shade for the Playground Benches
lessons.summary: A student gives two reasons for adding shade and answers a worry about cost.
lessons.subject: English language arts
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Identify a claim, two reasons and an answer to a worry.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original starting support text with 4 short sections and 7 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Identify the claim, reasons and response to a worry in a short opinion piece.
objectives.language: Use my first reason is and however to organize an opinion.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: What makes a reason strong?
beforeReading.background: Think about where students sit or rest during recess at your school.
beforeReading.hook: Four benches stand in the sun. Who wants to sit on a hot bench?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find the writer's claim, the two reasons and the answer to a worry.

vocabulary.definition: a cool place where the sun's light is blocked
vocabulary.example: Trees make shade on a hot day.

vocabulary.definition: a fact or idea that explains why
vocabulary.example: My first reason is comfort.

vocabulary.definition: feeling as if the room is spinning
vocabulary.example: Heat can make a person feel dizzy.

vocabulary.definition: costing a lot of money
vocabulary.example: A young tree is not expensive.

paragraphs.text: Our playground has four benches but no shade. I think our school should plant two shade trees or build a cloth roof over the benches. This is a small change that would help many students.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the writer want?

paragraphs.text: My first reason is comfort. On sunny days, the metal benches get so hot that nobody can sit on them. Students who want to rest or read must stand in the sun instead.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the first reason?

paragraphs.text: My second reason is health. Shade helps students stay cool and protects their skin. A student who is too hot can feel tired and dizzy, and then it is hard to learn.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the second reason?

paragraphs.text: Some people say trees and roofs cost too much. However, a young tree is not expensive, and parent volunteers might help plant it. A little shade today will help our school for many years.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the writer answer the worry?

activities.prompt: What does the writer want the school to add?

choices.text: A new set of metal benches
choices.why: The benches already exist, and the writer says the problem is that they are too hot.

choices.text: A longer lunch period outdoors
choices.why: The writer never asks for more time outside; the request is about shade.

choices.text: Shade over the playground benches

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the school should plant shade trees or build a cloth roof over the benches.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 3, a student who is too hot can feel “dizzy.” What does dizzy mean?

choices.text: feeling very hungry and thirsty
choices.why: The paragraph connects dizziness to being too hot and tired, not to being hungry.

choices.text: feeling excited and ready to play
choices.why: The paragraph says the student is tired, so feeling excited does not fit.

choices.text: feeling as if the room is spinning

activities.rationale: The writer says heat can make a student feel tired and dizzy, which describes feeling unsteady.

activities.prompt: Sort each detail by the job it does in the opinion piece.

items.text: The metal benches get too hot to sit on.
Shade protects students' skin.
Trees and roofs cost too much.
A young tree is not expensive.
Parent volunteers might help plant it.

activities.rationale: Paragraphs 2 and 3 give the reasons, and paragraph 4 states the worry about cost and then answers it with two details.

activities.prompt: How does the writer connect shade to learning?

choices.text: Too much heat can make students tired, and tired students find learning hard.
Shade makes the playground look nicer, so students enjoy math more.
choices.why: The writer talks about heat and tiredness, not about how the playground looks.

choices.text: Trees can teach students how plants grow during a science class.
choices.why: The writer never mentions science lessons about plants; the link is about feeling hot.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 says a student who is too hot can feel tired and dizzy, and then it is hard to learn.

activities.prompt: Why does the writer call the plan “a small change”?

choices.text: To show that the writer is not sure about it
choices.why: The writer gives two strong reasons and sounds sure, so the phrase is not about doubt.

choices.text: To make the plan sound easy and reasonable
To warn readers that it will not help much
choices.why: The next sentence says the change would help many students, so it is not described as useless.

activities.rationale: Calling the plan small makes it seem simple to accept, and the same sentence says it would help many students.

activities.prompt: Do you think the writer gives good reasons for adding shade? Use one reason from the text.
lookFor: States a clear opinion
Uses one accurate reason such as hot benches or skin protection
Explains why the reason matters
rubric: Connects the evidence to the position
activities.frame: I think the reasons are ___ because ___. The writer says ___.
activities.model: I think the reasons are good because they are about real problems. The writer says the metal benches get so hot that nobody can sit on them, so students cannot rest during recess.

activities.prompt: Choose one small change you would like at your school. Write your claim, give two reasons, and answer one worry with however.
lookFor: States a claim
Gives two different reasons
Answers one worry with however
activities.frame: I think our school should ___. My first reason is ___. My second reason is ___. However, ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Choose one small change you would like at your school. Write your claim, give two reasons, and answer one worry with however.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Identify the claim, reasons and response to a worry in a short opinion piece.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use my first reason is and however to organize an opinion.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Color-code the piece: claim in blue, reasons in green, worry in orange, answer in purple. Ask students which paragraph is easiest to find and why.
discussion: Which of the two reasons is stronger?
Why does the writer name the worry instead of leaving it out?
What other evidence would make the argument stronger?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think any detail in the text is a reason; ask whether the detail explains why the change is a good idea.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 3: reasons are in paragraphs 2 and 3, and the worry and answer are in paragraph 4.
Question 4: the link is that heat makes students tired and learning harder.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: I think the reasons are good because they are about real problems. The metal benches get so hot that nobody can sit on them.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.en: Read one paragraph at a time. Ask your student what the writer wants and which reason is the strongest. You can talk in any language, then ask for one sentence in English.
directions.es: Lean un párrafo a la vez. Pregunte a su estudiante qué quiere el autor y cuál es la razón más fuerte. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What does the writer want to add?
How does the writer answer the worry?
familySupport.noEnglishRequired: Family discussion can happen in any language; the student can practice explaining one idea in English afterward.

connections.speak: Tell a partner your claim and two reasons aloud.
connections.listen: Listen to an opinion and name the reason.

lessons.title: The Drum That Would Not Sound (a folktale)
lessons.summary: In this original tale, a village drum teaches a strong young drummer that listening comes before playing.
lessons.subject: English language arts
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain the theme of a tale using details from the story.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Identify the theme and turning point of a folktale and support them with details.
objectives.language: Use the words because and shows that to connect a detail to a theme.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: What can listening teach that strength cannot?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time you learned more by listening than by talking.
beforeReading.hook: The strongest drummer in the village strikes the great drum, and nothing happens. Why?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out why the drum is silent for Joro and what changes when Nuru tries.

vocabulary.definition: a person who takes care of something
vocabulary.example: Tavi was the keeper of the drum.

vocabulary.definition: great strength
vocabulary.example: He struck the drum with all his might.

vocabulary.definition: a pattern of sounds that repeats
vocabulary.example: Nuru tapped the rhythm of the river.

vocabulary.definition: a group that makes decisions for a community
vocabulary.example: The council chose a new drummer.

vocabulary.definition: to tell someone about danger before it comes
vocabulary.example: The drum warned the village of storms.

paragraphs.text: Long ago, a great drum hung in the middle of a valley village. When it sounded, everyone came from the fields, because the drum called people to the harvest and warned them of storms. For many years the old keeper, Tavi, played it. When his hands grew stiff, the council chose Joro, the strongest young man in the village, to take his place.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the drum do for the village?

paragraphs.text: Joro lifted the heavy sticks and struck the drum with all his might. The drum answered with a dull thud, like a stone dropped in mud. He struck harder, and then harder still. His arms shook and his face turned red, but the drum would not sing. The villagers whispered and shook their heads.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What goes wrong for Joro?

paragraphs.text: Nuru, a girl who swept the square each morning, watched from the well. “Perhaps the drum has not been asked,” she said softly. She pressed her ear to its cool skin and listened. She heard wind moving through the valley, the slow river, and the far-off cry of geese. Then she tapped the drum gently, in the rhythm of the river.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Nuru do differently?

paragraphs.text: The drum woke. Its deep voice rolled over the roofs and fields, round and warm as a loaf of bread. Joro stood with his sticks hanging in his hands. “I thought the drum wanted strength,” he said. Old Tavi smiled. “The drum wants a listener,” he said. “Strength is only what we have. Listening is what we give.”
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Tavi say the drum wants?

paragraphs.text: That autumn, Joro learned to listen first, and Nuru became his helper. One evening the geese flew low and the wind turned cold. Nuru heard the change, and together they beat the warning rhythm. The villagers brought in the grain and tied down the boats before the storm arrived. The drum has never been silent since.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does listening help the village?

activities.prompt: Why did the council choose Joro to play the drum?

choices.text: He had played the drum with Tavi for many years.
choices.why: The text says Tavi played the drum for many years, and it never says Joro had played before.

choices.text: He knew the rhythm of the river better than anyone.
choices.why: Nuru, not Joro, is the one who listens for the rhythm of the river.

choices.text: He was the strongest young man in the village.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the council chose Joro because he was the strongest young man in the village.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 2, Joro strikes the drum “with all his might.” What does might mean?

choices.text: careful patience
choices.why: The sentence says he struck harder and harder, which is about force, not about being careful.

choices.text: great strength
good luck
choices.why: Nothing in the sentence says luck helped him; it shows how hard he hit the drum.

activities.rationale: Joro uses all of his strength on the drum, and his arms shake, so might means great strength.

activities.prompt: The narrator says the drum's sound was “like a stone dropped in mud.” What does this comparison show?

choices.text: The sound was heavy and dead, with no ring to it.
The sound was bright and clear, like falling rain.
choices.why: A stone in mud lands with a dull, soft thud, so the comparison is not about a bright sound.

choices.text: The sound was so loud that it hurt the villagers' ears.
choices.why: The villagers whisper and shake their heads; the text never says that the noise hurt them.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 2 calls the sound a dull thud, and a stone dropped in mud makes a sound that is heavy and dead.

activities.prompt: What does Nuru understand that Joro does not understand at first?

choices.text: The drum is too heavy for one person to move.
choices.why: The text says Joro lifted the sticks and struck the drum; weight is never the problem.

choices.text: The drum must be listened to before it is played.
The drum only works when many people play together.
choices.why: Nuru plays the drum alone and it answers, so it does not need many players.

activities.rationale: Nuru listens to the wind, the river and the geese before she taps the drum, and then the drum answers.

activities.prompt: Which event is the turning point of the story?

choices.text: Nuru listens to the drum and taps a gentle rhythm.
Joro strikes the drum harder and harder.
choices.why: Joro's harder strikes show the problem getting worse, so they do not change the story's direction.

choices.text: The villagers tie down the boats before the storm.
choices.why: Tying down the boats comes after the change and shows its good results.

activities.rationale: In paragraph 3 Nuru listens and taps softly, and in paragraph 4 the drum finally sounds, so this is where the story turns.

activities.prompt: Which two details show that listening helps the village?

choices.text: Nuru hears the geese flying low and the wind turning cold.
Joro lifts the heavy sticks and strikes the drum.
choices.why: Joro's striking shows force, not listening, and the drum stays silent when he does it.

choices.text: The villagers bring in the grain before the storm arrives.
Tavi's hands grow stiff with age.
choices.why: Tavi's stiff hands explain why a new drummer is needed, not why listening helps.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 5 shows Nuru hearing the change in the geese and wind, and the villagers saving the grain and boats because of the warning.

activities.prompt: What lesson does the story teach? Use one detail from the story to explain it.
lookFor: States a lesson such as listening matters more than strength
Uses a detail such as Joro's silent drum or Nuru's gentle tapping
Connects the detail to the lesson
rubric: Explains how the detail shows the theme
activities.frame: The story teaches that ___. For example, ___. This shows ___.
activities.model: The story teaches that listening can matter more than strength. For example, Joro hits the drum with all his might and it stays silent, but Nuru listens first and it answers her. This shows that careful attention can work better than force.

activities.prompt: Think of a time when listening first helped you solve a problem. Write what happened and what you learned.
lookFor: Describes the problem
Describes how listening first changed what happened
States what was learned
rubric: Describes how listening first changed what happened
activities.frame: At first ___. Then I listened to ___. I learned that ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: Think of a time when listening first helped you solve a problem. Write what happened and what you learned.

teacherGuide.contentObjective: Identify the theme and turning point of a folktale and support them with details.
teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use the words because and shows that to connect a detail to a theme.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Draw a plot mountain and place the story on it: the drum is silent, Joro tries harder, Nuru listens, the drum sounds, the storm warning. Ask where the story turns.
discussion: Why does the author give Nuru a small job like sweeping the square?
What does Tavi mean by 'Listening is what we give'?
How is the drum like a person who must be asked before it answers?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may say the theme is only that Nuru is smart; point them to Tavi's words about strength and listening.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 5: the turning point is when Nuru listens and taps softly in paragraph 3.
Question 6: the two details are Nuru hearing the geese and wind and the villagers saving the grain.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The story teaches that listening can matter more than strength. Joro's hardest strikes could not wake the drum, but Nuru's gentle listening made it sing.
teacherGuide.sourceNote: Original reading lesson and questions authored for EduWonderLab; not official WIDA test material.

directions.en: Read one paragraph at a time. Ask your student why the drum is silent for Joro and what Nuru does differently. You can talk in any language, then ask for one sentence in English.
directions.es: Lean un párrafo a la vez. Pregunte a su estudiante por qué el tambor no suena para Joro y qué hace Nuru de otra manera. Pueden conversar en cualquier idioma y luego pedir una oración en inglés.

questions: What does Nuru do before she taps the drum?
What does Tavi say the drum wants?

lessons.title: The Fence Problem
lessons.summary: A garden story in which Priya tests rectangles with the same fence length to find which shape holds the most.
lessons.subject: English language arts and math
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how a character uses evidence to change a belief.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how a character tests an idea with numbers and how the story shows the result.
objectives.language: Use first, next and then to retell a series of tests, and use because to give a reason.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: Why is it better to test a hunch than to trust it?
beforeReading.background: Think about a time you were sure of something and then tested it.
beforeReading.hook: Twenty-four meters of fence can make many gardens. Which one holds the most tomatoes?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out what Priya tests and what she learns about the shape of the bed.

vocabulary.definition: the distance around a shape
vocabulary.example: The fence covers the perimeter of the bed.

vocabulary.definition: the amount of flat space inside a shape
vocabulary.example: The area of the bed is 36 square meters.

vocabulary.definition: a guess based on a feeling
vocabulary.example: Marcus had a hunch that long beds hold more.

vocabulary.definition: evidence that shows an idea is true
vocabulary.example: Priya wanted proof before she agreed.

paragraphs.text: On Saturday morning, Priya and her neighbor Mr. Okoye stood in an empty corner of the community garden with a roll of fencing. The roll was exactly 24 meters long, so the perimeter of the bed would be 24 meters. “We must use all of it,” said Mr. Okoye, “and the bed has to be a rectangle.” Priya's job was to choose its shape, because she loved puzzles.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What is the problem?

paragraphs.text: Marcus, who had come to carry buckets, had a confident idea. “Make it long and skinny,” he said. “Then it stretches farther, so it must hold more tomatoes.” It sounded sensible, but Priya wanted proof. She took out her graph paper and a pencil. “Let's test it,” she said.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Marcus think, and what does Priya do?

paragraphs.text: Priya started with Marcus's shape. A bed 10 meters long and 2 meters wide uses 10 + 2 + 10 + 2 = 24 meters of fence. Its area is 10 × 2 = 20 square meters. Next she tried 8 meters by 4 meters. That also uses 24 meters of fence, and its area is 32 square meters. “It grew!” said Marcus. “Keep going.”
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What do the first two tests show?

paragraphs.text: A bed 7 meters by 5 meters gave 35 square meters. Then Priya drew a square, 6 meters on each side. The fence was still 24 meters, but the area was 36 square meters, the biggest yet. She studied her list. As the two sides came closer in length, the area kept growing. “So with this much fence, a square holds the most,” she said.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does Priya notice?

paragraphs.text: Marcus scratched his head, then laughed. “I was sure long and skinny would win,” he said. “I guess you can't trust a hunch without testing it.” Mr. Okoye unrolled the fence around the square, and the three of them tied it to the posts. By noon, the first tomato seedlings were in the ground.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does Marcus change?

activities.prompt: How long is the roll of fencing?

choices.text: 36 meters
choices.why: Thirty-six is the area of the biggest bed, measured in square meters, not the length of the fence.

choices.text: 24 meters
12 meters
choices.why: Twelve is half of the fence length; it is the sum of one length and one width.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 1 says the roll was exactly 24 meters long.

activities.prompt: In paragraph 5, Marcus says you cannot trust a “hunch” without testing it. What is a hunch?

choices.text: a guess based on a feeling
a plan written on paper
choices.why: Marcus has not written anything down; his hunch is an idea he feels is true.

choices.text: a measurement from a tape
choices.why: A measurement would come from using a tape, but Marcus only says what he feels will happen.

activities.rationale: Marcus was sure long and skinny would win before any test, so a hunch is a guess based on a feeling.

activities.prompt: Another bed is 9 meters long and 3 meters wide. It uses all 24 meters of fence. What is its area?

choices.text: 12 square meters
choices.why: Twelve is 9 + 3, the sum of one length and one width, and not the area.

choices.text: 27 square meters
24 square meters
choices.why: Twenty-four is the amount of fence around the bed, not the space inside it.

activities.rationale: Area is length times width, so 9 × 3 = 27 square meters, as in the way Priya found 10 × 2 = 20.

activities.prompt: Put the shapes in the order that Priya tested them.

items.text: A bed 8 meters by 4 meters
A bed 7 meters by 5 meters
A square 6 meters by 6 meters
A bed 10 meters by 2 meters

activities.rationale: Paragraph 3 gives 10 by 2 and then 8 by 4, and paragraph 4 gives 7 by 5 and then the 6 by 6 square.

activities.prompt: What do Priya's results suggest about rectangles that use the same amount of fence?

choices.text: The longer one side is, the larger the area becomes.
choices.why: The areas grew from 20 to 36 as the sides came closer, so a longer side did not bring a bigger area.

choices.text: The area stays the same no matter what shape is used.
choices.why: The areas were 20, 32, 35 and 36 square meters, so they did not stay the same.

choices.text: The closer the sides are in length, the larger the area.

activities.rationale: Paragraph 4 says that as the two sides came closer in length, the area kept growing.

activities.prompt: Why does the author let Marcus laugh and say “you can't trust a hunch without testing it”?

choices.text: To show that he did not care about the garden
choices.why: Marcus stays to help tie the fence, so he clearly cares about the garden.

choices.text: To show that Priya was wrong about the shapes
choices.why: The tests showed that Priya's idea was right; Marcus is the one who changed his mind.

choices.text: To show that his thinking changed after he saw the proof

activities.rationale: Marcus says he was sure about long and skinny and then admits a hunch needs testing, which shows his thinking changed.

activities.prompt: Explain how Priya shows that a long, skinny bed does not hold the most. Use two numbers from the story.
lookFor: Says that the long, skinny bed has a smaller area
Uses two numbers such as 20 and 36 square meters
Explains that the same fence can make beds with different areas
rubric: Connects the numbers to the claim
activities.frame: Priya shows that ___. The long bed has an area of ___, but the square has an area of ___.
activities.model: Priya shows that long and skinny does not hold the most. The 10 by 2 bed has an area of 20 square meters, but the 6 by 6 square has an area of 36 square meters, even though both use 24 meters of fence.

activities.prompt: A friend has 20 meters of fence and a hunch that a 9 by 1 rectangle holds the most. Explain how to test the hunch and name one other shape to try.
lookFor: Says to find the area of each shape by multiplying length and width
Names another shape that uses 20 meters, such as 5 by 5 or 6 by 4
Compares the areas to decide
rubric: Says to find the area of each shape by multiplying length and width
Names another shape that uses 20 meters, such as 5 by 5 or 6 by 4
activities.frame: I would find the area of ___ by multiplying ___ by ___. Then I would compare it with ___.

lessons.transferPrompt: A friend has 20 meters of fence and a hunch that a 9 by 1 rectangle holds the most. Explain how to test the hunch and name one other shape to try.

Question 5: the areas 20, 32, 35 and 36 show that closer sides give a bigger area.

lessons.title: Words in My Pocket (a poem)
lessons.summary: An original poem about carrying words from home, planting new ones, and letting both languages grow.
lessons.subject: English language arts
lessons.alignmentStatus: Local instructional focus for the grades 6-8 cluster; Language Expectation mapping needs educator review.
lessons.languageFunction: Explain how images and metaphors build the theme of a poem.
lessons.taskComplexity: Original growing text with 5 short sections and 8 connected tasks; no numeric reading level is asserted.

objectives.content: Explain how a poet uses images and metaphors to show a change over time and a theme.
objectives.language: Use the words stands for and shows that to explain an image.

beforeReading.essentialQuestion: How can images show what it feels like to learn a new language?
beforeReading.background: Think about a word from your home language that you would like to share.
beforeReading.hook: The speaker says new words are seeds. What would it mean to plant a word?
beforeReading.purpose: Read to find out how the speaker's words change from stones in a pocket to a garden.

vocabulary.definition: a group of lines in a poem
vocabulary.example: This poem has five stanzas.

vocabulary.definition: to open into flowers
vocabulary.example: The flowers bloom in spring.

vocabulary.definition: twisted together in a mix
vocabulary.example: The vines grew tangled and bright.

vocabulary.definition: to speak in a very soft voice
vocabulary.example: She whispered one word in class.

paragraphs.text: When I came here, I carried my words like stones in my pocket, smooth and heavy, each one warm from my hand. They were the only things I had brought from home, and I held them tight.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the speaker carry?

paragraphs.text: At school the new words flew past me like birds I could not name. I opened my mouth, and a small, shaky sound came out. Someone smiled. The sound was not a failure; it was a seed.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What are the new words like?

paragraphs.text: I planted it each day: one word at breakfast, one word on the bus, one word whispered at the back of the class. The seeds were small. I watered them with questions and I waited.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the speaker plant the seeds?

paragraphs.text: Now my garden has two kinds of flowers. Some bloom in the language of my grandmother's kitchen, and some bloom in the language of the hallway. They grow side by side, tangled and bright.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: What does the garden hold now?

paragraphs.text: My pocket is no longer heavy. It is full of seeds and stones, and I know that the more I carry, the more I can say. Nothing was lost on the way. Everything was planted.
paragraphs.guidingQuestion: How does the speaker feel at the end?

activities.prompt: According to stanza 1, where did the speaker's first words come from?

choices.text: From the speaker's old home
From the noisy school hallway
choices.why: The hallway is where the speaker later hears new words, not where the first ones came from.

choices.text: From the friendly bus driver
choices.why: The bus is where the speaker whispers new words later, in stanza 3.

activities.rationale: Stanza 1 says the words were the only things the speaker had brought from home.

activities.prompt: In stanza 4, the two kinds of flowers grow “tangled and bright.” What does tangled mean?

choices.text: spread far apart from each other
choices.why: The flowers grow side by side, so they are close together and not spread far apart.

choices.text: twisted together in a mix
cut into small separate pieces
choices.why: The two languages are described as growing together, not as being cut apart.

activities.rationale: The poem says the flowers grow side by side, so tangled means twisted together in a mix.

activities.prompt: In stanza 2, the new words are like “birds I could not name.” What does this comparison show?

choices.text: The words seemed to move past the speaker and were hard to catch.
The words were soft and pretty like feathers and sang to the speaker.
choices.why: The speaker could not name the birds, so they are strange and hard to catch, not just pretty.

choices.text: The words were dangerous and made the speaker want to run away.
choices.why: The speaker feels shaky but then plants a seed, so the poem does not call the words dangerous.

activities.rationale: Birds that fly past and cannot be named show words that are moving too fast to hold, which is how the new language first feels.

activities.prompt: How do the main images change from stanza 1 to stanza 4?

choices.text: From a busy hallway to a quiet bus
choices.why: The hallway and the bus are places in the poem; the images that change are stones and plants.

choices.text: From a bright garden to a dark pocket
choices.why: The poem moves toward a bright garden and not away from it.

choices.text: From heavy stones to a growing garden

activities.rationale: Stanza 1 begins with stones in a pocket, and stanza 4 ends with a garden of flowers.

activities.prompt: What does “Nothing was lost on the way. Everything was planted.” suggest?

choices.text: The speaker has forgotten the language of home completely.
choices.why: Stanza 4 says flowers still bloom in the language of the grandmother's kitchen, so home words were not forgotten.

choices.text: The speaker plans to stop learning words in the hallway.
choices.why: Stanza 5 says the more the speaker carries, the more can be said, so learning goes on.

choices.text: The words from home still matter and grow beside the new ones.

activities.rationale: The stones from home and the new seeds are both in the pocket and in the garden, so nothing was lost.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentences to show how the images change in the poem.

segments.text: At first the speaker holds words tightly like
in a pocket. Later the new words are planted like
and grow into a

activities.rationale: Stanza 1 compares the words to stones, stanzas 2 and 3 call the new words seeds, and stanza 4 shows a garden.

activities.prompt: What is the theme of the poem? Use two images from the poem to explain it.
lookFor: States a theme such as both languages can live and grow together
Uses two images such as stones, seeds or the garden
Explains how the images show the theme
rubric: Connects each image to the theme
activities.frame: The theme is that ___. The poet shows this with ___ and ___.
activities.model: The theme is that a person can keep the words from home and learn new ones too. The poet shows this with stones that stand for home words and seeds that grow into a garden with two kinds of flowers.

activities.prompt: Write a metaphor that compares learning something new to growing something. Explain what the two things have in common.
lookFor: Writes a metaphor that says one thing is another
Names what the two things have in common
Uses a sense detail or an image
rubric: Writes a metaphor that says one thing is another
Names what the two things have in common
Uses a sense detail or an image

teacherGuide.languageObjective: Use the words stands for and shows that to explain an image.
teacherGuide.miniLesson: Draw a stone and a seed on the board. Ask students what each stands for in the poem, then ask where each image appears again at the end.
discussion: Why might the poet choose stones for the first words and seeds for the new words?
What does the garden with two kinds of flowers say about two languages?
How does the speaker feel in stanza 2 compared with stanza 5?
teacherGuide.misconception: Students may think the poem says home words are replaced by new words; point to stanzas 4 and 5, where both grow together.

scaffolds.modeled: Think aloud to find one detail that answers a question, then say which words proved it.
scaffolds.guided: Use the response frame and mark the evidence paragraph before answering.
scaffolds.independent: Answer without the frame and explain which choice you rejected and why.

answerNotes: Question 4: the images move from stones to a garden.
Question 5: both the stones and the seeds are in the pocket at the end.
teacherGuide.modelResponse: The theme is that a person can keep the words from home and learn new ones too. The stones stand for home words, and the seeds grow into a garden.
